items.title: The everyday ecology of children’s emotional experience
items.abstract: Emotional experiences are fundamental inputs to human development, yet we know surprisingly little about their distribution in everyday life. Research typically characterizes children’s emotional environments using global reports or brief observations, obscuring the real-time contexts in which emotions arise. Here, we used artificial intelligence to automatically transcribe and annotate daylong audio recordings from three samples totaling N=159 families with children aged 5 months-8 years old (48.43% female). Our findings reveal the architecture of children’s everyday emotional environments: positive speech was concentrated during play and music, and 25% of speech segments conveyed frustration, concentrated during routine caregiving. Mothers’ mental health did not predict affective speech, but lower child effortful control predicted more frustration in our toddler sample. Frustration peaked in early toddlerhood, suggesting that children’s growing independence at this age may reorganize family emotional environments. Overall, emotional speech appears to emerge from everyday activity, with meaningful shifts across development.

items.title: Structural Scarcity and the Bioethics of Priority Setting: A Structural Moral Ecology Framework
items.abstract: Abstract Background Healthcare priority setting under structural scarcity involves more than distributing limited resources. Institutional arrangements also shape who can access care, remain within treatment pathways, and benefit from available interventions. This paper develops Structural Moral Ecology (SME) as a normative framework for evaluating these conditions and their implications for distributive justice. Methods The paper employs conceptual and normative analysis, bringing Ecological Adverse Selection Theory into conversation with African relational ethics, ecostructural approaches to health ethics, and established theories of distributive and procedural justice. It distinguishes structural scarcity, understood as enduring conditions constraining the provision and use of care, from structural sorting, the mechanisms through which institutional arrangements distribute opportunities and burdens. The framework is applied to a constructed radiotherapy prioritisation case. Results The analysis establishes a distinction between justifying an immediate allocation decision and justifying the institutional conditions under which that decision becomes necessary. Although established allocation frameworks can address structural injustice, their application to particular decisions may leave institutional responsibilities insufficiently examined. Structural disadvantage may warrant accommodation, monitoring, escalation, or institutional remedy without automatically justifying a change in immediate allocation priority. The framework identifies three distinct normative judgements: duty attribution, duty specification, and duty prioritisation. It also develops an institutional capacity obligation connecting defensible decisions under existing constraints with continuing responsibility for fairer allocation conditions. Conclusions Structural Moral Ecology extends ethical assessment beyond the immediate distribution of scarce resources to the institutional responsibilities that persist after an allocation decision. By connecting allocation justice with continuing institutional accountability, it offers a framework for evaluating both the defensibility of present decisions and the conditions shaping access to care over time. items.title: Climatic Suitability and Invasion Risk of the Elm Zigzag Sawfly in North America.
items.abstract: The elm zigzag sawfly, Aproceros leucopoda (Hymenoptera), native to eastern Asia, is among the most concerning potential pests for elm trees (Ulmus spp.); elms form an important component in many North Temperate forests. This sawfly species invaded Europe in 2003 and spread rapidly across much of that continent. In 2020, it was recorded in North America, and it has since become established in several parts of the eastern United States and Canada. Sawfly infestations can cause severe elm tree defoliation, branch die-back that weakens tree health, and potentially tree mortality. Sawfly invasions have the potential to further exacerbate elm decline, especially in conjunction with other pressures, including Dutch elm disease (Ophiostoma ulmi). We used rigorous approaches from distributional ecology to explore climatic suitability for A. leucopoda across North America, considering various sources of uncertainty in the data. We found that, without control, the elm zigzag sawfly could establish populations across eastern Canada and much of the central-eastern and northeastern United States, as well as in the Pacific Northwest. More southern areas of North America were not climatically suitable for this species. Predicted suitable areas for the sawfly overlap broadly with elm distributions, highlighting the need to control this invasion to mitigate potential economic and environmental impacts.

items.title: A Narrowly Tuned Olfactory Receptor in the Sunda Pangolin Identifies 1-Octen-3-One as a Key Chemical Cue in Foraging Behavior.
items.abstract: The Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica) is considered a critically endangered species, partly due to its highly specialized diet, which consists mostly of ants and termites. Field observations have shown that pangolins rely on olfaction to locate ant and termite nests even from distances of several kilometers. However, the specific chemical signal used to locate food in the field remains unknown. Based on transcriptome sequencing, 1033 olfactory receptors (MjavORs) of M. javanica were identified and analyzed. Four MjavORs (OR118, OR171, OR215, and OR276) were functionally characterized using the Xenopus laevis oocyte system co-expressing CFTR, RTP1, and Gαolf. Notably, MjavOR215 showed a robust response to 1-octen-3-one, a compound released from termite nests. An odorant-binding protein, MjavOBP3, also demonstrated the highest binding affinity for 1-octen-3-one. Behavioral tracking assays confirmed that pangolins are significantly attracted to 1-octen-3-one, a volatile emitted from termite nests (p < 0.05), rather than to volatiles from termites themselves. These results clarify the molecular mechanisms underlying pangolin foraging, demonstrating that volatile from termite nests guide this behavior.

items.title: The Joint Impact of Deleterious Mutations, Dominance, and Gene Flow on Linked Neutral Variation in Structured Populations.
items.abstract: Most species are geographically structured, which leaves characteristic signatures in neutral genomic regions used to reconstruct demographic history. Yet, these signatures can be distorted by linked selection due to deleterious mutations. This can reduce genetic diversity through Background Selection, or increase diversity through Associative Overdominance. While their effects are well characterized in panmictic populations, they remain largely unexplored in structured populations. We investigated an Isolation-with-Migration model using simulations across a range of migration, selection, dominance, and recombination parameters. We quantified the effects of deleterious mutations on standard summary statistics by simulating either genotypes at neutral and deleterious mutations (genotype-based approach) or genealogies and deleterious mutations (Ancestral Recombination Graph-based approach). The latter recovered similar patterns, directly relating genomic patterns to underlying coalescent processes. For lower recombination rates, we found a Background Selection-driven regime for weakly codominant mutations, characterized by lower diversity and increased genetic differentiation. For recessive mutations, we identified an Associative Overdominance-driven regime, characterized by increased diversity and lower genetic differentiation. This is reflected in the genealogies: Background Selection shrunk coalescence times and led to lineage sorting topologies, while Associative Overdominance stretched coalescence times and led to incomplete lineage-sorting topologies. Migration strongly affected genetic differentiation and topology frequencies but had weaker effects on diversity and coalescence times. Our results provide evidence of a transition from Associative Overdominance to Background Selection for recessive deleterious mutations in an isolation-with-migration model. Importantly, these processes leave distinct signatures on genealogies, highlighting that Ancestral Recombination Graph-based approaches have the potential for inferring linked-selection in structured populations.

items.title: A Model-Specialist Predator Attacks a Batesian Ant Mimic as Readily as Its Model.
items.abstract: Batesian mimicry can protect palatable species when predators avoid their defended models, but resemblance to a model can also impose costs when predators actively target the model. We tested this potential cost using the ant-mimicking jumping spider Myrmaplata plataleoides (O. Pickard-Cambridge, 1869) and its model, the Asian weaver ant Oecophylla smaragdina (Fabricius, 1775), together with the aggressive ant-mimicking crab spider Amyciaea lineatipes O. Pickard-Cambridge, 1901, which routinely attacks O. smaragdina. We tested whether A. lineatipes differentially attacked the Batesian mimics and its model, and whether its responses differed when these prey were paired with less similar alternatives. In simultaneous-choice assays with living prey, A. lineatipes showed no differential attack probability between M. plataleoides and O. smaragdina. In contrast, A. lineatipes strongly preferred O. smaragdina over the non-ant-like salticid Thiania bhamoensis Thorell, 1887, M. plataleoides over the non-model ant Camponotus sp., and O. smaragdina over Camponotus sp. These controls show that the absence of a difference between M. plataleoides and O. smaragdina was not simply due to indiscriminate prey choice. We therefore interpret our main results as showing that the predator did not express differential attack preference between the Batesian mimic and its model under our experimental conditions; this could reflect limited discrimination or equivalent acceptance of both prey types. The findings indicate that model-specialist predation can impose a potential cost on Batesian ant mimicry, highlighting the importance of considering predator specialization when evaluating the fitness consequences of mimicry.

items.title: Seasonal Population Dynamics and Habitat Use of Dromiciops gliroides (Microbiotheriidae), an Endemic Marsupial of the Temperate Rainforest of Southern South America.
items.abstract: Dromiciops gliroides is an arboreal marsupial endemic to the temperate rainforests of South America, where it functions as a key seed disperser for several native plant species. To evaluate the ecological drivers shaping its activity patterns, we integrated demographic, spatial, and environmental data collected over three consecutive annual cycles in a forest stand of southern Chile. Population abundance, survival, and movement were estimated using capture-recapture analyses across five trapping grids (255 traps). We used Boosted Regression Trees to quantify the influence of microhabitat structure and climatic conditions on species detectability. Our results revealed pronounced seasonal dynamics: captures and recaptures peaked between late spring and early summer, and males were caught more frequently and moved farther than females during the reproductive season, a pattern compatible with a polygynous mating system but also with sex-specific detectability. Detection probability increased in areas characterized by a tall bamboo understory and the presence of key tree species (Eucryphia cordifolia, Lomatia dentata, and Nothofagus dombeyi), and captures were largely confined to periods when minimum temperatures exceeded ∼10°C, although seasonal timing and minimum temperature were weakly associated in our dataset. This study provides one of the first multi-year ecological datasets available for D. gliroides and provides new insights into its spatial ecology, seasonal dynamics, and habitat associations. Because these results derive from a single, structurally intact forest remnant, they should be read as a local demographic baseline rather than as range-wide values. Still, our findings highlight the importance of long-term monitoring to understand and conserve this ecologically pivotal and evolutionarily singular marsupial.

items.title: Resource Rich but Risky Patches: Primary Productivity Triggers Intraguild Predation of Insects by Livestock in Oak Savannas.
items.abstract: Theoretical models on intraguild predation (predation among organisms within the same trophic level, intraguild predation) assume a spatially heterogeneous primary productivity. Hence, resource-rich patches could attract both predators and prey, yet prey may suffer higher predation rates. This theoretical framework can be extended to antagonistic, size‑asymmetric interactions among herbivores in which negative effects arise not only from predation but also from other non‑trophic mechanisms. We analyzed antagonistic interactions driven by primary productivity among oak-defoliating Lepidoptera and livestock in Iberian oak savannas. Caterpillars defoliate oak canopies, but exclusion experiments have shown that free-range livestock predate/trample soil-pupating Lepidoptera. We used fine-scale multispectral imagery to assess the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) of oak canopies and surrounding pasture. Then, we tracked the visits of GPS-collared sheep in each tree of the study site, where we sampled oak-defoliating Lepidoptera caterpillars. NDVI of canopies and pasture were spatially correlated, and sheep grazed more often at more productive patches. Negative top-down effects (increased predation/trampling) outweighed positive bottom-up ones (increased food availability) in soil-pupating Lepidoptera, whose abundance was lower in productive pastures due to higher sheep activity. In contrast, species pupating in leaves/branches were more abundant in those trees, benefiting from increased productivity while avoiding predation, as their pupae were inaccessible to sheep. Irrespective of the underlying mechanisms (direct predation and/or trampling), our results show that assessments of antagonistic interactions between large herbivores and insects must incorporate landscape‑level variation in productivity and the movement abilities of both guilds.

items.title: An Attention Bias for Threat and a Safety-First Strategy: Trait Anxiety Selectively Facilitates Aversive Over Reward-Based Learning in Zebrafish (Danio rerio).
items.abstract: Trait anxiety reflects stable inter-individual differences in anxiety-like behavior and modulates an animal's assessment of risk-benefit trade-offs, thereby influencing its decisions in ecologically relevant contexts. Such decisions are often shaped by learning from both aversive and rewarding experiences. However, evidence on how anxiety affects these two types of learning remains inconsistent, suggesting that the effect may be task specific. Moreover, a direct comparison under a unified paradigm is lacking. Using zebrafish (Danio rerio) to address this gap, we screened for high- and low-anxiety individuals, characterized their food-shelter preference, personality traits, and baseline cortisol levels, then compared their cognitive performance across aversive (predator cue) and reward-based (social interaction) associative learning tasks. Our results demonstrate a clear task-specific effect: high-anxiety individuals performed better in aversive learning, but performed comparably to low-anxiety individuals in reward-based learning. Baseline cortisol levels did not differ between high- and low-anxiety individuals. The aversive-learning advantage in high-anxiety fish was partly explained by their personality, yet anxiety itself contributed unique variance, suggesting that the effect involves an interplay of personality co-variation, safety-first strategy, and sustained threat-related attentional bias. These findings suggest that a high-anxiety phenotype may confer greater survival fitness in high-risk environments. From a cognitive ecology perspective, this study provides insights into the potential evolutionary adaptive value of trait anxiety.

items.title: Contrasting selective regimes at seasonal-timing loci across the introduced range of the European corn borer.
items.abstract: Seasonal environments are ubiquitous and require organisms to synchronize life-history events with the appropriate season. For populations expanding into new geographic regions, successful establishment may require phenological shifts that align life-history events with local seasonal conditions, but it is unclear how selection contributes to this adjustment. We addressed this question by using pooled whole-genome sequencing to analyze introduced populations of the European corn borer moth, Ostrinia nubilalis, sampled across a latitudinal transect in the Midwestern United States, together with a laboratory population selected for extended diapause. Genome-wide differentiation among field populations was low, with no fixed differences or evidence of isolation by distance, consistent with weak population structure across the introduced range. Against this background, the seasonal-timing loci period (per) and Pigment dispersing factor receptor (Pdfr) showed contrasting patterns. Pdfr exhibited strongly reduced nucleotide diversity, a marked excess of rare variants, and low differentiation from the selected laboratory population, supporting recent directional selection across the transect. In contrast, per retained greater variation and showed a spatially oscillating allele frequency pattern consistent with geographically varying selection. Genome-wide scans identified additional candidates with diverse functions, including temporal regulation and metabolism. The core clock genes per and Clock were also implicated in clinal analyses of seasonal timing in the closely related Asian corn borer, suggesting that seasonal environmental gradients may repeatedly favor variation in shared components of the seasonal-timing network. Our findings indicate that spatially-uniform and spatially-varying selection can jointly shape seasonal adaptation across a weakly structured landscape.

items.title: Phage-Host Dynamics in Food Systems: Rethinking the "Lytic" and "Temperate" Paradigm.
items.abstract: Phage-host dynamics are central to food systems because bacteriophages can threaten microbial stability while serving as tools for microbial control. In fermentations, phages compromise starter culture performance and product consistency, whereas in foods, animal production, and processing environments they are increasingly used as biocontrol agents against foodborne pathogens. Temperate phages may also influence virulence, tolerance, competition, and horizontal gene transfer, including antimicrobial resistance gene mobilization, placing phage ecology within a One Health framework. These roles have traditionally been interpreted through a binary model in which virulent phages lyse and temperate phages persist. However, reports of pseudolysogeny, carrier state, and delayed lysis have long suggested that this distinction is incomplete. Recent large-scale studies showing that virulent phages can persist through colony purification and bacterial genome assembly workflows provide the central motivation for this review. These findings suggest that long-term non-lysogenic association may be more widespread than appreciated and challenge the assumption that "lytic" phages necessarily cause immediate host elimination. In food systems, this has implications for fermentation reliability, biocontrol, surveillance, and One Health interpretation. We argue that food systems are informative settings for reassessing phage lifestyle categories, and that "lytic" should be understood as infection potential rather than guaranteed ecological outcome.

items.title: Negotiating Young Children's Diets in Peri-Urban Peru: Caregiver Perspectives on Food Environments and Complementary Feeding.
items.abstract: Caregivers play a central role in shaping young children's diets during the complementary feeding period, yet there is limited understanding of how everyday food choices are negotiated within rapidly changing peri-urban environments in low- and middle-income countries. This qualitative study explored the drivers of food choices for children aged 6-23 months in peri-urban Peru. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with caregivers ( n = 18), home observations ( n = 10), and pile-sorting exercises, and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Findings reveal that caregivers' decisions emerge from dynamic interactions across three domains: the external food environment, including availability, pricing, and exposure to marketing and information; the household environment, encompassing affordability, accessibility, convenience, and culturally embedded practices; and the personal domain, including caregiver knowledge, skills, concerns, and children's preferences. Caregivers described ongoing tensions between aspirations to provide nutritious diets and the practical constraints of limited income, time pressures, and children's preferences. These findings illustrate how feeding practices are shaped by the interplay between structural conditions and lived experience, highlighting the constrained nature of caregiver agency in peri-urban contexts. Addressing complementary feeding in such settings requires focusing not only on knowledge, but also on addressing social and material conditions that shape what is possible in everyday life.

items.title: Tandem duplication of oxidosqualene cyclases and enzyme promiscuity of cytochromes P450 contribute to the diversity of triterpenoids in Eleutherococcus senticosus.
items.abstract: Triterpenoid saponins in Araliaceae plants exhibit remarkable structural diversity, with species-specific compounds like ginsenosides and ciwujianosides, yet the genetic basis remains elusive. Here, we report a chromosome-scale genome assembly of Eleutherococcus senticosus (Rupr. & Maxim.) Maxim. (1.39 Gb, 51,243 genes) and demonstrate that it shares a lineage-specific whole-genome duplication (WGD-α, Ks = 0.112) with Hedera helix. Phylogenomic analyses reveal a 4:4 syntenic relationship between these species, confirming their close evolutionary relationship. Notably, both E. senticosus and H. helix lack the dammarenediol-II synthase (DDS) gene, explaining the absence of ginsenoside-type saponins. Through genome mining and functional validation, we identify eight OSC genes, including a tandemly duplicated cluster on chromosome 18 unique to E. senticosus. Biochemical assays show that EsOSC4 and EsOSC12 synthesize tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol, representing the first enzymatic characterization of a tirucallane synthase in Araliaceae, while EsOSC13 produces lupeol. Site-directed mutagenesis establishes residue 372 (valine in EsOSC13, methionine in EsOSC4/12) as critical for this functional divergence. Moreover, we discover three promiscuous CYP716 enzymes (EsCYP716A244/A450/A452) capable of oxidizing β-amyrin, lupeol, and tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol at multiple positions, generating diverse oxidized derivatives. These findings reveal tandem duplication and enzyme promiscuity as primary mechanisms driving triterpenoid diversity in E. senticosus, with implications for synthetic biology applications in saponin production.

items.title: An Sfp2-like protein underlies tube foot temporary adhesion in the sea cucumber Apostichopus japonicus.
items.abstract: Temporary adhesion by echinoderm tube feet is essential for attachment, locomotion and feeding, yet its molecular basis remains poorly understood in Holothuroidea. Here, we combined ultrastructural, proteomic, phylogenetic and expression analyses to investigate the temporary adhesive system in the sea cucumber Apostichopus japonicus. Scanning and transmission electron microscopy revealed a highly specialized tube foot disc epidermis featuring abundant secretory pores, dense microvilli and two distinct types of adhesive secretory cells, whereas these features were absent in the non-adhesive homologous papillae. Proteomic analysis of tube foot footprints and discs, combined with bioinformatic screening, identified 20 high-confidence candidate adhesive proteins and one astacin domain-containing candidate de-adhesive protein. Notably, the 4085 amino acid multidomain protein Aj-Sfp2-like was relatively abundant in the footprint proteome and showed extensive predicted post-translational modification. Tissue expression and in situ localization confirmed that Aj-Sfp2-like transcripts are localized to the secretory epidermis of adhesive appendages (tube feet and tentacles), whereas no such expression was detected in the non-adhesive papillae. Phylogenetic and comparative domain analyses demonstrate that Aj-Sfp2-like belongs to the broadly conserved Sfp2-like protein family, sharing a homologous modular framework with asteroid-restricted Sfp1-like proteins. These findings provide the first molecular framework for understanding tube foot adhesion and de-adhesion in holothurians and broaden our understanding of the conserved and divergent basis of temporary adhesion across echinoderms.

items.title: The effect of protocol preregistration on study replicability, reproducibility and recognition: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background: The adoption of open science practices, particularly prospective protocol registration, is widely advocated to mitigate questionable research practices such as outcome switching and HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known). However, the empirical evidence regarding the impact of preregistration on studies’ quality and robustness remains fragmented. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantify the effect of protocol preregistration on study replicability, reproducibility, and academic recognition. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive literature search across multiple databases (including PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science) for studies published up to February 2025. We included meta-research studies reporting comparisons between (pre)registered and non-preregistered studies, in any field of research. Outcomes of interest included any assessment of reporting quality, availability of research materials, and data sharing for replicability; the proportion of statistically significant findings, effect sizes, and sample sizes for reproducibility; and number of citations and time to publication for publication recognition. Data were pooled using random effects meta-analysis, and outcomes that could not be quantitatively synthesized were analysed using Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM). Risk of bias was assessed with the RoBANS 2 tool. Results: The search yielded 2613 unique records, of which 49 cross-sectional retrospective meta-research studies met the inclusion criteria. No randomized controlled trials were identified. The included meta-research studies most commonly analysed randomized controlled trials in clinical medicine (n = 31), followed by studies in psychology-related fields (n = 7), systematic reviews (n = 5), and other research areas (n = 6). Meta-analysis revealed that preregistration is associated with an increase in transparent reporting (OR 2.51[1.76, 3.56]), a reduction in the reporting of favourable results (OR 0.49[0.29, 0.84]), and larger sample sizes. However, the effect on selective outcome reporting was inconclusive. The descriptive synthesis of outcomes not included in meta-analyses additionally supports the association between preregistration and improved transparent reporting, while also suggesting increased sharing of materials, code, and data. Conclusion: Preregistration is consistently associated with indicators of improved research replicability and reproducibility, including more transparent reporting, larger study sample sizes, and a lower likelihood of favourable findings. However, the certainty of the evidence remains very low because current evidence is derived almost exclusively from observational meta-research studies. More rigorous evaluations are needed to establish whether these associations reflect causal effects of preregistration.

items.title: Validation of webcam-based eye-tracking in human sign- and goal-trackers
items.abstract: Recently, psychology has shifted from ignoring individual differences to using them to understand the variability in human behaviour. A key example is how people respond to cues that predict rewards. When exposed to reward-predictive signals, sign-trackers treat the cue itself as a motivational magnet, showing strong attraction and attentional bias toward it even when it is irrelevant to reward delivery. In contrast, goal-trackers treat the cue simply as a predictor, focusing their attention on the reward location. Translating this animal model to humans is challenging, but researchers have successfully developed tasks that use fixation times to the stimulus or reward location as an index of attentional bias. However, researchers still frequently rely on sample-dependent methods (like the median split), which risk misclassifying participants in small laboratory samples and contribute to inconsistent findings regarding behavioural correlates.To collect larger and more diverse samples, behavioural science is moving online. Remote webcam-based eye-tracking has emerged as a low-cost, scalable alternative to expensive laboratory hardware, but it has never been validated for reward-based associative learning studies and for classifying sign-trackers and goal-trackers behavioural phenotypes. To bridge this gap, this study validates a novel webcam-based Pavlovian conditioning task by comparing a professional laboratory eye-tracker with a webcam used both in the lab and in participants' unsupervised home environments.We evaluated cross-method and cross-environment stability across these three setups. At the group level, Bayesian analyses showed strong equivalence in average gaze indices, demonstrating that shifting the device or environment does not alter core cognitive processes or introduce systemic bias. At the individual level, Intraclass Correlation Coefficients showed moderate-to-good absolute agreement along the tracking continuum, closely matching standard temporal test-retest variations. Crucially, individual phenotypic classification via median split remained highly stable, with the vast majority of participants maintaining their ST or GT assignment across laboratory and remote home environments.These findings successfully validate remote, webcam-based eye-tracking as a reliable and stable protocol for classifying sign-trackers and goal-trackers behavioural phenotypes. By overcoming the physical and financial constraints of traditional laboratory hardware, this scalable online task provides a clear opportunity to recruit large-scale samples and investigate diverse or specialised populations in an ecological environment.

items.title: Complementary behavioural signatures of a motor sequence memory following competing learning.
items.abstract: Learning a competing sequence may affect previously acquired motor sequence memories. To assess retention following competing learning, researchers typically examine changes in the number of correctly completed sequences, but this measure provides limited information about the temporal organisation of execution. We therefore compared correct-sequence count, indexing successful sequence production, with Key-Press Similarity (KPS), indexing cross-session similarity in keypress timing. In Experiment 1, participants learned an original sequence followed by a competing sequence and were tested after short or long retention intervals. Correct-sequence count improved for both sequences, whereas KPS showed a different pattern, with original-sequence KPS higher than competing-sequence KPS after the short but not the long interval. Original-sequence KPS was also higher in the short-interval group than in the no-interference control group and was positively associated with original-sequence correct-sequence count at test. Experiment 2 extended this approach to memory reactivation. Although no group-level KPS differences emerged, KPS for the newly learned sequence was positively associated with test correct-sequence count for both sequences at the short interval. Together, these findings show that successful sequence production and the temporal organisation of execution can follow different patterns during retention, revealing distinct but complementary behavioural signatures of motor sequence retention following competing learning.

items.title: Psychotropic medication use in early pregnancy: impacts on child socio-emotional and behavioral development.
items.abstract: Background Clinical symptoms of distress (anxiety or depression) affect around 10%-25% of women during the perinatal period, which, if left untreated, can adversely affect both maternal health and child development. Psychotropic medications are often first-line treatments for maternal distress in pregnancy, but their effects on child socio-emotional development remain underexplored. This study aims to compare socio-emotional and behavioral development of children at 18 and 36 months according to early pregnancy exposure to treated or untreated maternal distress. Methods This project is based on the Montreal Antenatal Well-Being Study, a prospective cohort study of 1,130 pregnant individuals from Quebec, Canada. Women self-reported their medication use and were categorized as: (1) Untreated maternal distress, (2) Psychotropic medication use, (3) Control group (no maternal distress, no psychotropic medication). Analyses of covariance were used to examine the associations between exposure groups and indices of child socio-emotional and behavioral development, assessed using the Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire and the Child Behavior Checklist. To better account for baseline symptom severity and treatment indication, propensity score weighting was used to create comparable groups with balanced covariates such as socioeconomic status and health care access. Results Approximately 9.4% of women reported psychotropic medication use in early pregnancy. Analyses of covariance showed that maternal psychotropic medication use was associated with child inhibited temperament at 18 months and greater social withdrawal at 36 months. Propensity weighting revealed that these associations were largely driven by unmeasured confounding, showing no lasting associations with medication. In contrast, children born to mothers with untreated distress had poorer socio-emotional development. Conclusions Our findings underscore the critical importance of appropriate statistical control of confounding in observational studies of maternal medication use and child outcomes. They also emphasize the impact of maternal distress on child development and the need for access to effective perinatal treatments.

items.title: "Surprised that men could Care?": gendered professional identity and occupational well-being among male clinical psychologists in India: a qualitative study.
items.abstract: Objective Clinical psychology is a care-oriented profession in which empathy and emotional attunement are central to practice and are often culturally associated with femininity. This study explored gendered professional identity, emotional labour, therapeutic practice, and occupational well-being among male clinical psychologists in India. Methods Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 14 male clinical psychologists registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India. Data were analysed using a six-phase thematic analysis approach. Results Five themes were developed: Pathways into Clinical Psychology; Systemic and Gendered Contexts; Negotiating Masculinity and Professional Identity; Learning and Professional Socialisation; and Sustaining Well-Being and Envisioning Change. Participants described navigating stereotypes associating care and emotional sensitivity with femininity, professional isolation, gendered client expectations, therapeutic boundary demands, financial pressures, and institutional constraints. Their accounts also reflected adaptive identity negotiation, professional learning, supportive relationships, reflective practice, and efforts to sustain occupational well-being. Conclusion Gendered expectations and institutional conditions intersected in shaping participants' professional identities and well-being. Gender-responsive supervision, peer-support networks, clearer professional structures, and greater institutional attention to clinician well-being may support more inclusive and sustainable professional environments.

items.title: Developing a culturally responsive survey of caregiving and cognitive health for older adults and their family caregivers in earthquake-affected Bantul, Indonesia: a cognitive interview pilot study.
items.abstract: Many older adults in Bantul, Indonesia, lived through the 2006 earthquake and now depend on family members for daily care. Their cognitive and functional health and the burden carried by their caregivers are rarely measured together, and no combined survey has been tested with Indonesian caregivers in a disaster-affected district. Guided by the caregiving stress process model, we combined six validated Indonesian-language instruments into one caregiver-reported survey: the AD8 and the Lawton IADL (stressors in the older adult), the Zarit Burden Interview and the six-item UCLA Loneliness Scale (caregiver outcomes), and the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale and the short-form Attitudes Toward Seeking Professional Psychological Help scale (caregiver resources). We pretested the survey through retrospective verbal-probing cognitive interviews with 17 participants (13 family caregivers and four health professionals who were also family caregivers). Transcripts were analysed with codebook thematic analysis based on Tourangeau's four-stage model of survey response and Willis's classification of question problems. Participants found the content relevant to their caregiving lives, but they reported three problems that arose from the combined battery rather than from any single scale: length and fatigue, unfamiliar medical and psychological terms, and a crowded online layout. Each problem was linked to specific items and revisions. Validated scales cannot be assumed to work well when they are combined and used in a new community. The next steps are a second round of cognitive interviews, brief measures of earthquake exposure, and psychometric testing in a large sample of caregiver and older adult dyads.

items.title: Factors associated with mammography screening stages in Hispanic/Latina women in the USA: a transtheoretical model and health belief model approach.
items.abstract: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among Hispanic/Latina women in the U.S. and they are more likely to be diagnosed at later stages. Understanding psychosocial factors associated with mammography screening is important for addressing these disparities. This study examined associations between Transtheoretical Model (TTM) stages of mammography screening and constructs from the Health Belief Model (HBM) and TTM, including self-efficacy, perceived benefits, barriers, susceptibility, and seriousness, as well as family support, among Hispanic/Latina women aged 40 years and older in the U.S.A. A cross-sectional design using self-report surveys was employed, with 473 Hispanic/Latina women recruited through multiple nonprobability sampling strategies. A one-way ANCOVA compared psychosocial factors across the three combined TTM groups (precontemplation/contemplation/preparation, relapse/inconsistent, maintenance), controlling for age. Statistically significant differences were found among the three combined TTM groups for self-efficacy (F(2, 469) = 13.08, p = 0.000), benefits (F(2, 469) = 5.21, p = 0.006), barriers (F(2, 469) = 6.90, p = 0.001), susceptibility (F(2, 469) = 8.37, p = 0.000), seriousness (F(2, 469) = 4.64, p = 0.01), and family support (F(2, 469) = 10.34, p = 0.000). These significant differences across the three combined TTM groups highlight the multifaceted nature of mammography screening behavior. Family support, often underrepresented in traditional health behavior models, was also associated with the combined TTM groups. In this study, family support was primarily reflected in family-related health communication and advice. These findings suggest that using the HBM and TTM as complementary frameworks, alongside family support, may inform culturally tailored interventions addressing individual beliefs and familial contexts to promote regular mammography screening among Hispanic/Latina women. Future longitudinal research should examine these factors across Hispanic/Latina subgroups and settings to better understand their relationships with mammography screening and inform targeted health promotion strategies.

items.title: Appearance-based concerns and psychosocial functioning following complex plastic surgery for female melanoma survivors: a qualitative study.
items.abstract: Melanoma is an aggressive form of skin cancer necessitating surgical removal. Following reconstructive surgery, melanoma survivors may experience body-image concerns and psychosocial distress, with females more likely to report a lasting impact on their wellbeing. This study aimed to explore the appearance-based concerns and psychosocial functioning of female melanoma survivors who had undergone reconstructive plastic surgery. Seven females who had undergone reconstructive plastic surgery as part of their treatment for melanoma, participated in semi-structured interviews which were analysed using interpretative phenomenological analysis. Three themes were developed: 'Constructing the melanoma-identity'; 'Relating to others: experiencing dismissal and self-stigmatisation'; and 'Grieving the life you had: adjusting and coping'. Findings highlight the impact of appearance changes upon participants' sense-of-self and identity. Psychologists could offer person-centred therapies aligned with concepts of post-traumatic growth and positive body-image. They may offer consultation and training to develop compassion for body-image concerns in multidisciplinary teams.

items.title: Lived emotional experiences of patients following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: a phenomenological approach.
items.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) involves significant emotional challenges, particularly during early recovery. However, broader emotional experiences in this period remain underexplored. To explore the emotional experiences of patients during early post-transplant recovery. A phenomenological study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital using purposive sampling. Ten clinically stable adult patients participated in semi-structured interviews conducted in their preferred languages. At least two interviews were conducted with each participant, while two participants required three interviews each. Each interview lasted approximately 40 minutes. Interviews were transcribed verbatim, translated into English where necessary, and analysed concurrently with data collection. Recruitment continued until data saturation was achieved, defined as the point at which no new themes or categories emerged from successive interviews. Data saturation, reflexivity, investigator triangulation, and COREQ guidelines supported methodological rigour. Five categories emerged: uncertainty and emotional distress; disrupted body image and altered self-identity; adaptive coping and emotional support; spiritual meaning-making and hope preservation; and emotional burden of dependency and isolation. Participants described treatment-related fears, physical changes, family and healthcare support, personal coping strategies, and spiritual practices. Despite support, some experienced guilt and loneliness. Emotional recovery following HSCT involves interconnected psychological, social, and spiritual experiences. Culturally sensitive, patient-centred psychosocial care may support emotional adjustment. Further longitudinal research is needed to inform interventions in the Indian sociocultural context.

items.title: Rooted in story: Implementation and evaluation of the Tree of Life intervention to promote cultural identity and hope for the future among refugee youth.
items.abstract: The Tree of Life (ToL) is an arts-based, culturally grounded intervention that features strengths-based and narrative approaches. This study implemented the ToL as an intervention to center refugee youth's voices in creating their life stories and promoting well-being. Specifically, this intervention aimed at fostering a positive sense of cultural identity and hope for the future among refugee youth. Refugee youth (N = 41) originated from seven countries participated in a 4-day intervention, followed by an evaluation focus group session. This manuscript's analytic goals are twofold. First, we explored the design and implementation of this intervention. We document the adaptations, youth responses to the materials and adaptations, and youth-led suggestions during the intervention implementation. Second, using reflexive thematic analysis, we analyzed the focus group evaluation data to understand refugee youth's experiences of and outcomes from participating in the ToL intervention. We identified three themes that showcase the aspects youth valued and their perspectives about the intervention's perceived impact: (a) authoring identity through reflection, (b) imagining and shaping possible futures and (c) realized uniqueness through social and cross-cultural connection. Based on our findings, we discuss implications and offer recommendations for future programs supporting refugee youth.

items.title: From shared space to shared resilience: How municipal co-working hubs build social capital among urban young adults.
items.abstract: This article examines how municipal co-working and learning hubs may support personal and community resilience among young adults aged 18-35. Drawing on the Integrated Resilience Model, we conducted 72 semistructured interviews with staff and young adults across five municipal hubs in Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel. Thematic analysis yielded eight themes concerning learning, initiative development, community events, supportive staff relationships, peer support, municipal connections, personal empowerment, and functional infrastructure. Participants described how accessible resources, repeated interaction, and opportunities to initiate activities supported self-organization, confidence, and belonging. Peer exchanges and relationships with municipal actors illustrated processes of bonding, bridging, and linking social capital. Findings contribute to community psychology scholarship on empowering community settings by specifying how everyday work and study environments can connect individual agency, peer networks, and public institutions. We conceptualize municipal hubs as public resilience infrastructure whose potential contribution to community resilience rests on opportunities for mutual support, participation, and collective initiative. For community practice, the findings highlight the importance of integrating accessible infrastructure, supportive staff relationships, peer connections, and institutional responsiveness.

items.title: "If not me, then who? If not now, then when?" Guidelines for partnering with lived experts of homelessness in research.
items.abstract: Individuals with lived experience of homelessness often engage with research and/or academic settings with lived histories of disrespectful or condescending treatment, often at the hands of researchers. However, research that meaningfully includes people who have lived expertise of homelessness is uniquely positioned to provide deeper insights into both the causes and the evidence-based solutions to homelessness. This paper describes the process of developing Guidelines for academic researchers partnering with lived experts of homelessness, and our finalized set of Guidelines. Our Guidelines include: strive to conduct research "with" versus "on" people; use respectful and inclusive language; create brave spaces that foster mutual respect between researchers and participants; be transparent in all stages of the research process; researchers should check their biases; researchers should be able to communicate across audiences; researchers should support participants' power and liberation; and always compensate lived expertise (and go beyond compensation to offer access to other valuable resources). Recognizing the historical and present marginalization, condescension, and disrespect that people experiencing homelessness have experienced at the hands of researchers, this work seeks to provide an alternative set of practices which explicitly shift power structures.

items.title: A cluster analysis of complex and "classic" post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms in a sample of ethnoracially minoritized and LGBTQ participants.
items.abstract: Ethnoracially minoritized and LGBTQ people are less likely to benefit from Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) treatments, and evidence points toward unaccounted for identity-based trauma as a reason for this disparity. Another potential pathway to this disparity is how identity-based trauma might shift PTSD symptom presentation. Complex trauma sequelae are known to be more intractable than Criterion A trauma sequelae, and identity-based trauma may contribute to the disparity by shifting symptoms toward complex PTSD. The importance of complex PTSD symptoms in the clinical presentation of a sample of ethnoracially minoritized (n = 120) and LGBTQ (n = 45) participants (total N = 138) were assessed using a TwoStep cluster analysis. Crucially, the statistical methods used for this study are intended for hypothesis generation and are not traditional null hypothesis significance testing. Findings from this cluster analysis may seed future null hypothesis significance testing. Cluster quality was good and resulted in low- and high-symptom clinical groups. For ethnoracially minoritized participants, both classic PTSD and complex PTSD symptoms determined group membership, whereas for LGBTQ participants, complex PTSD symptoms predominated. The results contribute to an emerging literature indicating that identity-based trauma may result in a clinical presentation similar to that of complex trauma.

items.title: Delusions of adequacy: Entitlement, deception, and mindfulness.
items.abstract: In higher education, addressing deception in knowledge production is challenging. This laboratory-based study examined whether manipulating self-entitlement influenced deceptive intent and the roles of self-deception and trait mindfulness in this process. Participants ( N = 278 university students in Indonesia, 83.8% female; mean age = 18.29, SD = 0.61) completed the trait mindfulness scale, were randomly assigned to a writing task designed to induce self-entitlement, completed a forward-looking paradigm to assess self-deception, and participated in a hypothetical knowledge-hiding task to measure self-reported deceptive intent. The results indicated that, compared with the no-entitlement group, individuals in the self-entitlement group reported higher levels of both self-deception and deceptive intent. The effect of self-entitlement on deceptive intent was mediated by self-deception, but in an unexpectedly opposite manner. Trait mindfulness was associated with a decreased intention to deceive others but not oneself. These findings suggest that, in educational settings, the interplay between self-deception and deception of others is more nuanced than previously understood.

items.title: Disorders of Ejaculation: AUA/SMSNA Guideline (2027).
items.abstract: Purpose The amendment of the Disorders of Ejaculation Guideline provides an update to the evidence-based guidance for clinicians on appropriate evaluation, diagnosis, and available treatments of premature ejaculation (PE) or delayedejaculation. Materials and methods The Pacific Northwest Evidence-Based Practice Center utilized Ovid MEDLINE and Embase databases to search for studies published between January 1, 2020 and December 19, 2024. Search strategies that were developed for the original Disorders of Ejaculation guideline were employed. The search identified 727 abstracts, 89 of which met inclusion criteria. In 2025, NV HEATHRES. INC. extracted data and assessed the quality of the evidence for outcomes on 25 studies to inform statement updates. Results A statement on non-pharmacological therapies for the treatment of PE was revised to reflect new evidence that indicates that some of these therapies may be effective. A new Expert Opinion statement on the potential use of PDE5i for the treatment of PE was written. Although there was evidence to support 2 new statements on the use of daily or on-demand clomipramine or glans hyaluronic acid injection for the treatment of PE, the Panel emphasizes that these treatments are to be used in the context of patient informed consent and at the behest of a trained clinician. Conclusions Although much of the evidence used to inform this Amendment supported existing statements, there was new data to support new statements on PDE5i, daily or on-demand clomipramine, and glans HA injection for the treatment of PE, although the latter 2 recommendations come with important caveats. Ultimately, the Panel recommends that shared decision-making should be the fundamental precept in the management of disorders of ejaculation regardless of the treatment option utilized.

items.title: Health professionals' notions of primary community health needs assessment: a qualitative study in Greece.
items.abstract: Background Understanding how primary health care (PHC) professionals perceive and respond to community health needs is essential for participatory and context-sensitive health planning. In Greece, dominant health surveys often overlook experiential dimensions of need, suppressing non-clinical indicators and excluding both professional and citizen voices. Methods This qualitative study involved three focus groups with 31 participants working or training in PHC, conducted in Thessaloniki, Greece, between May 2021 and June 2022. Andersen's Behavioral Model of Health Services Use (BMHSU) provided the structural framework, while data were analysed using principles of Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA), focussing on lived experience, meaning-making, and relational care. Results Health needs were described as dynamic, socially constructed, and frequently unexpressed-mediated by silence, stigma, or institutional neglect. Themes included the interpretive labor of frontline professionals, the ethical complexity of unspoken suffering, fragmentation between primary and tertiary care, role ambiguity, and professionals' disillusionment with rigid institutional structures. Despite structural limitations, participants expressed qualified support for community participation and called for evaluation models grounded in trust, local realities, and mutual accountability. Conclusions The study positions PHC not only as a clinical entry point but as a relational, ethical, and civic space. The findings suggest the need for co-designed tools that can assess both expressed and latent needs, inform inclusive planning, and support system responsiveness. Although the focus was on professionals' perspectives, the themes identified resonate across under-resourced or post-austerity settings and may inform broader European PHC reform.

items.title: Comparison of Infradian and Circadian Rhythms in Laboratory Rodents.
items.abstract: Infradian cycles are multi-day oscillations whose mechanisms are still poorly understood, while circadian rhythms have been extensively studied and are well-documented in mammals. In this study, we monitored the locomotor activity of three rodent species: CD-1 mice (Mus musculus), Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus), and white-tailed antelope squirrels (Ammospermophilus leucurus). We used Lomb-Scargle spectral analysis to verify the prevalence of circadian and infradian rhythms, the magnitude of the spectral power, and associations across species, rhythms, and sexes. Circadian rhythms were robust and were found for all animals. For infradian rhythms, the prevalence in mice was extremely low, whereas the prevalence in gerbils and squirrels was moderate in the 5- and 10-day ranges. In all cases, the strength of infradian rhythmicity was less than 10% of the strength of circadian rhythmicity. As no natural environmental cycle is documented to operate in the 5- to 10-day range, further studies are needed to determine whether an endogenous source may account for this weak but significant infradian rhythmicity.

items.title: Psychological resilience and quality of life among adolescents with and without chronic diseases following the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes.
items.abstract: Earthquakes can have substantial physical and psychological consequences because of their sudden and destructive nature. Adolescents with chronic diseases may be particularly vulnerable because disaster-related disruptions can compound ongoing healthcare and developmental needs. This study compared psychological resilience and health-related quality of life among adolescents with and without chronic diseases living in an earthquake-affected region. Data were collected using a Personal Information Form, the Child and Youth Resilience Measure (CYRM), and the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL). Adolescents with chronic diseases had significantly lower overall quality of life, as well as lower physical, psychosocial, school, and social functioning scores, than adolescents without chronic diseases. However, psychological resilience did not differ significantly between groups, and resilience was not significantly associated with PedsQL total or subscale scores. Multiple linear regression analyses showed that chronic disease status and housing damage were independently associated with lower PedsQL total scores, while having a family member trapped under debris was also significantly associated with PedsQL total score. Household income was the only significant predictor of psychological resilience. These findings suggest that post-earthquake support for adolescents should address not only continuity of healthcare for those with chronic diseases but also broader factors affecting recovery, including housing conditions, family-level disaster experiences, psychosocial support, school reintegration, and socioeconomic resources.

items.title: Classroom-Based Auditory Cognitive Training in Typically Developing Children.
items.abstract: Objectives The purpose of this study was to investigate the role of executive functioning in speech-in-noise perception, evaluate the efficacy of targeted auditory training in enhancing speech perception, and identify predictors of listening-related fatigue in typically developing children. The study addressed three questions: (1) To what extent do executive functioning skills predict children's speech perception accuracy in noise? (2) Does auditory cognitive training improve children's speech perception in noisy environments? (3) What is the relationship between executive functioning and listening-related fatigue in children? Design Eighty typically developing children aged 5 to 11 years underwent pre- and post-assessments of working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and speech perception in noise. Participants were randomly assigned to either the targeted auditory training group or a business-as-usual control group, with trained children assigned to 24 sessions spread over 6 weeks. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine the effects of group, time, and their interaction on executive functioning measures and speech perception accuracy. Pearson correlations were used to examine the relationship between individual differences in executive functioning and speech perception performance, as well as listening-related fatigue. Results Significant improvements in inhibitory control and cognitive flexibility were observed from pre- to post-test across both groups, but no significant group differences emerged, as these changes were not specific to the training condition. Higher inhibitory control was significantly associated with better speech perception in noise in a co-located listening condition, whereas age was the primary predictor in the spatially separated condition. No significant training effects were observed for speech perception in noise measures. In an exploratory analysis, listening-related fatigue was negatively associated with working memory capacity, though this finding should be interpreted with caution given that most children fell within the low-fatigue range and fatigue was assessed only at post-test. Conclusions The findings from this study suggest that while executive functioning skills, particularly inhibitory control, play a role in predicting speech perception accuracy in noise for typically developing children, targeted auditory training as implemented in this study did not yield significant improvements. The absence of fidelity data limits the interpretation of the null training effects, and future work should systematically measure training compliance to better understand when and for whom auditory training may be effective. The relationship between working memory and listening fatigue further highlights the importance of cognitive resources for children's listening experiences in classroom settings.

items.title: Preliminary Stakeholder Evaluation of a Novel Weight History Interview for Eating Disorders: A Qualitative Analysis.
items.abstract: Objective Measures of weight history, such as weight suppression (the difference between one's highest past weight and current weight), have been associated with behavioural, cognitive, and biological facets of eating disorders (EDs), including purging frequency, leptin levels, and future weight gain (Lowe et al. 2018; Lowe 2020). Given these consistent associations, it would be desirable to develop a systematic framework to gather patients' weight history in clinical settings. This study was the first stage in developing a weight history interview (WHI). Method Ten former patients and three clinicians from a residential ED treatment facility participated in separate focus groups to elicit feedback on the relevance, clarity, utility, and potential emotional impact of the first iteration of the WHI. Additionally, we administered surveys to gather quantitative feedback. Results Thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke 2006) of qualitative data identified seven themes highlighting participants' feedback and suggestions for future development of the WHI. Descriptive statistics of quantitative data largely reflected participants' mixed reactions. Conclusions Key stakeholders' feedback was used to identify suggested modifications for future versions of the WHI, including strategies to increase acceptability. The ultimate goal of this effort is to establish a weight history interview for use in clinical settings.

items.title: Synergistic effects of chronic and acute stress and racial discrimination on alcohol craving across Black and White young adults in the United States.
items.abstract: Background and aims Alcohol craving is an important proximal predictor of alcohol use; yet little is known about how chronic and acute forms of general and discrimination-based stressors synergistically interact to influence craving. This study aimed to examine the effects of chronic and acute stress and racial discrimination on daily alcohol craving and compare these associations between Black and White young adults in the United States. Design Observational study in which participants completed baseline assessments followed by a 17-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) protocol. Setting Non-treatment seeking, community sample from Western Pennsylvania, United States. Participants Young adults aged 21-30 (n = 166), who reported at least weekly alcohol use and at least three occasions of consuming 4+/5 + drinks for female/male participants in the past three months. 41.57% of participants identified as Black/African American and 58.43% of participants identified as White; 68.64% were assigned female at birth. Measurements Baseline assessments included sociodemographic characteristics and measures of chronic stress and racial discrimination. EMA protocol captured acute stress, discrimination, and craving. Results Between-person acute stress predicted higher craving [Unstandardized fixed-effect coefficient (B) = 1.17, standard error (SE) = 0.27, P Summary Effects of chronic and acute forms of general stress on alcohol craving appear to be consistent across Black and White young adults in the United States. Chronic and acute discrimination synergistically interact to drive alcohol craving in Black participants.

items.title: The Stanford Multifaceted Dissociation Questionnaire: A 9-Item Measure of Trait and State Dissociation.
items.abstract: Dissociation is a common and increasingly studied phenomenon with substantial relevance for mental health. To date, researchers have often relied upon broad conceptualizations and retrospective measures, making it difficult to identify a consistent subset of experiences for dissociation, explore their links to related phenomena, and differentiate habitual from momentary dissociation. To address these issues, we introduce the Stanford Multifaceted Dissociation Questionnaire (SMDQ), a 9-item measure that assesses three facets of dissociation and can be employed to assess either trait or state dissociation. In Study 1, we evaluated the content validity of the initial SMDQ item pool using feedback from individuals with lived experience of dissociation (N = 73) and content experts (N = 14), detailing our focus on detachment-type experiences that may help the dissociation construct to be more cleanly distinguished from other clinical phenomena. In Study 2 (N = 400), we described the item selection process and examined the factor structure, internal consistency, and convergent/discriminant validity of both the trait and state versions of the SMDQ. In Study 3 (N = 500), we further investigated the psychometric properties of both versions, including their factor structure, measurement invariance, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and convergent/discriminant validity. Across the studies, scores on the trait and state versions of the SMDQ showed strong content validity and a theoretically congruent factor structure, comprised of alteration in the perception of one's mind, body, and world (suggesting a tripartite model of dissociation). This structure was largely invariant across demographic groups and time. We also demonstrate good convergent and discriminant validity, internal consistency (ω > 0.80), and temporal stability over 1 week (r > 0.70 for the trait version). Overall, we conclude that the trait and state versions of the SMDQ are promising measurement tools that can enhance our understanding of dissociation's structure, antecedents, and consequences.

items.title: The Impact of Dissimilarity, Interaction, and Isolation Segregation Metrics on Cognitive and Functional Outcomes of Older Adults Enrolled in the H-EPESE Study.
items.abstract: ObjectiveWe examined the impact of residential segregation on cognitive outcomes and everyday functioning among older adults enrolled in the Hispanic Established Populations for the Epidemiological Study of the Elderly (H-EPESE).MethodsData from baseline, 2-, 5-, 7-, and 12-year follow-up visits were used. Residential segregation was characterized by dissimilarity, interaction, and isolation indices using Decennial Census data. Mixed-effects models were used to examine associations with cognition and everyday functioning.ResultsHigher residential segregation, as indexed by dissimilarity, was associated with both slower rates of cognitive and everyday functioning decline. Higher segregation, indexed by interaction and isolation indices, was only associated with slower rates of cognitive decline.ConclusionWe observed evidence of the "barrio advantage" for Hispanic older adult cognitive and functional health. Potential mechanisms for beneficial effects of co-ethnic living are discussed including access to cultural resources, greater social cohesion, and protection from discrimination.

items.title: The moderating role of cognitive reflection in the relationship between emotions and bullshit receptivity.
items.abstract: Although previous research has examined the role of cognitive reflection in bullshit receptivity, little deals with the effect of positive and negative emotions on pseudo-profound bullshit. This study aims to investigate the effect of emotion on bullshit and if this effect is moderated by cognitive reflection. A total of 217 subjects were randomly assigned to three experimental conditions, in which negative, positive, or neutral emotions were induced through a short film scene. Analyses were conducted using latent scores derived from the factors of the Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) , after verifying their dimensionality through a confirmatory factor analysis. Results indicated that positive emotions significantly increased receptivity to bullshit, whereas negative emotions did not produce a significant effect. Furthermore, cognitive reflection moderated the relationship between emotion and bullshit, so that as the level of cognitive reflection rises, the effect of emotion on bullshit receptivity weakens. There must be a high level of cognitive reflection to protect people from the effect of positive emotions on bullshit receptivity, whereas intermediate levels of cognitive reflection are enough to protect people from the effect of negative emotions on bullshit receptivity.

items.title: The development of children's normative beliefs about sharing strategies: A cross-cultural study in Uganda and the U.K.
items.abstract: Children's developing beliefs about social norms in middle childhood may lead to cultural differences in sharing behavior. However, we know relatively little about cultural differences in the development of children's normative beliefs, and the extent to which there is a difference between the sharing norms children endorse and their actual sharing behavior. To address this gap, we asked U.K. (N = 163, Female=88, Male=75; 54% White British; 29% Other British, 17% Other not British) and Ugandan (N = 185, Female=94, Male=91; 35% Alur; 24% Lugbara; 41% Other) children (aged 3.5-12 years, data collection: 2022-2024) and their caregivers what they "should" do in three sharing games. Caregivers and older children in the U.K. mostly endorsed egalitarian beliefs, while Ugandan participants' beliefs were more diverse. Societally unique patterns of beliefs emerged around age 5-6 but continued to develop through middle childhood. At older ages, children's egalitarian beliefs predicted their actual sharing in a separate Dictator Game. These results suggest that during middle childhood, children increasingly demonstrate both (i) a tendency to endorse adult-like (and culture-specific) normative beliefs about sharing, and (ii) a stronger tendency to conform to the normative sharing beliefs that they endorse.

items.title: Seroprotection and improved polyfunctional immunity conferred by a YF17D-vectored rabies vaccine
items.abstract: Rabies remains a major public-health challenge, with pre-exposure vaccination strategies constrained by the need for multiple doses and repeated healthcare visits. Here we describe YF-RabG, a live-attenuated rabies vaccine candidate based on the yellow fever 17D (YF17D) vaccine backbone that stably expresses the rabies virus glycoprotein (RabG). YF-RabG exhibited an attenuated phenotype and favourable safety profile compared with parental YF17D across several preclinical models, including neonatal and immunocompromised mice. A single immunization induced robust humoral and cell-mediated immune responses in non-human primates. Rabies virus-neutralizing antibody titres readily exceeded the widely accepted correlate of protection in mice, hamsters and non-human primates by several orders. Accordingly, vaccination conferred protection against lethal rabies challenge in a range of stringent mouse models, maintained seroprotective antibody levels for at least one year, and increased following a boost using a licensed rabies vaccine. Furthermore, the YF17D vector was readily adapted to accommodate glycoproteins from distant lyssaviruses, generating protective vaccine candidates against Mokola, Lagos bat and Lleida bat lyssaviruses. Collectively, these findings identify YF-RabG as a promising single-dose rabies vaccine candidate and highlight the versatility of the YF17D platform for lyssavirus vaccine development.

items.title: Sex and Gender Reporting and Female Participation Relative to Disease Burden in ClinicalTrials.gov
items.abstract: Importance: Assessing representation by sex assigned at birth and gender identity requires reporting of both in trials. If disclosure of full gender and sex participation from clinicaltrials.gov is limited, it poses challenges in characterization and understanding of those participant experiences. Objective: To determine how often ClinicalTrials.gov trials published trials report sex and gender, which characteristics are associated with reporting, and how participants' female share compares with that of the general public. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cross-sectional study of interventional trials registered to ClinicalTrials.gov, with or without US sites, with primary completion on or after September 27, 2008, and results first posted from January 1, 2009, through April 30, 2026. Exposures: Funder type, phase, US sites, enrollment, primary completion year, number of countries, and therapeutic area. Main Outcomes and Measures: Reporting of sex and gender, and the female participation-to-prevalence ratio (PPR; trial female share divided by the number of people with the condition). Results: Among 58,007 trials (median enrollment, 72 [IQR, 31 to 206]; 42,644 [74%] with US sites), 553 (0.95%) reported gender and 57,683 (99.44%) reported sex. Gender reporting was more common with National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding (odds ratio [OR], 9.05; 95% CI, 6.65 to 12.6), US sites (OR, 4.21; 95% CI, 2.96 to 6.22), and larger enrollment. Across 10 conditions (15,552 mixed-sex trials), median PPR ranged from 0.68 (95% CI, 0.64 to 0.71) for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to 1.05 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.09) for obesity and had a relatively lower female share in 8. Among the 10 conditions most prevalent in our cohort, 6,917 of 16,097 trial condition combinations (43.0%) reached a PPR of at least 0.90; odds of reaching it were higher for NIH-funded (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11 to 1.34) and lower for government-funded trials (OR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.33) as compared to industry-funded trials. Conclusions and Relevance: In ClinicalTrials.gov, sex reporting is nearly universal, whereas gender reporting is concentrated among NIH-funded, US-based, and larger trials. Female trial enrollment fell below the female share of people with the condition for most conditions, emphasizing the benefit of condition-specific benchmarks in clinical trials.

items.title: Practical evaluation of AI models to forecast a respiratory seasonal epidemic in Canada
items.abstract: Public health organizations can benefit greatly from infectious disease epidemic forecasting to guide and support interventions and policies that reduce morbidity. However, accurate and reliable epidemic forecasting remains notoriously challenging and is an evolving field in which new scientific advances continue to support forecasting efforts. Computational models that underpin artificial intelligence (AI) models are promising developments that may improve seasonal epidemic forecasting. This study aims to compare the performance of a selection of AI models previously identified as well adapted to epidemic forecasting, including machine learning (XGBoost), deep learning models (Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Transformer), time-series foundation model (Chronos), and a hybrid model: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), against statistical models (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Prophet) and a compartmental epidemiological model (CEM) in seasonal epidemic forecasting across Canada. The study uses weekly positivity-rate incidence of seasonal influenza A across eight Canadian provinces during the 2025/2026 season as a test case. Each model generated short-term (up to 5 weeks ahead) forecasts independently for each province from October 11, 2025, to March 28, 2026. We evaluated performance using mean absolute error (MAE) for each province. Our results show that AI models, specifically GRU, Transformer, and Chronos models, achieve lower MAE than CEM in four of eight provinces (Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, and Saskatchewan). Meanwhile, CEM and ARIMA outperform all AI models in three provinces (Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba) and one province (Nova Scotia), respectively. Furthermore, data pooling strategies that leverage multi-province data for the target virus or multi-virus data within individual provinces greatly improve deep learning models, and Chronos performs well under zero-shot forecasting in British Columbia. In contrast, Prophet always has the highest MAE, and PINN is worse than CEMs. Overall, AI models performed comparably to, or slightly better than, CEMs. However, these modest gains may not offset their lack of interpretability, high computational costs, and reliance on the specialized expertise required for implementation. We therefore conclude that AI models are best as a complement, rather than a replacement, to CEMs, which remain crucial for interpretability and informing decision-making.
