items.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
items.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

items.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
items.abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.

items.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
items.abstract: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.

items.title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
items.abstract: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.

items.title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
items.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

items.title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
items.abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

items.title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects
items.abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.

items.title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
items.abstract: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

items.title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

items.title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
items.abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

items.title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
items.abstract: Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken during a RAG repair journey. RagHarnessDebugger checks that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. We tested our approach on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements with two reader models and a replication set of separate contracts. Our debugger's audit layer exposed failure patterns that were hidden under aggregate metrics, policies acceptance cost of repairs vs regressions and policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealised repairs on development and replication sets. Our audit, together with a labeled error analysis and replay mechanism, allowed following the execution path all the way to the terminal decision - uncovering where missing repairs became lost. Our revised harness improved accuracy over the initial BM25-only baseline by 3.6 points on development contracts and 3.7 points on the replication set, and even improved our full contract access reference score by 1.1 on development and 2.4 on replication set. While our work here demonstrates how the debugger can conduct decision root-cause analysis for missed repairs, the true value lies with providing this debugger for judgment visibility serving continuous improvement of RAG decisions and their explainability. Keywords: agentic RAG, AI evidence repair, harness explainability, counterfactual replay, Jev, ContractNLI

items.title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
items.abstract: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

items.title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
items.abstract: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

items.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
items.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

items.title: VITAL: A Framework for Validating Agentic AI in Pharmaceutical Drug Development and Clinical Trial Operations
items.abstract: Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.

items.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
items.abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

items.title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
items.abstract: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.

items.title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models
items.abstract: Many real-world optimization problems involve optimizing black-box objectives for which only a limited number of evaluations are available. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for such problems, but its effectiveness often deteriorates in high-dimensional spaces. Recent work leverages diffusion models for black-box optimization, often through pre-training a reward-conditioned score network to steer generation towards high-reward samples. Alternatively, gradient-based guidance methods assume access to a differentiable reward function from which guidance gradients are queried. However, these approaches either require large amounts of labeled data for offline training or access to exact reward gradients, limiting their applicability in black-box settings. We propose BReaD (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model), a guidance sampling framework for optimizing black-box rewards without assuming access to a labeled dataset or reward gradients. The proposed method uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective and actively queries labels for the generated samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the total-variation distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution. Using Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as guidance signals, our method balances exploration and exploitation during generation and enables the discovery of high-reward regions in the data space. Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks demonstrate that our framework can effectively optimize black-box rewards in low-data scenarios.

items.title: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer for End-to-End Image Generation
items.abstract: Pixel-space diffusion learns visual representations and image generation jointly in a single end-to-end training stage, without a separately pretrained visual encoder. However, plain pixel-space Transformers still trail leading two-stage latent diffusion models in generation quality and training efficiency. We hypothesize that part of this gap arises from retaining one token per patch throughout the backbone, which does not explicitly encourage a visual hierarchy that summarizes related content at progressively coarser levels. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), which progressively group related tokens and represent each group with a single token. The main Transformer bottleneck processes these compact group tokens, and ungrouping restores features to their original image positions. A compression budget regulates the average compression ratio across the batch, allowing group memberships and counts to vary across images and diffusion timesteps during both training and generation. The model exhibits emergent semantic structure, learning to group coherent objects and object parts without segmentation labels. In text-to-image generation, HiT further learns to group caption words with image patches depicting the same concepts, without region annotations. HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ and reaches comparable generation quality to JiT using approximately 40\% of its cumulative training FLOPs. For text-to-image generation, HiT exceeds UniLiP's average score across five benchmarks with roughly $6\times$ fewer denoiser parameters and $3\times$ fewer forward FLOPs. These results suggest that learning a visual hierarchy within the generator breaks down the barrier to stronger image generation without external visual pretraining.

items.title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
items.abstract: We present the first complete implementation of $β$-reduction in the untyped $λ$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $θ$--$γ$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.

items.title: Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
items.abstract: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

items.title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
items.abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

items.title: Feedback and Resource Competition in Incoherent Feedforward Loops: When Is Cumulative Dose Ordering Preserved?
items.abstract: Biochemical coupling can change the expression levels and timing predicted by an incoherent feedforward loop (IFFL) model without changing cumulative dose ordering. We derive ordering conditions using shared-production identities and Metzler comparison bounds, with tail guarantees beyond finite computation. A nonlinear example exhibits delayed slope reversal at a fixed dose, on an $O(1/η)$ timescale as pathway mismatch $η$ vanishes. At one fixed joint fit, validated bounds establish decreasing cumulative output across 20-100 ng nominal burden, from zero to full target loading, at every positive finite observation time for a translation-blocking model and an RNA-decay model. Full loading at 20 ng reduces 48-hour cumulative output by 13.35% and 10.18%, respectively, while endpoint concentration in the first model changes by only +0.15%. Preserved ordering therefore does not ensure quantitative agreement.

items.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
items.abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

items.title: Molecular memory reduces timing noise in stochastic gene expression
items.abstract: Fluctuations in gene expression affect the timing precision of downstream events triggered when a gene product reaches a critical threshold. The first-passage time (FPT) to this threshold characterizes the timing of such events. In conventional single-step birth--death models, reaction waiting times are exponentially distributed and hence memoryless. In this setting, FPT noise exhibits a U-shaped dependence on the threshold, attaining its minimum near one-half of the steady-state mean. However, mRNA production and degradation often involve multiple sequential steps, leading to hypoexponential distributions of mRNA production times and mRNA lifetimes. Here, we investigate how molecular memory arising from multistep mRNA production and degradation affects FPT statistics in bursty gene expression. We calculate FPT statistics in the small-noise limit. Both multistep mechanisms reduce FPT noise, but through distinct mechanisms. Multistep burst arrival reduces mRNA copy-number fluctuations, thereby suppressing timing noise. Multistep degradation instead reshapes transient accumulation dynamics, reducing relative timing noise even when steady-state mRNA noise increases. The threshold that minimizes FPT noise remains close to one-half of the steady-state mean, except for multistep burst arrival with constant burst sizes, for which it shifts to lower values. Stochastic simulations support the analytical predictions within their regimes of validity and show that these qualitative conclusions persist beyond the small-noise approximation.

items.title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus
items.abstract: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

items.title: Earth-strength magnetic-field axis modulates non-spatial probabilistic decision-making in humans
items.abstract: Magnetoreception has been primarily studied in orientation and navigation, but whether Earth-strength magnetic fields influence non-spatial decisions remains unclear. Evidence for human magnetic responses is limited, and the transduction mechanism is unknown. Using a Go stone selection paradigm in which near-zero geomagnetic field and Larmor-frequency conditions previously showed lower black stone rates, we tested whether non-spatial choice depends on magnetic-field geometry. Fasted men played in pairs under ten static two-seat configurations varied component-wise at near-constant north-seat intensity. The north-seat black stone rate was lower under the two configurations with horizontal fields transverse to the geomagnetic field than under the other eight, which did not differ detectably. The difference emerged promptly, without evidence of outcome-driven learning or configuration-dependent associations with the partner's preceding actions, and process analyses linked it to the joint parity-choice outcome without isolating either step. A Larmor-frequency difference observed over the ambient field was not detected over horizontal-only or vertical-only backgrounds, suggesting a potential magnetoresponsive axis, although the background difference was statistically unresolved. Frequency, light-spectrum, and posture analyses support a radical-pair mechanism as a leading working hypothesis. These findings associate the geomagnetic field axis with human non-spatial choice, providing a paradigm linking magnetic sensing to decision processes.

items.title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
items.abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability. We then demonstrate that random internal perturbations allow individual bonds to estimate their mechanical dominance and locally adjust their stiffnesses to restore learning capacity. However, the forces associated with active learning bias these local measurements and interfere with restoration. Separating learning and repair into wake-like and sleep-like phases removes this interference and improves continual-learning performance. Our results suggest that the need for offline restorative phases can emerge from the mechanics of physical learning, even in systems without biological components.

items.title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
items.abstract: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.

items.title: Near Resonance, Less Ordered: Radius and Mass Ordering in Compact Multi-planet Systems
items.abstract: Compact multi-planet systems exhibit a tendency for planetary radii to follow ordered sequences with orbital position, suggesting that these non-random patterns preserve a fossil record of their formation. Here, we investigate whether ordering of planet radii and masses with orbital period is related to proximity to mean-motion resonances. We compare near-resonant and non-resonant systems using complementary rank- and inversion-based measures of ordering, while accounting for differences in planet multiplicity and uncertainties in the measured planetary properties. We find that radii and masses are less monotonically ordered in near-resonant systems than in non-resonant systems, with the primary radius analysis providing stronger evidence than the mass analysis. This result is opposite to the naive expectation that dynamical instabilities should erase the primordial ordering of initially resonant systems and leave non-resonant systems in a more disordered state.

items.title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
items.abstract: For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $Δ= [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not. We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $π$ to $π\circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $Δ(π) = -Δ(π\circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in. The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $σ$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.

items.title: Observational diagnostics of external photoevaporation at millimetre wavelengths
items.abstract: External photoevaporation is increasingly recognised as an important influence on protoplanetary disk evolution. However, there are no established molecular line diagnostics that can reliably distinguish external irradiation from variations in intrinsic stellar and disk properties. We use a large grid of thermochemical models to predict the fluxes of 48 transitions from eight species observable with ALMA, spanning a wide range of system properties and external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0. At fixed stellar and disk properties, all transitions generally brighten with increasing FUV field strength. HCO+ and CO fluxes increase monotonically in virtually all disks, whereas lower-excitation lines, particularly those of C2H and N2H+, respond weakly and non-monotonically. However, variations in stellar mass and disk size introduce substantial degeneracies, limiting the usefulness of individual line fluxes as tracers of external irradiation. We therefore assess all pairwise line flux ratios, which can significantly reduce these degeneracies, evaluating their correlation with the external field, the magnitude of their change across the FUV range, and predicted ALMA detectability. We identify 135 promising ratios, including several combining strong FUV sensitivity and high detectability with efficient single-tuning ALMA observations. The strongest diagnostics either contrast high- and low-excitation lines of the same or co-spatial species (e.g. CO J=8-7/J=1-0), probing different regions of the photoevaporative wind, or pair an FUV-sensitive wind tracer with comparatively insensitive emission arising closer to the disk (e.g. HCO+ J=3-2/C2H N=3-2). Our results provide a framework for identifying externally photoevaporating systems from spatially unresolved emission and constraining their incident FUV field strengths.

items.title: A novel method for dust evolution in protoplanetary disks and a new criterion for gap opening
items.abstract: We present the Grain Residence-Time Method (GRTM), a computationally efficient particle-tracking approach for studying dust evolution and trapping in protoplanetary disks. By reconstructing steady-state dust distributions from particle residence times, this method provides a way to obtain radial dust surface density profiles without directly evolving the dust as a fluid. We compare the GRTM with dust profiles computed via standard methods using the $\texttt{FARGO3D}$ code, which models the dust as a pressureless fluid, and find very good agreement over a wide range of parameter space. Finally, we investigate how dust gap formation depends on the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$) and Stokes number ($\mathrm{St}$), through a parameter study, establishing an empirical criterion for dust gap opening. In doing so, we have discovered a new regime of gap opening for small grains with $St \lesssim 10^{-2}$ and for planet mass well below Jupiter's, which is likely very relevant for gaps seen in ALMA images.

items.title: New Historical Guest-Star Candidates from Reassessed Chinese Records: Lunar Occultation of Planets
items.abstract: Ancient Chinese records of lunar occultations of planets have been used to test planetary theories and investigate long-term changes in Earth's rotation. However, certain records contain identification errors whose origins remain poorly understood; we propose that some of these errors may arise from misidentifying guest stars, such as novae or supernovae, as planets. We analyzed 67 errata on lunar occultations of planets from Liu Ci-Yuan's (2015) monograph using modern ephemerides and the open-source Python package \texttt{occultsky}, publicly available on GitHub. Using recorded dates and dynastic capital coordinates, we constructed observing windows anchored at solar noon and extending by $\pm 1$ day. Each window covered the preceding and recorded nights because the date may be off by one day. For each of the 67 records, we cataloged the apparent right ascension and declination $(α, δ)$ at the midpoint of the Moon's visibility window on each candidate night. The band swept by the lunar disk confines a possible transient to a narrow region a few degrees across; these midpoint coordinates serve as proxies for the implied guest-star positions. The catalog supplies candidate positions rather than identifications, enabling remnant and compact-object searches to test the guest-star hypothesis directly. If associations are established, these records could become dated guest-star candidates, and their dates could anchor remnant ages.

items.title: Planet Formation in a Warped Disc: Gravitational Instability and Misaligned Infall
items.abstract: We perform three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to investigate the impact of misaligned infall on a gravitationally unstable protoplanetary disc. The interaction between the disc and the infalling gas does not occur uniformly across all radii. As infall impacts the outer disc first, the outer disc experiences stronger torques than the inner disc, resulting in a warped disc where the angular momentum vector of the disc varies with radius. The surrounding infalling gas reprocesses stellar irradiation and re-emits it back towards the disc, resulting in a warmer disc. The higher temperatures cause the disc to become more gravitationally stable resulting in weaker spiral arms. However, over time, infall also continuously increases the disc mass, gradually altering the local conditions and strengthening gravitational instabilities despite the azimuthally averaged Toomre $Q$ indicating that the disc is stable against gravitational instability. Eventually, one of the spiral arms fragments, forming a giant planet by gravitational instability in a disc warped by misaligned infall. Hence, the impact of infall on gravitational instability in general will vary depending on the infall and disc properties due to the balance between the stabilising and destabilising effects. We also find that infall alters the expected signatures of gravitationally unstable discs by introducing asymmetries in scattered-light, continuum, and molecular line emission.

items.title: Crowd model with anticipation and interactions: an exclusion process based mean-field game
items.abstract: Mean-field games (MFG) is a powerful framework to describe competitive optimization processes. A natural field of application is crowd dynamics, where pedestrians are considered to optimize their path, while interacting with the others. Despite its success to incorporate anticipation in describing pedestrian behavior, the mean-field games framework neglects microscopic granular effects, rendering its results less realistic in various applications (bottlenecks, evacuations etc.). In this work, we consider an explicitly interacting microscopic model, namely an asymmetric simple exclusion process and derive the corresponding mean-field game. This mean-field game is applied to an evacuation setting and the differences from the standard MFG based on non-interacting Langevin dynamics, as well as the correlations induced by the granular interactions are discussed.

items.title: Unveiling the mutual inclination distribution in astrometric surveys
items.abstract: Mutual inclination in three (or more) body systems (triple stars, circumbinary planets, multi-planetary systems, etc.) is a tracer of their formation and evolution. Gaia Data Release 4 will provide for the first time a catalog of orbital solutions for three-body systems. Because astrometry is only sensitive to the motion in the plane of the sky, there is a degeneracy in the orbital solutions leading to two possible solutions for the mutual inclination in three-body systems. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian framework to circumvent this degeneracy and unveil the mutual inclination distribution in the population. We tested our methods on simulated datasets, and showed that it reliably recovered the injected mutual inclination distributions in various cases. The method is thus promising for the statistical analysis of Gaia DR4 three-body systems.

items.title: 3D and 2D Radiation Non-ideal MHD modeling of the decay of FUor outbursts
items.abstract: FU Orionis (FUor) outbursts are high-accretion events in protoplanetary disks thought to be driven by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). Although these outbursts span a wide range of observed durations and can thermally process and potentially transport disk material, the physical processes governing their decay remain poorly understood. We present a three-dimensional radiative non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation of the decay of an MRI-driven FUor outburst, complemented by a suite of two-dimensional models that explore its dependence on disk properties. During the decay, rings and gaps form naturally within the inner disk. Magnetic flux preferentially concentrates in the gaps, while the rings remain comparatively weakly magnetized. We show that MRI-active rings act as ``magnetic dams,'' confining magnetic flux within adjacent gaps. As the rings cool below the MRI activation temperature, non-ideal MHD effects decouple the gas from the magnetic field, allowing the trapped flux to diffuse outward. This outward diffusion can sometimes transiently reactivate MRI in neighboring rings, producing localized reheating events that we term ``Reactivation.'' By comparing otherwise identical two- and three-dimensional simulations, we find that MRI heating is systematically less efficient in two dimensions, leading to outburst durations shorter by a factor of $\sim3$--4. Our model suite further shows that the decay timescale depends primarily on the disk surface density and distance from the central star, with only a weak dependence on the magnetic field strength. We further derive an empirical relation linking the outburst duration to these quantities.

items.title: Exomoons and Exorings with the Habitable Worlds Observatory. III. Icy Moons and Rings Often Outshine Their Planets
items.abstract: If we could observe the Solar System's giant planets with the upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), the dominant sources of reflected near-infrared light would not always be the planets themselves. In fact, the brightest sources are split roughly evenly between the giants and their icy companions: at the locations of the giant planets, the dominant point sources would be Jupiter, Saturn's rings, Uranus, and Triton (Neptune's icy moon). Motivated by these Solar System cases in which rings or moons outshine their host planets, we investigate the detectability of analogous exomoons and exorings with HWO. We compute the expected signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) for moons and rings with the same albedos as their Solar System counterparts over a range of sizes, system distances, and star to planet+moon or star to planet+ring separations. We find that reflected light from Triton-analog exomoons and Saturn-analog exorings is detectable with HWO over a broad parameter space. In the nearest systems, icy Titan-sized moons are detectable at star-moon separations of ~2 AU and icy Earth-sized moons out to ~6 AU. Moreover, Saturn-like exorings are likely to be the brightest point sources in many extrasolar systems, capable of greatly outshining any planets, while remaining potentially detectable at system distances out to 100 pc. These results highlight the need for further work to develop methods for identifying and disentangling exoring and exomoon signatures from exoplanet signals in HWO observations, where these sources will be blended and spatially unresolved.

items.title: Does succinic acid treatment improve metabolic health in a male murine model of early ageing?
items.abstract: Ageing associates with obesity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired glucose homeostasis. Previously, we documented that succinic acid (SA) treatment improves mitochondrial function and adiposity; however, the effects on ageing are unknown. Therefore, we determined the effect of SA treatment on metabolic health in 19 aged male mice (Age; 16 months), randomized to receive vehicle (Veh, n = 8) or SA (n = 11) and compared to young controls (Young; 6 months) (n = 24). After 6 weeks of treatment, insulin tolerance (IT), glucose tolerance (GT), pyruvate tolerance (PT) and physical activity (PA) were assessed. Body mass (BM), epididymal white adipose tissue (EWAT) and heart mass (HM) were measured at study end. Soleus muscle and EWAT underwent mitochondrial respirometry. Mice in the Age group had higher HM and EWAT (both P 0.05). PA was ∼50% lower in the Age group (8778 ± 5774 vs. 4132 ± 1523 rev/day), though Age-SA had 48% higher PA (Age-SA 6118 ± 2203 rev/day). SA treatment did not affect BM (37.8 ± 2.7 vs. 37.7 ± 3.2 g), EWAT (1.4 ± 0.4 vs. 1.3 ± 0.4 g) or HM (0.17 ± 0.01 vs. 0.19 ± 0.04 g, Age-Veh vs. Age-SA, all P > 0.05, respectively). GT AUC differed by group (P = 0.019), with Age-SA having lower AUC (Young 47120 ± 8751 vs. Age-SA 37180 ± 5383 AUC, P 0.22). SA reversed the age-associated reduction in complex I+II-driven respiration in adipose (P < 0.05). Ageing elevated adiposity, impaired pyruvate tolerance and reduced adipose mitochondrial function, though SA was partially restorative in mitigating these age-associated effects, warranting further study.

items.title: Predicting others' actions through one's own motor style: Behavioral and neural evidence for a kinematic similarity effect.
items.abstract: Predictive processes during action observation are known to benefit from motor expertise, but it remains unclear which factors drive successful prediction in everyday actions, where everyone can be considered an "expert." We hypothesized that prediction accuracy is modulated not only by expertise per se, but by the degree of fine-grained kinematic overlap between the observer's and the agent's motor repertoire, here operationalized as motor similarity. In Study 1 (N = 90, action execution), we introduced a continuous, multidimensional, kinematics-based metric of inter-individual motor distance, and used it to quantify each participant's motor style relative to others. In Study 2 (N = 20, behavioral) and Study 3 (N = 21, behavioral and EEG), we then tailored action-observation tasks to each participant by selecting movements that varied parametrically in similarity to their own motor style, while verifying that stimuli across similarity levels carried equivalent amounts of action-relevant kinematic information. Behavioral results consistently showed that motor similarity enhances perceptual prediction: observers were more accurate when viewing actions that were closer to their individual motor style. Electrophysiological data further revealed that beta-band modulation, a neural signature associated with prediction uncertainty, is amplified over sensorimotor regions when participants observed more dissimilar movements. Together, these findings demonstrate that the degree of agent-observer kinematic overlap is a key determinant of prediction processes, extending beyond traditional expertise-based accounts.

items.title: Triggered electromyography-guided progressive fascicular subdivision to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in conjoined twin spinal cord separation: a dual-configuration case series.
items.abstract: Purpose Surgical separation of conjoined twins with fused caudal spinal cords requires identification of a safe neural cleavage plane, yet anatomical boundaries are often indistinct. Triggered electromyography (tEMG) has been used to determine nerve root ownership, and iterative subdivision with sequential stimulation has been reported in pygopagus twins, but the sequence and its endpoint have not been standardized. This study describes a tEMG-guided progressive fascicular subdivision approach to identify a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in two conjoined twin configurations. Methods We monitored two cases (pygopagus and ischiopagus) using multimodal intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, including tEMG, transcranial motor evoked potentials, somatosensory evoked potentials, and free-running electromyography. A dual-twin color-coded electrode configuration enabled simultaneous independent mapping of both nervous systems. Progressive fascicular subdivision with re-stimulation of each bundle was performed until a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval was identified. Results Case 1 involved pygopagus twins with a fused conus medullaris at S2. Case 2 involved ischiopagus twins with syringomyelia involving both spinal cords and an anterior sacral meningocele. In both cases, progressive fascicular subdivision identified a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval, which guided microsurgical separation. Motor function and anal tone were unchanged at 6-month follow-up. Conclusion Triggered electromyography-guided progressive fascicular subdivision identified a bilaterally tEMG-silent interval in both pygopagus and ischiopagus configurations, including one with complex intrinsic spinal cord pathology. This interval reflects absence of detectable somatic motor activation in the monitored muscles and does not exclude sensory or autonomic fibers; its value as an intraoperative reference requires validation in larger series.

items.title: Using binocular rivalry to assess cultural differences in spatial-frequency processing of faces.
items.abstract: Cultural experience shapes attention, memory, and some aspects of visual processing, but it remains unclear whether it influences perceptual selection when incompatible images compete for awareness. We preregistered a binocular rivalry study to test whether Eastern and Western observers differ in the relative weighting of low- versus high-spatial-frequency information during initial perceptual competition. Forty-nine Western participants (U.S.-born, ≤ 2 years abroad) and 43 Eastern participants (recent East Asian arrivals, ≤ 5 years in the U.S.) viewed dichoptic pairs of spatially filtered faces (Albert Einstein, Marilyn Monroe). Image size was varied across five levels to shift retinal spatial frequency content, allowing estimation of each observer's "balance point"-the size at which low-pass and high-pass filtered faces were equally dominant. In a second component of the study, a filtered image of one face was pitted against an unfiltered image of the other face to assess the competitive strength of isolated spatial-frequency bands against broadband-image rivals. Increasing retinal image size enhanced the dominance of high-pass information. However, mean balance points did not differ between cultural groups, and no reliable association emerged with measures of participants' levels of acculturation or cultural values. The results suggest that the initial outcome of perceptual competition in binocular rivalry is largely independent of cultural background and that the mechanisms governing this competition operate similarly across observers from different cultural backgrounds. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The study was preregistered online ( https://osf.io/pgyqv ). Final analyses deviated from the plan in that we used the quickpsy Package in R (instead of fitting a 2nd-degree polynomial using MATLAB's curve fitting toolbox) to generate a cumulative normal curve which better characterized the relationship between image sizes and task performance. This also allowed us to use t tests rather than ANOVAs. In addition, sample sizes exceeded the original plan to allow for exclusions and for exploratory individual difference analyses. After reviewing the stereopsis test measure-but without comparing data from the two groups-the team decided that getting six of the nine circles correct (instead of the preregistered criterion requiring nine out of nine circles) would be sufficient to demonstrate stereopsis. We did not use response times as an exclusion criterion for individual trials, and our additional exploratory analyses focused on the self-report measures of culture rather than those included in the preregistration. We deemed these exploratory analyses to be more of interest, given the focus of the paper, than those originally planned or the sample characteristics did not support further follow-up analyses (e.g., uneven distributions of urban/rural background and gender). Data and code are available at https://osf.io/st473 and https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ST473 .

items.title: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths.
items.abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

items.title: Dietary interventions and stroke clinical outcomes: a systematic review.
items.abstract: Optimal nutrition is biologically essential for supporting neural repair mechanisms post-stroke, yet clinical guidelines provide limited and non-specific dietary recommendations that are largely extrapolated from primary cardiovascular prevention rather than stroke recovery populations. To systematically review and synthesise evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of food-based or whole-diet interventions on clinical outcomes in adults with stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA), including disability, neurological function, cognition, mood, quality of life, and stroke recurrence. Following Cochrane and PRISMA guidelines, four databases (Medline, Embase, CINAHL, CENTRAL) were searched to February 2026 for RCTs testing oral dietary interventions (≥4 weeks) in adult stroke/TIA survivors. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2. Eight RCTs (n=15,974) were included (1 low risk, 6 some concerns, 1 high risk). Quantitative meta-analysis was precluded by marked heterogeneity. Interventions included salt substitution (n=2), Mediterranean diets (n=2), ketogenic diet (n=1), partial meal replacement (n=1), Trigona honey (n=1), and soy milk (n=1). Reduced-sodium salt substitution decreased stroke recurrence (RR 0.86, 95%CI 0.77-0.95) and mortality (RR 0.88, 95%CI 0.82-0.96) in large Phase III trials, while Mediterranean diets improved quality of life (EQ-5D mean difference: 10.1, 95%CI 1.8-18.4). For functional recovery, small Phase I/II pilot trials yielded exploratory, domain-specific proof-of-concept signals (e.g., post-exercise soymilk enhancing walking performance; Trigona honey improving MoCA scores), but were constrained by high susceptibility to Type I errors and effect size overestimation. Ketogenic diet improved NIHSS (5±2 vs 7±2, p<0.01) and disability (mRS: 2±1 vs 3±1, p<0.05), but was accompanied by high adverse event rates (keto-flu 25%, GI distress 15%, hyperlipidemia 10%). Salt substitution and Mediterranean diets show clear promise for secondary prevention and recovery. Given the limited and heterogeneous evidence base, high-quality, phase-specific RCTs are urgently needed to establish stroke-specific nutrition strategies.

items.title: Health-related quality of life in patients with solid cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors: the ARON-MOUSEION-18 systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Background Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) contributes to the value of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), but assessment and reporting remain heterogeneous. Methods This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261330878). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for RCTs of adults with solid tumors comparing ICI-based regimens with non-ICI controls and reporting global HRQoL with the EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL scale or EQ-5D-3L/5L visual analogue scale (VAS). Pooling required a visit-specific adjusted between-group estimate with a 95% confidence interval (CI) or standard error. Random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood, Hartung-Knapp adjustment) were used. Clinical relevance was assessed using instrument-specific MID benchmarks. Results Eighty-two RCTs were included: 42 in the quantitative and 40 in the narrative synthesis, 40 reported EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL, 10 EQ-5D-3L VAS, and 14 EQ-5D-5L VAS. All pooled trials evaluated anti-PD-1-based regimens. The pooled LSMD for EORTC QLQ-C30 GHS/QoL was 1.78 points (95% CI 0.71-2.86; p = 0.002; I2 =71.9%). Neither EQ-5D VAS differ significantly. Most trial-level estimates were below the MID, and no trial showed clinically meaningful deterioration. Favorable estimates were concentrated in open-label active-control, advanced/metastatic and lung cancer trials. Conclusion Anti-PD-1-based therapy results in no clinically important difference in global HRQoL compared with non-ICI controls: the small average advantage is below the MID and concentrated in open-label active-control trials. Interpretation is shaped by trial design, comparator, setting, assessment timing, and incomplete PRO reporting. Standardized PRO reporting is needed across cancer settings and ICI classes.

items.title: The Clinimetric Spectrum of Poor Response After Treatment for Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy.
items.abstract: Introduction/aims Clinicians regularly modify treatment in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) because of insufficient response, yet it is unclear how changes over time in the recommended outcome measures inform these decisions. We therefore explored which changes were observed in patients deemed to have an insufficient treatment response. Methods We selected patients with CIDP who were previously included in various prospective studies, in whom first-line treatment was changed within 6 months due to deterioration or insufficient improvement. Changes in two disability and two impairment measures were analyzed according to commonly used minimal clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds. Results We included 16 patients. Median time to treatment change was 12 weeks (IQR 6 to 19). In seven patients (44%), treatment change coincided with deterioration on all available outcome measures, and this occurred within 12 weeks of treatment in 6 patients. Earlier change was associated with more severe baseline disability and impairment, and greater magnitude of deterioration. In seven patients (44%), treatment was changed despite (limited) improvement on one or two outcome measures; all of these observations occurred after 12 weeks. Discussion Earlier treatment change seemed to be associated with clear deterioration on most outcome measures, while later treatment changes were mainly associated with insufficient improvement, reflected by a combination of improvement and worsening in different clinical outcome measures. Our findings suggest that poor response to treatment requires a nuanced consideration of multiple outcome measures, taking the magnitude and consistency of change into account in relation to treatment duration.

items.title: Beyond memory strengthening: noradrenergic control of memory specificity.
items.abstract: Emotionally significant events are typically remembered better and for longer than mundane experiences. This emotional memory enhancement critically depends on arousal-induced norepinephrine release within the brain. Beyond memory strengthening, recent work shows that noradrenergic activity also shapes the specificity, detailedness, and temporal precision of memories during both early consolidation and systems consolidation. In this review, we synthesize recent findings from human and animal research spanning molecular, circuit, systems, and behavioral mechanisms to propose an integrative framework for how emotional arousal-induced noradrenergic activity affects neural systems that regulate memory specificity and systems consolidation dynamics. The proposed framework refines current models of memory under emotional arousal and may have relevant implications for stress-related psychopathologies.
