items.title: Spine shortening osteotomy improves gait quality after one year in tethered cord syndrome: a retrospective case series.
items.abstract: Objective Tethered cord release (TCR) remains the gold standard treatment for tethered cord syndrome (TCS), yet repeat TCRs often fail to restore neurological function. Spine shortening osteotomy (SSO) has been proposed as an alternative for revision untethering or complex tethering anatomies, but its effect on ambulatory performance has not been quantified. This study evaluates whether SSO improves walking function in patients with recurrent or complex TCS using instrumented gait analysis (IGA). Methods A retrospective cohort of all patients undergoing SSO at Amsterdam Medical Centre between 2012 and 2022 was assembled. Indications were revision surgery or anatomically complex tethering. Preoperative and 12-month postoperative gait assessments employed two-dimensional IGA. Standardized video recordings yielded the Edinburgh Visual Gait Score (EVGS), walking speed, and kinematic variables . Results SSO was performed in 12 patients (mean age 38 ± 14 years); complete gait data were available for nine. Median EVGS improved significantly from 13 to 7 (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z = -2.38, p = 0.018). Walking speed increased not significantly by 0.10 m.s -1 (z = -1.661, p = 0.097), four patients (44%) experienced a clinically meaningful gain >= 0.1 m.s -1 . No significant changes were observed in secondary kinematic parameters. Conclusions SSO provided improvement in gait quality in patients with recurrent or complex TCS, while effects on speed are heterogeneous. Limitations include the small, heterogeneous cohort and reliance on 2-D analysis. Larger, multicenter studies are needed to confirm these findings, refine patient selection, and inform guideline development for SSO in TCS.

items.title: Foraging reveals systematic suboptimality that is amplified in a mouse model of Alzheimer disease.
items.abstract: Adaptive decision-making extends beyond selecting among discrete alternatives. It requires the dynamic organization of actions as costs, opportunities, and goals evolve over time. Foraging captures this complexity in an evolutionarily conserved behavior that integrates spatial, temporal, and reward-related information across successive actions. These demands make foraging an ecologically grounded framework for investigating Alzheimer disease, in which spatial cognition, temporal organization, cost evaluation, and behavioral flexibility are frequently disrupted. We examined foraging-related action selection in control C57BL/6J mice and APP NL-G-F knock-in mice using a controlled task in which travel distance, food texture, and pellet size altered the costs and benefits of available strategies. Bayesian multinomial modeling showed that control mice flexibly redistributed their behavior across conditions, whereas APP NL-G-F mice showed impaired cost integration, increased withdrawal, and reduced behavioral flexibility rather than a generalized performance impairment. Comparison with a classical reward-rate-maximization benchmark revealed substantial suboptimality in both groups. Control mice selected the rate-maximizing behavior on 53% of trials, compared with 45% in APP NL-G-F mice and exhibited lower regret. These systematic departures suggest that behavior was shaped by cognitive, motivational, or contextual constraints not represented in the normative model, with Alzheimer-disease-relevant dysfunction associated with greater suboptimality. Group differences were greatest when optimal behavior was highly sensitive to competing costs. By preserving the distribution of behavior across strategies, this study establishes foraging-related action selection as a framework for detecting disease-associated disruptions that may be obscured by conventional measures of choice or overall task performance.

items.title: Signatures of Performance Monitoring in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder and At-risk Groups: Midfrontal Theta Predicts Divergent Behavioral Adaptation.
items.abstract: Background Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) has been robustly linked to increased performance monitoring, most consistently indexed by an increased error-related negativity (ERN). However, the role of response-related midfrontal theta oscillations, a key neural mechanism supporting cognitive control and behavioral adaptation, remains incompletely understood in OCD and at-risk populations. Methods EEG was recorded from 180 adults (46 OCD, 39 unaffected first-degree relatives, 39 with adverse childhood experiences, and 56 controls) during an arrowhead flanker task. Response-related midfrontal theta power (4-7 Hz) was investigated alongside behavioral indices, including error rates and post-error slowing. Group differences in neural and behavioral data, trial-wise theta-behavior relationship, and associations with clinical symptoms were investigated. Results Error-related increases in midfrontal theta were robust across participants. Relative to the combined non-OCD sample, individuals with OCD exhibited enhanced error-related theta power, while unaffected first-degree relatives and individuals with adverse childhood experiences did not differ from controls. Single-trial analyses revealed altered neural-behavioral coupling: greater theta predicted slower and less accurate performance on subsequent trials in OCD, and, contrarily, improved subsequent performance in controls. Consistent with these findings, individuals with OCD showed prolonged post-error slowing. Across participants, error rate and PES were associated with worry and depressive symptoms, whereas theta power was associated with age and depressive symptoms. Conclusions OCD is characterized by enhanced error-related midfrontal theta together with an altered association between neural error signals and adaptive behavioral adjustment. These findings suggest that abnormal performance monitoring in OCD reflects not only exaggerated error processing but also disrupted implementation of cognitive control.

items.title: Cerebellar anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) attenuates the decline in sequential prediction during social mentalizing.
items.abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests that the posterior cerebellum is critically involved in mentalizing, particularly through its role in extracting regularities from social action sequences and using them to predict others' actions and intentions, thereby supporting smoother and more coordinated social interactions. Previous work using a trait-prediction task found no significant behavioral effects of cerebellar anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), potentially because the relatively low task difficulty left limited room for stimulation-related improvements in performance. The present study therefore examined the effects of cerebellar anodal tDCS using a more difficult adaptation of the trait-prediction task. Using a double-blind sham-controlled protocol, 61 participants received either anodal stimulation (n = 31) or sham stimulation (n = 30) targeting the cerebellum before completing the adapted trait-prediction task. Results revealed that while accuracy scores remained stable for participants who received anodal stimulation, they decreased for participants who received sham stimulation. Reaction times decreased across trials in both stimulation conditions, with no significant difference between conditions. The findings suggest that cerebellar anodal tDCS attenuates the decline in the prediction of action sequences over time during social mentalizing, supporting a potential contribution of the cerebellum in sustaining predictive social sequencing.

items.title: From Variability to Synchrony: Non-linear Development of Auditory Neural Responses During the First Year of Life.
items.abstract: In humans, the first year of life is characterized by rapid developmental changes, including substantial brain maturation. As a result, neural responses to auditory stimuli undergo marked changes during this period. In this study, we followed 69 infants across their first year of life and recorded high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG) at 2 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months postpartum. Infants were presented with pure beep tones to examine the development of neural responses to auditory stimulation. We analyzed event-related potentials (ERPs), inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), and event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) responses to the beep tones and controlled for arousal state during stimulus presentation. We found that with increasing age, neural responses became more pronounced and showed reduced trial-to-trial variability. Phase synchronization increased from 2 weeks to later developmental stages in a broad low-frequency range (0.5 Hz to 13.6 Hz), indicating improved temporal alignment of brain responses over time. However, phase synchronization decreased from 6 to 12 months, suggesting a developmental transition towards more differentiated brain activity. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that auditory maturation during the first year of life follows a non-linear trajectory driven by dynamic changes in neural synchronization, reflecting the progressive refinement of functional neural circuits. Our results thus provide a critical benchmark for understanding the neural dynamics underlying sensory development during this period.

items.title: Neuropathic pain: Opportunities and challenges for immune-based therapeutics.
items.abstract: Neuropathic pain develops as a result of a lesion or a disease affecting the somatosensory nervous system and is associated with substantial disability, poor quality of life, and high health care costs. Current management is dominated by neuron-focused interventions that provide modest benefits and are often poorly tolerated. Accumulating evidence from experimental and clinical research implicates neuroimmune mechanisms in the development and persistence of neuropathic pain, yet their clinical relevance and therapeutic potential remain uncertain. In this review, we outline the latest clinical evidence on the contribution of immune processes to neuropathic pain and review interventions that act on neuroimmune mechanisms, including novel neuroimmunomodulation therapies. Focusing on human data, we outline key challenges and future directions for the field, including establishing whether observed neuroimmune changes cause neuropathic pain, designing trials that are explicitly equipped to investigate heterogeneity in treatment effects, and testing novel interventions.

items.title: Noncoding functions of FMR1 transcript in riboregulation of human neurodevelopment.
items.abstract: The noncoding functions of protein-coding messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are largely ignored. Here, we demonstrate an unexpected noncoding role of FMR1 mRNA in human neurodevelopment. A loss of FMR1 and its protein product, fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP), leads to the neurodevelopmental disorder fragile X syndrome (FXS). Neurons derived from FXS patients display hyperexcitability and immature morphology, whereas FMRP knockout (FMRP-KO) neurons that retain FMR1 transcript expression do not. Multi-omics analyses reveal key metabolic differences between FXS and FMRP-KO neurons. Although both FXS and FMRP-KO neurons exhibit reduced mitochondrial respiration, only FXS neurons exhibit elevated glycolysis. We further discover that the FMR1 transcript riboregulates the levels of the glycolytic enzyme lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) by inhibiting the binding of LDHA mRNA to insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 2 (IGF2BP2). Finally, the FMR1 transcript, independent of FMRP, rescues glycolytic and cellular deficits of FXS neurons. Together, these results suggest that FMR1 is a dual-function RNA in human neurodevelopment.

items.title: Association between the timing of low-dose aspirin and recurrence after simple coil embolization of small unruptured intracranial aneurysms.
items.abstract: To investigate factors associated with recurrence after low-dose aspirin combined with simple coil embolization for small unruptured intracranial aneurysms (SUNIA), with emphasis on aspirin timing. Single-center prospective cohort of 105 SUNIA patients (January 2022-June 2023), excluding stent-assisted cases. Patients received preoperative 3-day oral aspirin (n = 65) or intraoperative intravenous aspirin (n = 34), each followed by oral aspirin for 12 months per center protocol. Twelve-month follow-up compared recurrence rates. Univariate and exploratory multivariate Cox regression and bootstrap ROC analyses were performed. Ninety-nine patients formed the analysis set; six died before 12 months and were censored. Fourteen (14.1%) had recurrence. Crude 6-month recurrence was 0/65 versus 7/34 (20.6%; P < 0.001). Because six patients died before 12 months and were censored, 12-month recurrence was estimated by Kaplan-Meier: 6.5% (95% CI 2.5-16.4) in the preoperative 3-day group versus 30.2% (17.6-48.9) in the intraoperative group (log-rank P < 0.001). Exploratory multivariate Cox analysis (14 events, 5 covariates) identified the strongest association for intraoperative aspirin timing (HR = 5.52, 95% CI 1.63-18.69), followed by wide-neck aneurysm (HR = 3.65, 1.01-13.22), subtotal/partial embolization (HR = 3.42, 1.04-11.25), and elevated hs-CRP (HR = 1.34, 1.12-1.61); irregular aneurysm was not significant after adjustment (HR = 3.53, 95% CI 0.91-13.77). Combined exploratory ROC AUC was 0.882 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.769-0.967). Preoperative 3-day aspirin was associated with lower observed recurrence than intraoperative administration. Because allocation was not randomized and recurrence was ascertained with different imaging modalities across groups, this association cannot be separated from detection differences and cannot establish causality or justify routine protocol adoption.

items.title: Elevated concentrations of 78 Se and 208 Pb isotopes in cerebrospinal fluid but not in blood plasma from patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
items.abstract: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor neuron degeneration and muscle atrophy, ultimately leading to death through respiratory failure. In addition to genetic factors, environmental exposures have been investigated as potential ALS risk factors. Elevated concentrations of cadmium, lead and selenium have previously been detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood from ALS patients, suggesting an association between metal dysregulation and disease progression. Here, we conducted a detailed analysis of CSF and blood plasma from seven ALS patients and seven healthy controls, where samples were collected using ultraclean techniques. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) was used to measure isotopes of a wide range of elements. Significantly higher concentrations of 208Pb and 78Se (p < 0.01) were recorded in CSF but not in plasma of ALS patients compared to controls. Interestingly, no significant differences were observed for the 206Pb and 207Pb isotope concentrations as such. However, the 208Pb/207Pb ratio was elevated in CSF of ALS cases compared to controls, which might be due to biological isotope fractionation, or exposure to lead from different geological sources. Taken together, our data supports previous reports of Pb and Se contributing to ALS pathogenesis. The results also suggest that investigating metal dyshomeostasis at the isotope level can improve understanding of disease pathologies, especially for conditions and diseases where metal exposure is a risk factor.

items.title: Clinical characteristics and oncologic outcomes of young adults with squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue: A multicenter retrospective study.
items.abstract: The prognostic significance of young age in squamous cell carcinoma of the mobile tongue and floor of mouth remains controversial. We compared clinicopathological characteristics and oncologic outcomes between young and older patients undergoing surgery. This multicenter retrospective study included patients treated with primary curative-intent surgery at 13 high-volume European cancer centers between 2012 and 2022. Patients were stratified as young (≤40 years) or older (≥55 years); those aged 41-54 years were excluded. Clinicopathological variables, recurrence, overall survival (OS), and disease-specific survival (DSS) were compared. Among 375 patients, 133 were young and 242 older. Younger patients were more often never smokers (67.2% vs 47.5%; p = 0.001), non-drinkers (95.1% vs 74.5%; p < 0.001), and had early pT disease (62.9% vs 48.3%; p = 0.009) and lower tumor grade (p = 0.041). Pathological nodal involvement, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, and extranodal extension were comparable. Younger patients had higher odds of positive margins (18.3% vs 10.5%; OR 1.898; p = 0.034). In advanced pT disease, perineural invasion was more frequent in younger patients (71.4% vs 54.5%; p = 0.042). OS, DSS, and recurrence did not differ significantly between groups. After adjustment for pT, pN, tobacco exposure, and alcohol consumption, age was not associated with OS or DSS. Young adults show lower tobacco and alcohol exposure and more favorable local tumor features without improved oncologic outcomes. Young age should not be considered an inherently favorable prognostic factor. Further translational studies are warranted to clarify the biological mechanisms underlying early-onset disease.

items.title: Longitudinal associations between maltreatment, bullying victimization and externalizing problems in children and adolescents: Evidence from Brazilian High Risk Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Background Empirical evidence consistently demonstrates elevated rates of maltreatment and bullying victimization among children and adolescents with externalizing problems. However, most research has been conducted in high-income countries (HICs), with limited understanding of these developmental processes in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Objective To examine longitudinal associations between maltreatment, bullying victimization, and externalizing problems in an LMIC context. Participants and setting Participants were 2511 children and adolescents (aged 6-18 years) from the Brazilian High-Risk Cohort Study. Methods Caregiver reports were used to assess study variables across three waves. A Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) was applied to data from T1 (mean age = 10.20, SD = 1.90), T2 (mean age = 13.50, SD = 1.92), and T3 (mean age = 16.58, SD = 1.03). Results At the within-person level, both maltreatment at T1 (β = 0.08, p = .024) and bullying victimization at T1 (β = 0.08, p = .016) were associated with externalizing problems at T2. Maltreatment at T2 was positively associated with externalizing problems at T3 in males (β = 0.14, p = .031), and negatively associated in females (β = -0.26, p = .003). Conclusions Our study highlights longitudinal associations between maltreatment, bullying victimization, and externalizing problems, which vary between sexes and developmental stages. These findings underscore the importance of prioritizing child and adolescent mental health in Brazil. More broadly, the results highlight the need for research in other LMICs to identify both global and context-specific mechanisms underlying the development of externalizing problems.

items.title: Microstate-specific functional connectivity in alcohol use disorder using resting-state EEG.
items.abstract: Introduction Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is often described as a "disconnection syndrome", reflecting neural dysfunction associated with chronic alcohol use. However, previous studies on functional connectivity of resting-state EEG (rsEEG) in AUD have reported inconsistent findings, possibly due to overlooking the brain's dynamic nature. Methods We examined rsEEG in 26 young adults with AUD and 35 healthy controls (HC), using microstate analysis to characterise transient brain states and to estimate functional connectivity within each state. Results Although microstate map topologies were comparable between the two groups, the temporal dynamics of the AUD group were biased towards microstates C and D. Particularly within microstate C, the AUD group showed significantly greater functional connectivity across most frontal-occipital channel pairs, whereas significantly reduced functional connectivity was observed in the interhemispheric channel pairs. Moreover, compared with conventional functional connectivity estimates, microstate-specific functional connectivity yielded superior classification performance in distinguishing the two groups. In addition, the AUD group showed less stable hub-like properties in microstate C, indicating diminished network efficiency. Conclusions Our findings suggest that transient EEG properties, exemplified by microstate-specific functional connectivity, provide informative neural markers for characterising the impact of alcohol use on the brain.

items.title: A Plasma eMTBR-Tau Immunoassay for Detection of Advanced Insoluble Tau Pathology.
items.abstract: Blood biomarkers that reflect neurofibrillary tau burden, a defining hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD), remain limited. Endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau 243 (eMTBR-tau243) has shown promise when measured by mass spectrometry; a scalable immunoassay could broaden research access and support clinical evaluation. To determine whether plasma levels of eMTBR-tau measured by a novel immunoassay are associated with tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology defined by neuropathology and tau positron emission tomography (PET). This cross-sectional study included brain donors with antemortem plasma from 2 US autopsy cohorts, and individuals with plasma samples and tau PET from 2 imaging cohorts in Canada and Sweden, with visits between 2002 and 2025 depending on the cohort. Plasma eMTBR-tau measured with an immunoassay and eMTBR-tau243 measured with mass spectrometry. Plasma eMTBR-tau levels across neuropathologic Braak neurofibrillary tangle stages (I-VI, ranging from tangles confined to the entorhinal region to widespread neocortical tangles) and tau-PET Braak stages (0-VI), expressed as fold changes. Correlations with regional tau-PET standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs; higher values indicating more tau tangles), discrimination of regional tau-PET positivity (area under the curve [AUC]), and correlation with mass spectrometry-based eMTBR-tau243. The study included 728 participants in 4 cohorts (median age by cohort, 71.0-83.5 years; 41.3%-56.6% female). In the 2 autopsy cohorts (n = 241 and n = 240), eMTBR-tau age- and sex-adjusted geometric means were 0.0021 pg/mL and 0.0040 pg/mL, respectively, at Braak stages I-II vs 0.107 pg/mL and 0.101 pg/mL at Braak stage VI (50.5-fold [95% CI, 26.3-97.0] and 25.2-fold [95% CI, 15.8-40.3] higher for stage VI vs stages I-II; P < .001 for both cohorts). In one imaging cohort (n = 99), compared with tau-PET Braak stage 0, eMTBR-tau levels were 11.0-fold (95% CI, 6.9-17.5) higher at stages III-IV and 59.9-fold (95% CI, 39.5-90.7) higher at stages V-VI. Among participants positive for amyloid-β (Aβ) in another imaging cohort (n = 50), the Spearman rank correlations for eMTBR-tau with tau-PET SUVRs were ρ = 0.52 (95% CI, 0.28-0.70) in Braak regions I-II, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.61-0.86) in regions III-IV, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.75-0.91) in regions V-VI (all P < .001). Immunoassay and mass spectrometry measurements were strongly correlated (Spearman rank correlation, ρ = 0.93 in all participants [n = 108] and ρ = 0.96 in Aβ-positive participants [n = 54]) and discriminated tau-PET positivity similarly (n = 102; AUC range, 0.96-0.99 for the immunoassay and 0.97-0.99 for mass spectrometry). A plasma eMTBR-tau immunoassay identified neocortical tau pathology in autopsy and tau-PET cohorts and correlated strongly with mass spectrometry measurements, a proof of principle that eMTBR-tau can be measured by immunoassay as a marker of advanced neurofibrillary tangle pathology.

items.title: Cross-Domain Transfer of Depression Voice Biomarkers Depends on the Outcome Instrument: Leakage-Controlled Cross-Sectional Evaluation Study.
items.abstract: Voice-based depression screening is commercializing rapidly, yet whether voice biomarkers generalize across clinical settings is largely untested. Generalization is usually framed as a question about populations, but it is also a question about the outcome instrument a model is scored against, an effect confounded with other between-study differences in the literature. We tested whether depression voice biomarkers transfer between perinatal and general-psychiatric speech in both directions under strict leakage control and whether transfer depends on the screening instrument. In a cross-sectional, online US study, 390 pregnant participants at a mean of 22 (SD 1) weeks' gestation (analytical sample n=316) participated in 446 sessions; each participant provided 4 voice recordings and completed the modified 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) and modified 9-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (mEPDS-9). We extracted 375 acoustic descriptors and 330-dimensional Population Dynamics Foundation Model community-health embeddings. Discrimination area under the curve (AUC) was assessed under leakage-controlled cross-validation, with feature and classifier selection inside training folds only and a permutation negative-control harness, across a prespecified grid of 4 speech tasks×4 outcome definitions. The prenatal-trained model was applied to 2 general-psychiatric corpora (Distress Analysis Interview Corpus-Wizard-of-Oz, n=189; Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, n=219) under pure held-out inference, and the open-source Kintsugi Depression/Anxiety Model (DAM), trained on 35,000 individuals, was applied to all 3 cohorts without refitting, with Benjamini-Hochberg multiplicity control. In the prenatal cohort, the preregistered outcome was at chance (AUC 0.494, 95% CI 0.431-0.560); no cell in the 16-cell grid survived adjustment under either modeling paradigm. The prenatal-trained model did not transfer to either general-psychiatric corpus (AUCs 0.505 and 0.478). Reverse transfer depended on the screening instrument. The DAM reached an AUC of 0.706 to 0.708 on general-psychiatric speech. In the same participants, it performed at chance against the PHQ-8 (AUC 0.510, 95% CI 0.411-0.609) but discriminated against the mEPDS-9 (AUC 0.645, 95% CI 0.541-0.744), a paired difference of 0.135 (95% CI 0.019-0.248; unadjusted post hoc P=0.02). Exploratory item-level analysis suggests a mechanism: the DAM tracked affective-distress items (crying r=0.26, sadness r=0.21, and overwhelmed r=0.20) but not somatic PHQ-8 items; only crying survived adjustment across 17 tests. Transfer varied by elicitation task (pregnancy narrative 0.653, 95% CI 0.550-0.753; open-ended speech 0.597, 95% CI 0.486-0.699; scripted reading 0.544, 95% CI 0.434-0.651), though these were not formally compared. Cross-domain comparison showed a compound shift: population, elicitation task, and outcome instrument differed together, while only the instrument could be varied on its own. Whether a depression voice biomarker transfers may depend not only on the population but also on whether the outcome instrument captures what the model can detect. Validation should state the population, elicitation task, and outcome instrument together; a tool validated against one instrument should not be assumed to work against another.

items.title: Expanding Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Genetic Spectrum via Systematic Screening of Adult-Onset Neurologic Disease Genes.
items.abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) shares genetic architecture with other neurologic disorders, whose causal variants may be overlooked by targeted sequencing. Here, we evaluated the occurrence of pathogenic variants in genes linked to adult-onset neurologic disorders among individuals with ALS. Short-read WGS was performed in retrospectively collected ALS (Gold Coast criteria) and primary lateral sclerosis (PLS) (consensus diagnostic criteria) patients consecutively recruited at an Italian tertiary referral center (2013-2023), extensively phenotyped to exclude mimics. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic single-nucleotide variants/indels (American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines) and short tandem repeat expansions across 453 genes, including established ALS genes and other neurodegenerative disease genes, were systematically screened and validated. C9orf72 expansions (>30 repeats) were routinely screened by fragment analysis and repeat-primed PCR. A total of 856 patients with ALS and PLS (median age at onset 61.8 years, 38.5% women) were enrolled. Among them, 168 (19.6%) carried pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants or short tandem repeat expansions in genes associated with adult-onset neurologic disorders, mostly autosomal dominant. Of these, 41 (4.8% of the cohort) harbored variants in non-ALS/frontotemporal dementia (FTD) genes (ataxias, neuropathies, myopathies, movement disorders, mitochondrial diseases, and hereditary spastic paraplegia [HSP]). Repeat expansions accounted for 11.9% of cases, while 0.6% carried both sequence variants and repeat expansions. Family history of ALS/FTD (p = 2.132e-06), other neurodegenerative disorders (p = 0.0006934), and earlier age at onset (p = 0.024) were enriched among variant carriers. Variants in genes associated with upper motor neuron (UMN) involvement (ataxias/HSP) did not predict an UMN-predominant phenotype (odds ratio 1.54, 95% CI 0.39-6.07, p = 0.54), while the association between neuropathy/myopathy genes and a lower motor neuron-predominant phenotype was not statistically estimable. Beyond established ALS pathways, enrichment was observed in mitochondrial, metabolic, and proteostasis pathways (false discovery rate ≤0.05). Although the absence of a control cohort limits assessment of variant enrichment, the identification of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in genes associated with adult-onset neurologic disorders other than ALS/FTD in patients with ALS supports the inclusion of broader gene panels to advance precision medicine in ALS.

items.title: Robustness of Plasma P-Tau217 Diagnostic Thresholds for Alzheimer Disease Across Various Clinical Populations and Laboratory Environments.
items.abstract: Blood-based biomarkers (BBMs), especially plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p-tau217), could scale Alzheimer disease (AD) clinical-biological diagnosis, but clinical use requires thresholds transferable across laboratories and populations. We compared Lumipulse p-tau217 with other BBMs; evaluated amyloid-anchored thresholds across centers, analyzers, reagent lots, and clinical populations; and assessed second-line CSF adjudication of gray zone results. This multicenter, cross-sectional diagnostic-classification study included an exploratory Brussels cohort and 3 external validation cohorts. Brussels participants were cognitively unimpaired or impaired and had Aβ status determined by amyloid-PET or CSF Aβ42 and tau status by tau-PET or CSF p-tau181. Validation cohorts comprised consecutive Paris memory-clinic patients, patients with early-onset neurodegenerative dementia in Bordeaux, and individuals with monogenic frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Plasma p-tau217 was measured locally on Lumipulse analyzers. BBMs and ratios were compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. In Brussels, a Youden cutoff and dual 95% or 97.5% sensitivity/specificity cutoffs were derived; intermediate values defined gray zones. Among 411 participants (mean age 70.5 years; 51.6% female), p-tau217 showed the best diagnostic performance; p-tau217/Aβ42 did not improve performance or reduce gray zones. In Brussels, p-tau217 discriminated Aβ+ from Aβ- status (AUC 0.96, 95% CI 0.93-0.98; p < 0.0001). The 0.193 pg/mL Youden cutoff (95% CI 0.178-0.213) yielded 91.5% sensitivity (95% CI 84.7-95.5) and 91.6% specificity (95% CI 84.8-95.5) and detected neocortical tau-PET positivity with 98.5% sensitivity and 81.8% specificity. In Paris, sensitivity/specificity for clinical-biological AD were 93.2% (95% CI 85.1-97.1)/93.0% (95% CI 81.4-97.6); in Bordeaux, sensitivity/specificity for clinical-biological AD were 95.7% (95% CI 79.0-99.2)/92.3% (95% CI 66.7-98.6). Specificity in monogenic FTLD was 88.4% (95% CI 75.5-94.9). False-positive classifications were enriched in FTLD with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Dual thresholds yielded gray zones in 15.4%-24.8% of Paris patients; second-line CSF testing resolved 86.2%-88.9% of gray zone cases. Lumipulse plasma p-tau217 thresholds were transferable across centers, analyzers, reagent lots, and heterogeneous clinical populations, supporting evaluation of plasma-first pathways with confirmatory testing for gray zone values. Values below 0.193 pg/mL made neocortical tauopathy unlikely. Limitations include cross-sectional design, specialized Western European recruitment, unavailable race/ethnicity data, heterogeneous reference standards, incomplete AD copathology adjudication in monogenic FTLD, and no cross-platform comparison.

items.title: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins.
items.abstract: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5' GGGGCC 3' sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR20) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR20. We sought to identify DPR-related cell surface uptake factors using µMap high-resolution proximity labeling. DPR-iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR20-induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR50, we found PR50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR50 or GR50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. These results suggest CSPG4 participates in poly-PR/poly-GR internalization and transmission.

items.title: Struggling minds in lower ranks: Stronger ACC-OFC-amygdala coupling despite reduced selection of effortful options in subordinate male rats.
items.abstract: Social hierarchy can influence how individuals allocate effort to obtain rewards, but the neural mechanisms underlying rank-related differences in effort-based decision-making remain unclear. We investigated whether social rank is associated with effort-based choice and local and interregional neural activity in male rats. Twenty-one male Wistar rats were classified as dominant, intermediate, or subordinate based on repeated tube-test performance. Rats then performed a T-maze effort-based decision-making task in which they chose between a high-reward/high-effort option (six food pellets with a 30-cm barrier) and a low-reward/no-effort option (two food pellets without a barrier). Local field potentials were recorded from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and amygdala (AM). Dominant rats selected the high-reward/high-effort option more frequently than intermediate and subordinate rats, whereas response latency did not differ significantly among social-rank groups. Subordinate rats exhibited greater theta and high-gamma power in the ACC, OFC, and AM, as well as greater low-beta power in selected regions. Interregional coherence differed across social-rank groups in a frequency- and pathway-specific manner. Subordinate rats generally showed greater low-beta and high-gamma coherence in the OFC-AM, OFC-ACC, and ACC-AM pathways, whereas dominant rats showed greater theta coherence in the OFC-ACC and ACC-AM pathways. Several associations between neural measures and choice behavior were observed, particularly for low-beta and high-gamma activity and coherence, although these relationships varied across social-rank groups and neural pathways. These findings indicate that social rank is associated with differences in effort-based choice and with frequency- and pathway-specific alterations in ACC-OFC-AM neural dynamics. Overall, the findings suggest that social experience and hierarchical position are associated with distinct patterns of cortical-limbic activity during effort-based decision-making.

items.title: Astrocyte-associated water channel changes following buprenorphine administration in a rat model of diffuse traumatic brain injury.
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a significant concern, with millions sustaining a TBI each year. The vast majority are categorized as mild, in which diffuse pathologies are the hallmark and multiple cell types are affected, including astrocytes. Buprenorphine (bup), a semi-synthetic opioid, is a common human and veterinary analgesic. Previous studies from our group showed that a single dose of slow-release bup administered acutely following TBI alters astrocyte morphology at 1 day and 4 weeks post-injury in a region-specific manner. The current study expands on these findings by examining how four major astrocyte-associated proteins, GFAP, SWELL1/LRRC8A, TRPM4, and AQP4, are affected by such a dose of bup. Adult male rats received either a sham or TBI via a central fluid percussion injury model, followed by saline or bup 15 min following injury. Protein quantification at 1 day and 4 weeks post-injury revealed region- and time-dependent effects of acute bup administration. At 4 weeks following TBI, bup treatment was associated with reduced cortical SWELL1 and TRPM4, and reduced hippocampal and thalamic AQP4 expression. Collectively, these findings suggest that a single post-injury dose of bup can alter the regional expression of major astrocyte-associated proteins beyond the acute phase following diffuse TBI.

items.title: A Perfused Placenta-Based Model for Training in Cerebral Cavernous Malformation Microsurgery.
items.abstract: Declining operative exposure during residency has increased the need for realistic and accessible surgical simulation models for the acquisition of microsurgical skills. Human placenta has previously been used as a biological substrate for vascular microsurgical training. In this study, we present a placenta-based training model integrated with a 3-dimensional-printed craniotomy to reproduce key steps of microsurgical resection of cerebral cavernous malformations. Human placental tissue was combined with a 3-dimensional-printed pterional craniotomy to create a microsurgical training platform. A cavernous malformation was simulated using placental subunit fragments and clots, which were encapsulated and embedded within the placental parenchyma. The model was perfused through cannulation of umbilical vessels. The simulation procedure reproduced the main surgical steps: dural opening, vascular dissection, lesion exposure, intracapsular dissection with piecemeal removal and dural closure. The model was tested by 2 experienced neurosurgeons and 2 senior residents, who evaluated the simulator using a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire assessing realism, tissue consistency, instrument handling, training value, and overall usefulness. The model could be assembled in a mean time of 16 minutes at negligible costs and standard instrumentation. Up to 8 simulations could be obtained from a single placenta, increasing the model's cost-effectiveness. Evaluators rated the simulator favorably across all the investigated domains. Experts completed the procedure in a mean time of approximately 16 minutes, whereas residents required approximately 35 minutes. The described placenta-based model represents a feasible and reproducible platform for training microsurgical removal of cerebral cavernous malformation and may serve as a complementary tool in neurosurgical training programs.

items.title: Neurocognitive Alterations Manifested as Reaction Time Deficits Following ACL Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies.
items.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is associated with changes in cognitive-motor processing that may persist beyond physical recovery and are not fully identified by conventional physical performance assessments. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate neurocognitive function as expressed through cognitive-motor performance following ACLR compared with healthy individuals, with particular emphasis on reaction time and higher-order cognitive outcomes. Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase) were searched from inception to December 2025. Eligibility criteria included observational studies on cognitive-motor outcomes in individuals from ACLR recovery and healthy controls. Data extraction followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools. Random-effects models were used to calculate standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2, subgroup analyses and publication bias evaluations. Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participants Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participantswere included. Neurocognitive performance showed a significant impairment in reaction time from ACLR recovery with a moderate effect size (standardized mean difference = 0.56, 95% confidence interval 0.41-0.71, p < 0.001) and high heterogeneity (I2 = 78%). In contrast, pooled analyses showed no statistically significant differences for error rate, accuracy, visual memory, or visual motor speed. Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with persistent reaction time deficits, whereas pooled analyses of error rate, accuracy, visual memory, and visual motor speed did not demonstrate statistically significant differences compared with healthy controls. This pattern suggests selective impairment in the temporal efficiency of cognitive-motor processing rather than generalized cognitive dysfunction. Reaction time may represent a potential marker of altered cognitive-motor processing following ACLR; however, prospective studies are needed to determine its prognostic value and clinical utility for post-ACLR assessment and return-to-sport decision making.

items.title: Integrated Network Toxicology, Machine Learning, and Structural Biology Identify a Candidate Gene Network Linking Predicted Acetyl Tributyl Citrate Targets to Alzheimer's Disease.
items.abstract: As a common plasticizer, acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) poses a potential public health risk, yet its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is unclear. This study seeks to identify candidate molecular links between computationally predicted ATBC targets and AD-associated transcriptional alterations. We combined differential gene expression and co-expression results from two AD-related transcriptomic datasets with in silico ATBC target predictions from ChEMBL, PharmMapper, and SwissTargetPrediction, followed by machine learning feature selection, network toxicology, and molecular docking. We identified sixty-nine overlapping candidate genes shared among AD differentially expressed genes, AD-associated WGCNA modules, and computationally predicted ATBC targets. Among these, three genes-Interferon-stimulated gene 20 kDa (ISG20), Cytochrome P450 26A1 (CYP26A1), and β-1,3-Galactosyltransferase-1 (B3GALT1)-were further prioritized through machine learning. Docking scores were - 5.1 kcal/mol for ISG20, - 5.4 kcal/mol for CYP26A1, and - 4.6 kcal/mol for B3GALT1. These computational results suggest plausible binding poses. Our integrated analysis nominates ISG20, B3GALT1, and CYP26A1 as candidate molecular links between predicted ATBC targets and AD-associated transcriptional changes, providing a computational foundation for experimental validation.

items.title: A hierarchical study of depression and subcortical gray matter volume in adults with HIV.
items.abstract: Depression is highly prevalent in people with HIV (PWH). However, brain imaging studies of depression in PWH have been rather limited. We used a hierarchical approach to systematically investigate the impact of depression on subcortical volume in adults with HIV, focusing on the medial temporal lobe (MTL), the basal ganglia (BG), and the diencephalon. 99 PWH were included in the analysis (41-70 years old, 65% Black/African American, 25% female). Depression status was determined via the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Gray matter volume (GMv) of MTL, BG, diencephalon, and their subfields were estimated using FreeSurfer (v8.0.0). Linear regressions were performed in a hierarchical fashion to examine the association between depression and GMv of subcortical regions and subregions. The impacts of clinical and demographic factors were also examined. Depression was associated with lower GMv in the MTL (p = 0.014), but not the BG (p = 0.179) or diencephalon (p = 0.264). For subfields, depression was strongly associated with lower GMv in the hippocampal formation and most of its subfields, as well as in the basolateral and cortical-like regions and subnuclei of the amygdala. None of the viral factors were associated with any significant changes in GMv, including detectable viral load, nadir CD4, current CD4 count, and disease duration. In PWH, depression was associated with lower subcortical GMv, especially within the hippocampal formation and the basolateral amygdala, largely in accordance with the general population. Future longitudinal studies are needed to answer whether these associations continue or even grow throughout aging, and whether clinical factors play a role.

items.title: Taurine metabolism: a potential target for neuroprotection in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
items.abstract: Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammals and plays essential roles in cellular homeostasis, mitochondrial function, calcium regulation and neuronal survival. Taurine availability varies markedly across tissues, species and sexes, reflecting the balance between endogenous synthesis, dietary intake, transport and efflux. Although reduced taurine levels have been reported in some aging tissues, recent longitudinal studies indicate that circulating taurine does not decline universally with age, and its value as a biomarker of aging remains debated. Alterations in taurine or its transporter SLC6A6 have been described in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease and retinal degenerations. Preclinical studies indicate that taurine supplementation mitigates excitotoxicity, stabilizes mitochondrial function, reduces neuroinflammation and supports myelination and synaptic balance. Despite this strong mechanistic rationale, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided trials and a clearer definition of optimal therapeutic windows. In this review, we summarize the general properties of taurine and its metabolic regulation. We examine taurine's neuroprotective properties across different neurodegenerative conditions and discuss future perspectives for targeting taurine metabolism as a promising but largely unexplored strategy for intervention in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.

items.title: The role of prefrontal sharp wave ripple-like events in working memory and behavioral performance.
items.abstract: Sharp wave ripples (SWRs) in the hippocampus are well known for their roles in memory processes; however, the occurrence and functional relevance of ripple-band events in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) during awake states remain unclear. Here we investigated the presence and characteristics of ripples in the PFC of monkeys performing a delayed-match-to-sample task. We analyzed local field potential signals, focusing on ripple activity, and compared ripple properties between a passive pre-training condition and the active post-training task, and, within post-training, between sessions with low and high behavioral performance. Ripple-triggered spiking increased in the post-training condition, peaking before the ripple, during the first stimulus (encoding), the working-memory delay (maintenance), and the second stimulus (retrieval). In the post-training condition, when the animals had to actively hold information in working memory, ripple peak frequency was consistently higher than in the passive pre-training condition during both the maintenance and the second-stimulus periods. Within the post-training task, higher behavioral performance was accompanied by lower ripple power during the maintenance period. Consistent with a physiological role for these events, ripple-band amplitude was phase-coupled to the ongoing delta rhythm. Together, these findings indicate that awake PFC SWR-like events are modulated by working-memory demand and task performance, and provide new insight into cortical ripple dynamics during active cognitive processing.

items.title: Deep learning MGMT promoter methylation status prediction in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma using multiparametric MRI: Benchmark vs. real‑world performance.
items.abstract: Preoperative determination of O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter methylation status is of major prognostic and predictive relevance in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, yet currently depends on invasive tissue sampling. This study investigates deep learning-based strategies for MGMT prediction from multiparametric MRIs, with particular emphasis on robustness and generalizability under heterogeneous, multicenter conditions. A total of 949 glioblastoma cases were analyzed, integrating public benchmark data from the Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge (BraTS) with multi-institutional private cohorts acquired across diverse scanners and imaging protocols. Four complementary experimental settings were designed to compare reproduced literature baselines, private-only training, whole-brain end-to-end models, and segmentation-guided region-of-interest (ROI) pipelines. Tumor delineation was performed using an nnU-Net framework with expert quality control, and multiple three-dimensional convolutional neural network architectures were evaluated. Model performance was highest on the homogeneous BraTS benchmark, where a whole-brain DenseNet121 achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.80. However, marked performance deterioration was observed when models were evaluated on independent held-out multicenter test set. In contrast, segmentation-guided ROI-based approaches showed a more stable performance profile in this preliminary independent held-out multicenter test. Explicit lesion localization was associated with reduction in false-positive classifications, suggesting a potential benefit for performance stability across heterogeneous datasets, although validation in external cohorts from institutions not represented during training is required. Collectively, these results demonstrate that upstream methodological choices, especially tumor segmentation and ROI definition, remain critical determinants of performance in MRI-based radiogenomic modeling. Future studies should emphasize prospective multicenter validation, domain-shift harmonization, multimodal data integration, and uncertainty-aware deep learning to enhance robustness and interpretability.

items.title: Unique response patterns and high reinforcing efficacy characterize self-administration of combined fentanyl and methamphetamine.
items.abstract: Recent clinical data indicates combined use of fentanyl and methamphetamine (FENT+METH) is climbing, leading to increased adverse health events and deaths. However, preclinical rodent research has not extensively characterized responding and behavioral patterns associated with combined FENT+METH. We aimed to: (1) assess and characterize fixed ratio responding for fentanyl (FENT) alone and in combination with methamphetamine (METH) across sexes; (2) compare the rewarding efficacy of FENT- or METH-alone to that of FENT+METH. Male and female Long Evans rats were trained to self-administer FENT, METH, or FENT+METH (2.5 µg/kg/inf FENT, 0.05 mg/kg/inf METH, 2.5 + 0.05 FENT+METH) under long access conditions for fourteen days, followed by ten days of extinction and one day of drug-induced reinstatement. In a separate cohort of animals, progressive ratio responding was used to compare rewarding efficacy between polysubstance and single drug conditions (5 µg/kg/inf FENT, 0.1 mg/kg/inf METH, 5 + 0.1 FENT+METH). Female FENT animals displayed the greatest long access responding, while no differences were observed between drug conditions in males. Across sex, FENT+METH produced distinct response patterns compared to FENT- or METH-alone, producing mostly separate, evenly spaced infusion events, while single drug self-administration produced 'burst-like' responding, with grouped infusions and greater time between infusion events. FENT+METH animals displayed perseverative behavior during extinction, failing to reach extinction criteria. METH-alone engendered the highest responding under drug-induced reinstatement. Under the present experimental doses, FENT+METH had greater reinforcing efficacy than FENT- or METH-alone. The present findings highlight, across both sexes, the unique response patterns and increased rewarding efficacy produced by FENT+METH self-administration.

items.title: IMPROving MYelin imaging in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (IMPROMYMS study): protocol for a prospective longitudinal study.
items.abstract: It is increasingly recognized that patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) may experience disability progression in the absence of clinical relapses and new lesions, a phenomenon known as progression independent of relapse- and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) activity (PIRMA). The biological basis of this type of progression remains poorly understood. Demyelination is the central pathological hallmark of RRMS. Conventional clinical MRI protocols focus primarily on detecting focal lesions. However, advanced imaging techniques that quantify myelin content can provide additional insights beyond visible lesions, helping to better understand the mechanisms that drive clinical deterioration. Therefore, this study named IMPROving MYelin imaging in patients with relapsing-remitting Multiple Sclerosis (IMPROMYMS study) aims to apply myelin imaging techniques to study clinically defined disease progression in patients with RRMS, by assessing myelin content and comparing it to patients with RRMS without progression of the disease. In total, 97 patients with RRMS will be included and followed for 2.5 years. Participants will undergo MRI scanning at baseline and after 2 years and have regular clinical follow-up visits. Besides conventional MRI, advanced imaging sequences will be scanned, including gradient spin echo (GRASE), multi-echo gradient echo (ME-GRE), diffusion and functional MRI. Additionally, blood samples will be collected longitudinally to assess circulating biomarkers of neuroaxonal damage and astrocytic activation. Participants can also use the smartphone symptom-monitoring app MS Sherpa to enable more frequent monitoring of functional changes in daily life. In addition, 30 healthy controls will be scanned once as a reference group. In this study, we expect to find radiological prognostic markers of an increased risk of developing PIRMA, so that disease management strategies can be altered accordingly.

items.title: Neurocognitive profiles structure heterogeneous treatment response to bumetanide in neurodevelopmental disorders: secondary analysis of a multiple baseline single-case experimental design.
items.abstract: We performed a secondary analysis of the Bumetanide for Developmental Disorders (BUDDI;EUDRA-CT-2020-002196-35) trial to examine whether baseline neurocognitive profiles are associated with differential behavioral and cognitive treatment response. Participants (7-19 years) with atypical sensory reactivity and ASD, ADHD, epilepsy, or TSC diagnoses received 6-months of bumetanide treatment (max 3.0 mg/day) within a multiple-baseline SCED. Neurocognitive functioning was assessed across multiple domains and used to derive subgroups via cluster analysis. Behavioral outcomes were captured using a parent-reported PROMset and standardized questionnaires. Linear mixed models and subgroup comparisons were used to evaluate change over time. Of 119 participants enrolled, 105 completed baseline and 85 follow-up assessments At the group level, memory improved after six months (B = 0.65, 95%CI = 0.45to0.85, pFDR < .001, d = 1.07), while processing speed decreased (B = - 0.25, 95%CI = - 0.42to - 0.07, pFDR < .001, d = - 0.49). Cluster analysis identified four neurocognitive subgroups with distinct baseline profiles and differential treatment responses: individuals with weaker functioning showed the largest memory improvements, whereas those with preserved functioning showed greater behavioral improvement alongside declines in processing speed and visuomotor integration. Across subgroups, neurocognitive and behavioral changes did not align, and correlations were small (r < 0.30). In this study, neurocognitive profiling based on a standardized test battery was associated with distinct patterns of change during treatment. The dissociation between neurocognitive and behavioral outcomes indicated domain-specific and non-linear treatment effects. These findings provide a basis for linking variability in real-world change to individual neurocognitive characteristics within a defined clinical context.Trial registration: EudraCT (2020-002196-35) registration date 24-04-2020. Protocol: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-022-04033-8.

items.title: Beyond "more is better": a contextual framework for understanding synchrony in psychotherapy.
items.abstract: Research on interpersonal synchrony in psychotherapy has yielded inconsistent findings, challenging the assumption that greater synchrony is inherently beneficial. Building on recent meta-analytic evidence, we propose a contextual framework in which the psychological meaning of synchrony emerges from the interaction between two complementary levels: relatively stable, trait-like individual-specific synchrony signatures of patients and therapists, and state-like therapeutic processes unfolding within particular relational contexts. From this perspective, the same synchrony pattern may reflect adaptive coordination, therapeutic change, or maladaptive interaction, depending on the individuals involved and the clinical circumstances. We further emphasize the multidimensional nature of synchrony across behavioral, vocal, physiological, facial, and linguistic modalities. Rather than asking whether greater synchrony predicts better outcomes, future research should examine how the interplay between trait-like synchrony patterns and state-like changes contributes to therapeutic outcomes, and which combinations are beneficial for particular patients, with particular therapists, and under specific clinical conditions.

items.title: Ecology of Chagas disease vector Triatoma sanguisuga in Delaware: distribution, habitat, host use and Trypanosoma cruzi infection
items.abstract: Chagas disease is a vector-borne disease caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by triatomine bugs. The disease is increasingly recognized as an emerging public health threat in the United States (US). Little is known about the Chagas disease system in the Mid-Atlantic US despite the presence of a native T. cruzi vector species, Triatoma sanguisuga. The species is widespread throughout the eastern US, and the Mid-Atlantic comprises the northernmost portion of its geographic range. Triatoma sanguisuga has been implicated in autochthonous T. cruzi transmission to humans in other parts of the US but has never been formally studied in the Mid-Atlantic. To fill this knowledge gap and increase public health preparedness, we investigated T. sanguisuga in Delaware and eastern Maryland. We aimed to collect baseline information about the species, including its habitat, feeding patterns, and T. cruzi infection rates across land use intensities. We collected 151 T. sanguisuga specimens in all three DE counties and two counties in MD, and identified standing dead trees as an important local habitat for the species. Twenty specimens (13.2%) were submitted by community members who had found the bugs in or around human homes and businesses. We detected T. cruzi infection in 23 of 150 (15.3%) specimens and identified 24 vertebrate host species, including humans, from 95 specimens. We detected a stage-structured blood feeding pattern wherein juvenile bugs ("nymphs") were reptile-associated (which are refractory T. cruzi hosts)and adult bugs were mammal-associated (which are competent T. cruzi hosts), which was reflected in a significant difference in T. cruzi infection prevalence between adults and nymphs. Our findings reveal the multiscale network that sustains T. cruzi transmission in Delaware while also providing practical public health information on a local vector-borne disease system.

items.title: Natural language processing of title vocabulary in ecology papers: country comparison and trend detection
items.abstract: I analyzed titles of 2,188,788 ecology-related papers (1990–2025) from OpenAlex with natural language processing to map country-level research interests and temporal change. The corpus was the union of (i) papers in SCImago Ecology and Ecology, Evolution, Behavior and Systematics venues and (ii) papers whose OpenAlex primary_topic fell in subfields 1105 (Ecology, Evolution, Behavior and Systematics) and 2303 (Ecology). Country comparisons used weighted log-odds of 1–3-word phrases extracted from titles. For the 15 countries with the largest shares of ecology papers, relatively frequent distinctive phrases often began with biome or landscape terms and then named particular organisms. Japan stood out for island-nation landscape words, prefecture, the specific epithet japonica , environmental DNA, and native or economically important species. Emerging phrases shared across countries included microbiome, metabarcoding, environmental DNA, and machine learning, whereas mitochondrial DNA and polymerase chain reaction declined in title share—consistent less with method abandonment than with once-novel terms becoming routine. Title differences do not rank research quality; they describe what each national community puts in titles. In addition, historical changes in ecological methods and a broadening of focus from individual organisms toward communities, ecosystems, and microbial assemblages as wholes also became clear.

items.title: Occlusal Macrowear Patterns and Initial Tooth Contacts in Patients With Temporomandibular Disorders and Asymptomatic Controls.
items.abstract: Background Previous studies investigating the aetiological role of occlusion in temporomandibular disorders (TMD) have primarily focused on forms of malocclusion, whereas occlusal wear patterns and initial tooth contacts have received comparatively little attention. Objective This study investigated possible associations between occlusal wear facets, centric initial tooth contacts, and the tissue-specific localization of TMD-related symptoms. Methods A total of 52 fully dentate individuals were included in this blinded study. Occlusal wear facet patterns of 24 individuals with symptoms involving the bilaminar zone of the temporomandibular joint and/or the mandibular retractor muscles (patient group: P) were compared with 28 asymptomatic individuals (control group: C). Individual interocclusal silicone records were obtained in a habitual pain-free mandibular position, documenting the first tooth contact during gentle closure. Occlusal Fingerprint Analysis (OFA) was applied to quantify and compare wear facet patterns and initial contact. Results No significant between-group differences were observed for premolars or molars in any quadrant (p = 0.072-0.869). The P-group exhibited significantly more pronounced wear facets on maxillary incisors (p = 0.015-0.047). In 58% of the P-group, initial occlusal contacts were anterior, compared with 14% in the C-group, representing a significant between-group difference (p = 0.002). Conclusions Occlusal wear facets may reflect the power stroke. The position and orientation of initial contacts in a relaxed, pain-free mandibular position may be functionally relevant. Wear facets indicating premature incisor contacts may reflect increased retractor muscle activity and associated posterior mandibular displacement, potentially resulting in increased loading of the bilaminar zone. However, causal relationships remain unclear and require further investigation.

items.title: Life-history trade-offs: the constraints underlying mosquito-borne pathogen transmission.
items.abstract: Mosquito-borne pathogen transmission models typically assume that vector life-history traits vary independently. While survival, reproduction, and immunity are shaped by evolutionary forces to maximize fitness, life-history theory predicts that resource and physiological constraints create trade-offs among these traits. These trade-offs can shape pathogen development and transmission in nonintuitive ways. We argue that incorporating trade-offs into epidemiological and ecological modeling could improve predictive capacity for disease establishment and spread. Environmental variation alters resource allocation and, thus, trait covariation, so environmental variability may have cascading effects on transmission potential. This perspective unifies infection biology, local adaptation, vector-pathogen coevolution, invasion dynamics, and vector control under a common mechanistic framework to improve predictions of disease risk in a rapidly changing world.

items.title: Characterizing wildlife's behavioral response to humans.
items.abstract: Human-wildlife interactions are critically important across biodiversity conservation, public health, and urban sustainability. Defining wildlife behavioral responses to humans is essential for managing these interactions, yet existing knowledge remains fragmented. We provide a framework to understand and predict behavioral responses to humans. We classify responses into four categories-avoidance, attraction, defense, and unresponsive-that generate diverse ecological and societal consequences. The prevalence of these response types varies across spatial and temporal scales in context-dependent ways because animals adjust their perceived risk-reward balance in response to humans, as well as nonhuman ecological, internal, and abiotic factors. By providing a common framework to explain this variation, we highlight opportunities to improve the prediction and management of human-wildlife relationships in a human-dominated world.

items.title: Emerging integral impact of microplastic (MP)-metal interactions on environmental dynamics.
items.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) can sorb and transport metal contaminants under certain conditions, forming composite particulate-chemical systems with complex environmental and toxicological behaviour. Their sorption capacity is governed by polymer chemistry, surface oxidation, aging state, particle size, and environmental conditions including pH, salinity, and dissolved organic matter. Weathering enhances oxygen-containing functional groups and surface roughness, thereby increasing metal-binding affinity, while plastisphere biofilms further modulate adsorption-desorption dynamics via extracellular polymeric substances and redox-active metabolites. These processes regulate metal speciation, mobility, and bioavailability across aquatic systems. Ecotoxicological evidence indicates that metal-loaded MPs alter exposure geometry through ingestion-driven desorption, epithelial retention and tissue-specific redistribution, leading to oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, immune disruption and developmental toxicity. Interaction outcomes vary from synergistic enhancement of metal toxicity to antagonistic sequestration, depending on polymer-metal affinity and organism physiology. Although advances in spectroscopy, elemental mapping, and multi-omics approaches have improved mechanistic understanding, current knowledge is constrained by environmentally unrealistic exposure scenarios, limited chronic and nanoscale investigations, and a lack of standardized analytical protocols. This review synthesizes environmental chemistry, plastisphere ecology and toxicological mechanisms to provide a systems-level assessment of MP-metal interactions and highlights priorities for risk-based evaluation of these emerging hybrid contaminants.

items.title: Carboxymethyl cellulose-regulated poly(vinyl alcohol) ionic networks for recyclable strain sensing.
items.abstract: Conductive hydrogels are promising soft materials for flexible sensing, electronic skins, and human-machine interaction; however, integrating mechanical robustness, stable ionic transport, environmental adaptability, and reprocessability within a fully physically crosslinked network remains challenging. Here, we report a Hofmeister-effect-assisted multi-interaction strategy for constructing a physically crosslinked ionic hydrogel based on polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), termed P-MC. Freeze-thaw-induced PVA microcrystals serve as reversible load-bearing junctions, while concentrated MgSO₄ simultaneously provides mobile ions and promotes polymer-chain association through the Hofmeister effect. CMC forms a semi-interpenetrating network with PVA, and ethylene glycol regulates water-polymer interactions to improve environmental stability. The resulting P-MC hydrogel exhibits a tensile strength of 0.87 MPa, a fracture strain of 525.09%, favorable biosafety, anti-drying and anti-freezing performance, and thermal reprocessability. Distinguishable electromechanical responses are retained after five recycling cycles. By mounting two P-MC sensors on the index finger and thumb and processing the resulting dual-channel resistance signals using a one-dimensional convolutional neural network, six hand gestures are classified with a test accuracy of 99.44%; direct testing of the trained model on two additional volunteers yields accuracies of 95.00% and 96.67%. Additional demonstrations include joint-motion monitoring and core-sheath fiber-based triboelectric output. This work establishes a Hofmeister-regulated physical-network design strategy for recyclable, environmentally adaptable, and intelligently interactive flexible electronics.

items.title: Strategies for improving the performance of bioelectrochemical systems for wastewater treatment and pollutant removal: A comprehensive review.
items.abstract: Bioelectrochemical systems (BESs) integrate microbial metabolism with electrochemical reactions and provide a novel technique for wastewater treatment, pollutant removal, and resource recovery. However, their practical application remains constrained by mass transfer limitations, material costs, and performance deterioration. This review critically examines strategies for improving BES performance by linking the system bottlenecks to electrode engineering, microbial regulation, reactor and operating optimization, and integration with complementary treatment processes. Particular attention is given to the different transformation and recovery pathways of nitrogen, phosphorus, recalcitrant organic contaminants, and metals. And it is emphasized that removal efficiency does not adequately represent mineralization, detoxification, or resource recovery. BES performance can be improved through electrode modification, microbial regulation, reactor and operating optimization, and process integration. Electrode modification enhances surface properties, conductivity, and catalytic activity. Microbial regulation promotes the formation of active and stable electroactive communities and biofilms. Reactor design and operating conditions affect mass and ion transport, local reaction environments, and electron allocation, while coupling with complementary treatment processes can overcome limitations in separation, mass transfer, and refractory pollutant transformation. This review focuses on analyzing the key engineering trade-offs between performance improvement and material costs, additional energy consumption, and environmental impact. Future progress therefore requires standardized and comprehensive performance assessment, long term validation with real wastewater, pilot scale demonstration, and integrated evaluation of treatment performance, resource recovery, cost, environmental burden, and operational stability. It is hoped that this review will facilitate the transition of BES from laboratory research to practical applications in wastewater treatment and resource recovery.

items.title: Hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid disrupts intestinal health and gut microbial networks of the native earthworm Metaphire guillelmi in agricultural soil.
items.abstract: Hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid (HFPO-DA), a short-chain PFAS alternative to perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), is increasingly detected in agricultural soils, but ecologically relevant indicators of its toxicity to native soil invertebrates remain insufficiently defined. Here, using wheat-field soil as a realistic exposure medium, we exposed Metaphire guillelmi to HFPO-DA (0.02 and 0.2 mg kg -1 ) for 28 days and included PFOA at equivalent doses as a benchmark. We integrated oxidative stress biomarkers, digestive enzyme activity, the 8-hydroxy-2-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), histopathology, integrated biomarker response version 2 (IBRv2), transcriptomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, LEfSe, and microbial network analyses to establish a multi-level indicator framework for assessing the risks associated with PFAS alternatives. HFPO-DA yielded a lower relative IBRv2 value than PFOA at 0.2 mg kg -1 after 28 days, yet it generated specific adverse effects, including elevated DNA damage and visible intestinal epithelial injury even at 0.02 mg kg -1 . Transcriptomic analyses revealed concentration-specific changes in genes associated with fatty acid metabolism and PPAR signaling at the low dose, and with oxidative phosphorylation, neurotransmitter-related pathways, and Hedgehog signaling at the high dose. Gut microbial analyses further showed that 0.2 mg kg -1 HFPO-DA reduced α-diversity, altered the relative abundances of bacterial taxa, and simplified co-occurrence networks. Collectively, these results indicate that HFPO-DA can impair intestinal health, alter gut microbial communities, and induce transcriptional changes in a native earthworm. Our findings support using integrated host-microbiome indicators as early-warning tools to evaluate hidden ecological risks associated with emerging PFAS alternatives in agricultural soils.

items.title: Ecotoxicological Effects of Plastics and Cerium in a Soil Sentinel Caenorhabditis elegans: Modulating Role of Particle Size.
items.abstract: The increasing exposure risk of rare earth elements (REEs) in soil has raised widespread concern. However, the combined effects of REEs and coexisting pollutants remain relatively poorly understood. Herein, we address this knowledge gap by systematically investigating the particle size-associated toxicological effects between a representative REE (cerium, Ce) and polystyrene nanoplastics (60 nm NPs) versus microplastics (10 μm MPs) in nematodes (Caenorhabditis elegans). Notably, exposure of Ce alone decreased malondialdehyde (MDA) contents and peroxidase (POD) activities by 21.3% and 14.8%, respectively, while significantly increased adenosine triphosphate (ATP) contents by 65.6%, compared to control groups. Under co-exposure, NPs induced more severe oxidative injury, whereas this effect was less pronounced in the presence of MPs. While, the coexistence of MPs significantly decreased the contents of protein and glycogen by 49.8% and 31.0%, respectively, suggesting the potential changes of energy metabolism. These distinct toxic outcomes were closely linked to plastic size-associated metabolic reprogramming. Specifically, NPs-Ce mixtures perturbed the metabolisms of glycerophospholipid, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, beta-alanine, and glutathione, consistent with observed oxidative damage. In contrast, MPs-Ce mixtures primarily affected maltose, thiamine, arginine, and proline metabolisms, aligning with altered energy metabolism. Collectively, our findings provided novel mechanistic insights into biological responses to Ce-plastic mixtures, underscoring the crucial role of particle size in determining ecotoxicological outcomes in organisms.
