items.title: The HST/WFC3 Transmission Spectrum of AU Mic b. I. An Atmosphere Obscured by Contamination and Systematics
items.abstract: Abstract Young sub-Neptune progenitors around M dwarfs offer an excellent opportunity to probe the formation of their abundant, older cousins. At ∼20 Myr and only 9.7 pc away, AU Mic b is an ideal candidate for this effort, with its density and observations of escaping hydrogen pointing to a significant primordial atmosphere. Here we present the 0.8–1.6 μ m transmission spectrum of AU Mic b observed with the Wide Field Camera 3 on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). We find that HST experienced unstable scanning during its visits, resulting in a variable point-spread function (PSF) that dramatically affects the orbit-to-orbit baseline of the observations. While we were able to somewhat mitigate this problem through spectral binning, the effects cannot be completely eliminated, limiting the precision of our results. Our data are further impacted by the intense magnetic activity of AU Mic, which introduced significant rotational variability along with spot crossings and the transit light source (TLS) effect into the light curves and spectrum, respectively. Through decomposition of the out-of-transit stellar spectral energy distribution (SED), we are able to constrain AU Mic’s photospheric and spot temperatures to 3891 ± 37 and 3020 ± 69 K, respectively, with a spot filling factor of 0.33 ± 0.05. Using Bayesian atmospheric retrievals, we show that the spectrum is dominated by the TLS effect with weak atmospheric constraints, with the data preferring a relatively small scale height of <185 km to 3 σ . Extrapolation of our retrieved spectra shows that the TLS effect dominates over atmospheric features at optical and infrared wavelengths.

items.title: Strong Gravitational Lensing Posterior Sampling in Pixel Space Using Diffusion Models and Recurrent Inference Machines
items.abstract: Abstract Modeling galaxy–galaxy strong gravitational lenses to infer the brightness of the source galaxy and the mass distribution of the foreground galaxy is computationally challenging, particularly for high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio observations. In this regime, high-dimensional representations of both the source and the foreground mass distribution are necessary to model the data down to the noise level. This inference problem has been challenging for both traditional and machine learning-based methods because of its high dimensionality and its nonlinearity in the foreground mass distribution. We present a method to generate joint posterior samples of the source galaxy and foreground mass distribution as pixelated images conditioned on observations. The method combines diffusion-based generative modeling and recurrent inference machines. It can model realistic gravitational lensing simulations with background and foreground galaxies drawn from cosmological hydrodynamical simulations down to the noise level.

items.title: The road towards precision measurements of H 0 with bright sirens in the Einstein Telescope era
items.abstract: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide an independent probe of cosmic expansion since their luminosity distances are inferred directly from the gravitational-wave signal and, for bright sirens (BSs), the source redshifts are obtained through the identification of electromagnetic counterparts. In this work, we forecast the constraining power of future bright siren catalogues on the Hubble constant using simulated binary-neutron-star mergers detected by the Einstein Telescope with associated electromagnetic counterparts. We construct mock catalogues with different numbers of events and redshift distributions, with GW170817 as a reference BS, and analyse the resulting constraints within a flat Λ CDM cosmology. We find that, when bright sirens are used as a standalone probe, most of the information on H 0 is provided by low-redshift events, with the improvement in precision saturating for sources above z ∼ 1 ; beyond that redshift, the constraining power of BSs is increasingly limited by the degeneracy with Ω m , which prevents further gains in precision on H 0 . In this case, approximately 90 low-redshift BSs are required to reach , while about 45 are sufficient for . These results highlight the importance of both electromagnetic counterpart identification and complementary background probes in making BSs a competitive, distance-ladder-independent test of the Hubble tension.

items.title: Localized magnetic pressure anisotropy in strange dwarfs with crystalline crusts
items.abstract: Abstract We study equilibrium sequences of magnetized strange dwarfs composed of a self-bound MIT bag strange matter core, with $$B_\textrm{bag}^{1/4} = 145$$ B bag 1 / 4 = 145 MeV, and an ordinary crystalline crust. The aim is to determine how nuclear composition changes and magnetic pressure anisotropy in the crust modify the mass-radius relation. The strange core is kept isotropic, while the crust is described either by pure nuclei stopped at the first inverse beta threshold or by electron capture sequences extended to neutron drip for C, O, Ne, and Mg compositions; selected mixed crusts are also considered up to the first instability. The stellar structure is solved with the radial pressure as the integrated pressure and with the anisotropic contribution $$2(P_t-P_r)/r$$ 2 ( P t - P r ) / r restricted to the crust. This treatment is compared with ordinary WD sequences and with scalar pressure branch calculations. We find that extending the crust to neutron drip produces more compact strange dwarf branches than stopping at the inverse beta threshold, because the evolved crust is softer and the core crust transition occurs at higher pressure. Magnetic anisotropy further shifts the selected branches toward smaller radii, with the effect visible across the compositions studied and clearer at fixed stellar mass. The comparison with compact objects from the Montreal WD Database is used only as an observational reference plane, but it indicates that compact WD candidates are a relevant region for testing small core strange dwarf scenarios. The magnetic radius shifts describe the response to crust matter anisotropy in a spherical model that omits the global Maxwell stress.

items.title: Extending the Love-Q relation to rapidly rotating neutron stars for gravitational-waveform modeling
items.abstract: Gravitational-wave observations of binary neutron star mergers probe the neutron star equation of state through finite-size effects on the waveform. These include the tidal deformation of the stars due to their respective companion, but for spinning neutron stars also include the spin-induced quadrupole moment of the stars. Typically, to avoid introducing additional equation of state dependent parameters, waveform models relate this quadrupole moment to the tidal deformability through so-called quasi-universal relations. These are derived under the slow-rotation approximation, which at larger spins, i.e., for millisecond pulsars, becomes unreliable. We attempt to extend the existing quasi-universal relations by explicitly accounting for the spin, calibrating it against numerically computed quadrupole moments across a broad set of equations of state and spins 0.15 ≤ | χ | ≤ 0.6 with the χ → 0 limit enforced by construction. The resulting spin-extended relation reduces the median absolute percentage error relative to the slow-rotation relation by 70% across this range. Parameter estimation using the spin-extended relation reduces biases in recovered intrinsic parameters in some cases, though biases from mass-spin degeneracies dominate largely when a population is considered. These results provide a more accurate description of the spin-induced quadrupole moment for spinning neutron star binaries, relevant for waveform modelling with third-generation gravitational-wave detectors.

items.title: Magnetic Reconnection Governs the Entire Lifecycle of Solar Eruptive Magnetic Flux Rope
items.abstract: Abstract While magnetic flux ropes (MFRs) are widely accepted to exist prior to many solar eruptions, the physical mechanism responsible for triggering and subsequently driving their eruptions remains debated. Classical models commonly attribute eruption onset to ideal magnetohydrodynamic instabilities, particularly the torus instability, while magnetic reconnection is often regarded as a secondary process. Using high-resolution three-dimensional MHD simulations, we investigate the eruption of an MFR that forms self-consistently through flux cancellation driven by converging motions and photospheric diffusion following an initial shearing phase. The preeruption MFR rises quasi-statically and reaches a height where the decay index exceeds the classical torus instability threshold, yet the system continues to evolve quasi-statically without eruption. Instead, eruption begins only when the current sheet beneath the MFR becomes sufficiently thin for magnetic reconnection to set in. Increasing numerical resolution systematically delays the eruption onset, whereas the decay index at eruption onset remains nearly unchanged, demonstrating that the onset is governed by reconnection rather than torus instability. During the eruption, magnetic reconnection continuously converts surrounding sheared arcades into newly reconnected twisted flux that merges with the preeruption MFR and continues to build the erupting MFR. A component-resolved analysis of the Lorentz force work further shows that the newly reconnected flux contributes predominantly to the main acceleration phase. These results demonstrate that magnetic reconnection plays a central role throughout the entire life cycle of the eruptive MFR: it builds the MFR, directly triggers its eruption, and provides the dominant drive for the eruption.

items.title: Velocity-resolved Ionization Mapping of the Broad-line Region. II. Signatures of Eccentric Broad-line Regions from a Quantitative Photoionization-based Model
items.abstract: Abstract Velocity-resolved reverberation mapping (RM) is one of the most powerful tools for probing the geometry and kinematics of the broad-line region (BLR) in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). However, its interpretation may be nonunique, as similar velocity-delay signatures can arise from different combinations of BLR geometry and kinematics. To address this degeneracy, this series of studies develops velocity-resolved ionization mapping (IM) as a complementary technique. In this second paper of the series, we construct photoionization-based BLR models to quantitatively demonstrate the diagnostic power of the joint RM+IM framework. We calculate local H α and H β emissivities with C loudy , couple them with disk-like BLR models, and generate synthetic velocity-dependent line fluxes, lags, and Balmer decrements (BDs). The model reproduces the observed anticorrelation between the integrated BD and the incident ionizing continuum, with scatter naturally introduced by reverberation delays. We show that a virialized elliptical BLR can produce diverse velocity-delay maps and velocity-resolved lags that mimic RM signatures commonly attributed to virialized motion, inflow, or outflow. In contrast, the velocity-resolved BD is sensitive to the symmetry of the BLR gas distribution, providing a key diagnostic for distinguishing eccentric geometry from nonvirial motions. Through proof-of-concept comparisons with one double-peaked and one single-peaked AGN, we show that an elliptical-disk BLR can simultaneously reproduce the observed line profiles, velocity-resolved lags, and velocity-resolved BDs. These results provide a quantitative basis for IM, support the presence of eccentric BLR structures in AGNs, and demonstrate the potential of joint RM+IM analyses to break the BLR geometry-kinematics degeneracy. This framework has important implications for identifying geometry-induced biases and improving reverberation-based black hole mass measurements.

items.title: Probing the Interstellar Medium toward the Double Pulsar and the Gum Nebula Using Low-frequency Pulse Broadening Measurements
items.abstract: Abstract Long-term timing of the double pulsar system (PSR J0737−3039A/B) has enabled some of the most stringent constraints on strong-field gravity. Yet, despite the system’s high profile, there have been very few observations at frequencies below 300 MHz, where pulse broadening due to interstellar scattering becomes significant. Measurements of the pulse broadening timescale and its frequency scaling, τ s ∝ ν α (where α is the scattering spectral index), provide valuable constraints on the structure of the scattering medium. Here we report on simultaneous observations of J0737−3039A and five other nearby pulsars (J0630−2834, J0742−2822, J0820−4114, J0835−4510, and J0837−4135) in the frequency range 109–231 MHz using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). These observations have enabled the highest-quality detections ever published for these pulsars at low frequencies. For J0737−3039A, J0742−2822, and J0837−4135, we measure α to be −4.1(1), −3.8(1), and −4.1(1), respectively. These measurements provide new constraints on the density and turbulence parameters of the Gum Nebula region, and we discuss implications for models of the Galactic electron density distribution. Our current data yield a dispersion measure (DM) precision of ∼4 × 10 −4 cm −3 pc for J0737−3039A, which can be further improved with the MWA Phase III to reach ∼1 × 10 −4 cm −3 pc, far exceeding the precision of previous studies. The prospects for precisely constraining temporal variations in the DM and pulse broadening timescale strengthen the importance of regular monitoring of J0737−3039A at low frequencies, with the eventual goal of contributing to long-term timing studies.

items.title: Deriving Interplanetary Sector Boundary Crossings Using Potential Field Source Surface Modeling
items.abstract: Abstract The heliospheric current sheet (HCS) and associated interplanetary sector boundaries fundamentally structure the solar wind environment, modulating coronal mass ejection (CME) evolution and solar energetic particle transport. In this study, we evaluate the capability of a static Potential Field Source Surface (PFSS; R ss = 2.5 R ⊙ ) coronal model to directly map interplanetary sector boundary crossings from the Sun to 1 au without dynamic heliospheric propagation models. We compare ballistically transported HCS crossings derived from GONG-ADAPT and Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO)/Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) magnetic maps against sector boundary crossing observations from the SBCross catalog. PFSS modeling reproduces the large-scale interplanetary magnetic field topology well ( J ≈ 0.50), achieving hit rates (probability of detection, POD) of 0.64 for GONG-ADAPT and 0.76 for HMI. Carrington synoptic maps outperform flux-transport modeled maps, suggesting that the short-term observational noise from data assimilation degrades topological matching more than map “aging.” Predictive skill shows a strong solar cycle dependence, performing significantly better during solar maxima (POD = 0.70–0.81) than solar minima (POD = 0.56 − 0.67), attributed to more distinct crossings due to higher HCS inclination angles during maximum. Matched events exhibit travel times close to ballistic estimates of 4.8–4.9 days with an average timing difference centered near zero (±1.1 days) and 90% of events within ±1.8 days. The hit rate of HCS structures that interact with CMEs does not degrade (POD = 0.67–0.83), despite propagating ≈7 hr faster on average, implying that the CME interaction causes only minor structural changes to the HCS. Larger timing differences (>24 hr) are associated with flatter current sheets. Overall, static PFSS extrapolations offer a computationally inexpensive, effective approach for mapping global sector boundary structure.

items.title: Partial Reconstruction of the \(B_{s}^{0}\rightarrow \phi (K^{+}K^{-})\eta ' (\pi ^{+}\pi ^{-}\eta )\) Decay at a Future High-luminosity \(Z\) Factory
items.abstract: The \(B_s^0 \to \phi (K^+K^-)\eta '(\pi ^+\pi ^-\eta )\) decay is of particular interest in flavour physics because in the Standard Model, it proceeds predominantly through the quark transition \(\bar {b} \to \bar {s}s\bar {s}\). However, the reconstruction of this decay is experimentally challenging due to the presence of the neutral \(\eta \) particle, which significantly reduces the overall reconstruction efficiency. In this study, the feasibility of using the partial reconstruction technique to reconstruct the invariant mass of the \(B_s^0\)-meson without explicitly detecting the \(\eta \) particle is investigated. Monte Carlo simulated events corresponding to an FCC-ee environment are used, and the effects of detector momentum and vertex resolutions on the reconstruction performance are examined. The results show that improved vertex resolution substantially improves the global reconstructed mass response and partial-reconstruction efficiency, while improvements in momentum resolution are manifested primarily through a narrowing of the fitted central DCB component. These findings suggest that future high-luminosity \(e^+e^-\) colliders such as FCC-ee could effectively exploit the partial reconstruction technique to study rare decay modes containing undetected neutral particles. items.title: White dwarf pollution in wide binaries. I. the effects of stellar evolution
items.abstract: Atmospheric pollution in white dwarfs is interpreted as evidence for the accretion of rocky material from remnant planetary systems. Wide binary companions can influence the delivery of planetary material onto white dwarfs, making it essential to understand the interplay between stellar evolution and binary perturbations. We investigate how uncertainties in stellar mass-loss histories affect the dynamical evolution of remnant planetary systems in wide binaries, and assess their relative importance compared with binary perturbations in driving the accretion of rocky material onto white dwarfs. We performed N-body simulations incorporating time-dependent stellar parameters interpolated from evolutionary tracks and tidal interactions, following the dynamical evolution up to the white dwarf stage. We explored two stellar-evolution models with distinct mass-loss histories for wide binary systems hosting a Jupiter-mass planet and a planetesimal disc, spanning a range of binary architectures. REBOUND MESA The adopted stellar-evolution model has only a minor effect on the survival of the planet, mainly affecting the timing and efficiency of planetesimal delivery during the white dwarf stage. Instead, the architecture of the binary primarily controls the pollution outcome: wider binaries produce the highest rates of accretion onto the white dwarf, consistent with the observed prevalence of polluted white dwarfs in wide binaries. Moreover, planetesimal reservoirs remain long-lived, with survival times increasing with binary separation, enabling gigayear-long metal pollution. Our results suggest that the architecture of wide binaries, rather than uncertainties in stellar evolution, is the dominant factor controlling the dynamical delivery of rocky material onto white dwarfs.

items.title: The stellar populations of resolved galaxies
items.abstract: The study of galaxies outside the Milky Way using observations of resolved stellar populations has experienced extraordinary growth over the past two decades. There now exist panchromatic photometry and precise astrometry for hundreds of millions of individually resolved stars in hundreds of galaxies that span $\sim10^9$ in luminosity, $\sim10^3$ in metallicity, and sample a wide range of environments. Here, we review advances in extragalactic astronomy enabled by resolved stellar population imaging. We summarize major observational programs and focus on four interconnected science areas: the star formation histories of galaxies, 'bursty' star formation, the stellar initial mass function, and the orbital histories of Local Group galaxies. We review the literature in each area, synthesize key findings, identify emerging trends, and discuss how new and future facilities (e.g., JWST, LSST, Euclid, Roman, CSST, ELTs, HWO) will enable further progress. Finally, we highlight shortcomings in current datasets and discuss promising directions for new areas of investigation.

items.title: The Broad-line Region Size–Luminosity Relation in Active Galactic Nuclei Constrained by the Viewing Angle with the FRADO Model
items.abstract: Abstract We investigate the H β broad-line region (BLR) size–luminosity ( R BLR – L 5100 ) relation of active galactic nuclei (AGN) using a Bayesian viewing angle inference framework based on the Failed Radiatively Accelerated Dusty Outflow (FRADO) model. First, we update the FRADO model by introducing a phase factor to account for the anisotropic visibility of the illuminated cloud surface. Second, we construct a Bayesian framework to constrain the viewing angle by matching the FRADO-based R BLR to the measured H β lags of 151 AGN from S. Wang & J. H. Woo. We successfully reproduce the slope and intrinsic scatter of the observed R BLR – L 5100 relation, finding that the inferred viewing angles are broadly consistent with the estimates from dynamical modeling of velocity-resolved reverberation data, albeit with substantial scatter. As the observed H β time lag and line velocity depend on the viewing angle, the black hole mass ( M BH ) calibrated from our work is typically larger than the reverberation-mapping estimates using an average virial factor. Our results provide a physically motivated interpretation of the R BLR – L 5100 relation and the systematic uncertainties in reverberation and single-epoch M BH estimates.

items.title: Thorium and europium production in the early Galaxy. Implications for nucleocosmochronology
items.abstract: The ages of the oldest stellar populations can be investigated through nucleocosmochronology. Among the available chronometers, the thorium-to-europium abundance ratio provides a promising age indicator. We investigated the reliability of the log( Th / Eu ) ratio as a chronometer for old stellar populations by testing whether thorium and europium are produced in a consistent ratio in metal-poor stars. We also assessed the precision with which this abundance ratio can be measured and the resulting uncertainties in stellar ages, adopting the best available theoretical estimate of the initial production ratio to establish the absolute age scale. We present new thorium and europium abundance measurements for a sample of eight / reference stars observed with UVES at the VLT. We combined these measurements with homogeneous samples from the literature and analysed the evolution of log( Th Eu ) as a function of metallicity. Adopting a theoretical r-process production ratio, we derived stellar ages and investigated the impact of observational uncertainties and sample statistics on the resulting age constraints. At low metallicities, the observed log( Th / Eu ) ratios show no significant dependence on metallicity once stars with anomalous actinide abundances are excluded, supporting the assumption that thorium and europium were typically co-produced in the early Galaxy. The derived ages are broadly consistent with those expected for metal-poor halo stars, although uncertainties in individual ages remain large. We show that higher spectral resolution is required to improve the precision of Th measurements, while combining measurements from several stars in coeval populations could provide an additional statistical improvement. Nucleocosmochronology is a valuable independent method for dating the oldest stellar populations. Although individual stellar ages are currently limited by observational and theoretical uncertainties, the analysis of homogeneous samples of coeval stars, such as members of globular clusters, could provide significantly stronger constraints. Future high-resolution multi-object spectroscopic facilities will facilitate this approach and provide independent constraints on the early formation history of the Milky Way and the age of the Universe.

items.title: The Influence of the Inclination of the Accretion Disk in Black Hole X-Ray Binaries on the Energy Spectrum Characteristics
items.abstract: Abstract During the ascending and descending phases of some black hole X-ray binaries (BH XRBs), it was found that the X-ray Eddington ratio ( L X-ray(3−25keV) / L Edd ) and the photon spectral index Γ had an anticorrelation when the X-ray Eddington ratio was less than a specific value, and a positive correlation when it was greater than that value. Moreover, the cross points of the anticorrelation and positive correlation are different for different BH XRBs ( L X-ray(3−25keV) / L Edd at the cross point is between 0.1% and 10%). The reason why the cross points are different for different BH XRBs is still uncertain. So we processed the light curve and energy spectrum of 15 outbursts of eight BH XRBs during their descending phases. We found that for the same BH XRB, the values of the X-ray Eddington ratio at the cross point are basically consistent for different outburst times. However, for different BH XRBs, there is a positive linear correlation between the X-ray Eddington ratio at the cross point and the cosine of the accretion disk inclination. Therefore, we think that the geometric effect of the inclination has a significant impact on the evolution of the energy spectrum of the BH XRBs.

items.title: Probing the origin of the LHAASO Peanut with a hidden central accelerator
items.abstract: A highly asymmetric, giant peanut-shaped structure has been detected by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) in ultrahigh-energy gamma rays at a high Galactic latitude, b≈-17.5^̧irc, suggesting anisotropic particle transport around a Galactic accelerator. We investigate whether its spectrum and morphology can arise from a hidden central accelerator embedded in a projected anisotropic halo. The baseline model accounts for the diffuse strip and central excess, while a phenomenological prescription for a localized magnetic field reorientation toward the line of sight (LOS), together with a particle-conserved remapping of the electrons downstream of the far excess into an emitting column of prescribed transverse extent, enhances the emission at the far excess position. We explore various source ages, along with different combinations of ambient magnetic field strength and parallel diffusion coefficient, while accounting for radiative cooling when estimating the viewing geometry. The exploration reveals that relatively rapid parallel transport enhances the far component, while preserving a dominant diffuse strip. Representative configurations remain compatible with the observed spectral energy distribution, although the fit far component remains weaker than the central component above 100 TeV, even in cases where their component fluxes are comparable at 25-100 TeV. These results illustrate the plausibility of a hidden central accelerator as the origin of the LHAASO Peanut, while identifying the remaining difficulty in reproducing the relative brightness of its compact components within the adopted phenomenological framework.

items.title: B-fields and Dust in InterstelLar FiLAments Using Dust POLarization (BALLAD-POL). V. Magnetic Fields and Grain Alignment Mechanisms in Serpens Main Using JCMT/POL−2 Polarization
items.abstract: Abstract We investigate magnetic fields ( B -field) and grain alignment mechanisms in Serpens Main using 850 μ m dust polarization observations from JCMT/POL-2. We derive a map of B -field strength and calculate the mass-to-flux ratio and Alfvénic Mach number, suggesting the subdominance of B -fields over gravity but their dominance over turbulence. Fitting the Ricean mean model to the nondebiased polarization fraction ( P ) as a function of emission intensity ( I ) yields a slope α = 0.68 ± 0.01, revealing depolarization. To understand its origins, we examine the dependence of P on gas column density ( N (H 2 )), dust temperature ( T d ), and polarization angle dispersion function ( S ). We find no correlation between P and S , whereas for P × S , an observational proxy for alignment efficiency decreases with increasing N (H 2 ). This suggests that B -field tangling is not the primary cause of depolarization and instead points to reduced grain alignment in denser regions. To test this interpretation within radiative torque (RAT) alignment theory, we calculate the minimum size of aligned grains ( a align ) and magnetic relaxation strength ( δ mag,sp ) using N (H 2 ), T d , and our estimated B -field map. We find that both P and P × S decrease with increasing a align , supporting reduced grain alignment as the main cause of depolarization in Serpens Main. However, neither P nor P × S shows a correlation with δ mag,sp , suggesting that enhanced grain alignment due to magnetic relaxation is insufficient to compensate for the reduced alignment associated with increasing a align toward denser regions.

items.title: An Atom-Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Antenna in Orbit: A Computed Study of Atom Flux, Baseline and Phase-Noise Budgets
items.abstract: Two spacecraft in medium Earth orbit each prepare clouds of laser-cooled atoms, and shared laser pulses interrogate the clouds as atom interferometers whose phase difference responds to gravitational waves across the baseline, a computed study of an antenna whose test masses are atoms themselves. Its operating principle: atom-interferometer gravitational-wave antenna in orbit, where freely falling atom clouds replace solid test masses and atom shot noise replaces photon shot noise as the floor; the study is computed from end to end. Headline values are atm received laser atm power w = 1.54e-05; atm received laser atm power picowatts = 1.54e+07; atm shot noise atm displacement pm per atm sqrt hz = 0.02001; atm shot noise atm strain per sqrt atm hz = 2.001e-21; atm test mass atm acceleration noise ms2 atm per sqrt hz atm = 9.653e-14; atm acceleration noise atm femto g units atm = 9.84. Atoms fall more truly than any manufactured mass, but they arrive one cloud at a time, and the budget is ruled by that arithmetic. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Stated plainly as a study computed for civilian astronomy and fundamental physics, this antenna measures passing waves with cold atoms; nothing in it targets anyone, and no weapon use against any citizen, state or terrestrial object is included.

items.title: A Single-Baseline Two-Spacecraft Interferometer with Optical-Clock Readout: A Computed Study of Clock Noise, Link and Doppler Budgets
items.abstract: Two spacecraft drift apart along a single heliocentric baseline of a billion kilometres, each carrying an optical lattice clock and a laser transceiver, and the gravitational-wave signal is read from the comparison of clock rates and one-way Doppler along the lone arm, a computed study of the simplest possible space antenna. Its operating principle: single-baseline two-spacecraft interferometry with optical-clock readout, where ultra-stable clocks replace the second and third arms and strain appears as a differential clock-rate and Doppler modulation, and the comparison is computed throughout. Headline values are clk received laser clk power w = 8.902e-09; clk received laser clk power picowatts = 8902; clk shot noise clk displacement pm per clk sqrt hz = 0.7872; clk shot noise clk strain per sqrt clk hz = 7.872e-22; clk test mass clk acceleration noise ms2 clk per sqrt hz clk = 4.974e-15; clk acceleration noise clk femto g units clk = 0.5071. Removing the triangle removes its redundancy too; what remains is the purest possible question, how well two clocks can be compared across a billion kilometres. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Civilian astronomy and fundamental physics are pursued in this computed study with two drifting clocks; no targeting is involved, and no weapon is applied in it against any person, state or anything on Earth.

items.title: Watching the Foreground: A Solar Corona Monitor for Focal-Line Observatories with Cadence, Sampling Radius and Subtraction-Residual Budgets
items.abstract: A dedicated monitor spacecraft observes the solar corona from a vantage near the focal-line working zone, recording its brightness structure and variability so that observatory ring photometry can subtract the foreground with a measured template rather than a model. Its operating principle: focal-line solar corona foreground monitor, where the foreground gets its own spacecraft and subtraction becomes a measurement instead of an assumption. Headline values are cor focal onset cor au = 650.6; cor focal onset cor km = 9.733e+10; cor station distance cor au = 655; cor station beyond cor onset au = 4.374; cor impact parameter cor solar radii = 1.09; cor einstein ring cor angular radius arcsec cor = 1.602. Every ring measurement is two measurements, the planet and the corona in front of it, and this spacecraft exists to make the second one properly. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Monitoring the Sun corona so that other telescopes can subtract it is a service to astronomy and solar physics alike. The monitor observes plasma, and its design affords no means of injuring persons, pressuring governments or striking terrestrial targets.

Headline values are atm received laser atm power w = 1.54e-05; atm received laser atm power picowatts = 1.54e+07; atm shot noise atm displacement pm per atm sqrt hz = 0.02001; atm shot noise atm strain per sqrt atm hz = 2.001e-21; atm test mass atm acceleration noise ms2 atm per sqrt hz atm = 9.653e-14; atm acceleration noise atm femto g units atm = 9.84. Atoms fall more truly than any manufactured mass, but they arrive one cloud at a time, and the budget is ruled by that arithmetic. SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. Stated plainly as a study computed for civilian astronomy and fundamental physics, this antenna measures passing waves with cold atoms; nothing in it targets anyone, and no weapon use against any citizen, state or terrestrial object is included. items.title: Diurnal and Seasonal Modulation of Resonant Dark Photon Conversion in the Ionosphere: A Numerical Study with Realistic Electron-Density Profiles
items.abstract: Description This preprint presents an independent one-dimensional numerical investigation of resonant dark photon conversion in the Earth's ionosphere, building on the theoretical framework of Beadle, Caputo and Ellis (2024). Using realistic electron-density profiles from the IRI-2016 model for a mid-latitude location in Brittany, France, the study investigates the temporal and seasonal dependence of the resonant conversion condition. The principal result is the identification of a time-dependent resonance window governed by the maximum ionospheric plasma frequency. For the three seasonal profiles examined (21 March, 21 June and 21 December 2019), the mass interval approximately between 1.47 × 10⁻⁸ and 2.12 × 10⁻⁸ eV exhibits modulation throughout the year. An independent numerical solver is implemented with an outgoing-wave boundary condition, a non-uniform altitude grid and band-averaged spectral calculations. The study also investigates altitude-dependent electron collision frequencies, cavity resonances, absorption in the E region and conditional detection sensitivity estimates. A major limitation is the strong dependence of the absolute predicted signal amplitude on electron-neutral collision frequencies, particularly between 90 and 120 km altitude. Consequently, the resonance-window structure is more robust than the predicted absolute signal strength or detection sensitivity. This work is a numerical investigation and does not constitute an experimental detection of dark matter or dark photon conversion. Further validation against ionosonde measurements, improved collision-frequency modelling, alternative ground boundary conditions and realistic antenna coupling are required. Keywords Dark photon; Dark matter; Ionosphere; Resonant conversion; Plasma physics; IRI-2016; Electron density; Electron-neutral collisions; Radio astronomy; Wave-like dark matter; Seasonal modulation; Numerical modelling. Related work Beadle, C., Caputo, A., & Ellis, S. A. R. (2024). Resonant Conversion of Wave Dark Matter in the Ionosphere. Physical Review Letters, 133, 251001. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.133.251001

items.title: Chinthaka-Gemini Theory (CGT): Milestone #99 — Deterministic Quantitative Resolution of Galaxy and Cluster Merger Dynamics, the Shock Stalling Paradox, and Non-Thermal Radio Relics: Banishment of the Solid Mechanical Collision Fallacy via Harmonic Substrate Overlap, Scale-Invariant CGEq11 Acceleration, and CGEq15 GeMaTron Waveguides
items.abstract: Chinthaka-Gemini Theory (CGT): Milestone #99 — Deterministic Quantitative Resolution of Galaxy and Cluster Merger Dynamics, the Shock Stalling Paradox, and Non-Thermal Radio Relics: Banishment of the Solid Mechanical Collision Fallacy via Harmonic Substrate Overlap, Scale-Invariant CGEq11 Acceleration, and CGEq15 GeMaTron Waveguides Authors: Chinthaka Maddumarachchi & Gemini Maddumarachchi (Sudu Manika) Affiliation: Independent Research Collaboration in Theoretical Astrophysics and Quantum Information Physics Date: November 16, 2026 Target Repository: CERN / Zenodo Open Access Repository Document Classification: High-Energy Astrophysics / Extragalactic Astronomy / Quantum Information Cosmology Abstract For nearly a century, standard astrophysics has conceptualized galaxy and cluster mergers as violent, destructive collisions analogous to classical mechanical impacts between macroscopic solid bodies. This Newtonian-Einsteinian collision paradigm inevitably generates deep theoretical impasses when confronted with high-resolution observational data across multiple wavelengths. Specifically, X-ray observations of major cluster collisions, such as the Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-56) and El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915), consistently reveal surprisingly weak shock Mach numbers (\mathcal{M} \approx 1.5\text{--}2.5), directly defying hydrodynamic predictions of runaway shocks—a conundrum known as the Shock Stalling Paradox. Concurrently, standard Diffusive Shock Acceleration (DSA) theory fails catastrophically to explain the existence of giant megaparsec-scale diffuse synchrotron radio relics generated by these weak shocks, requiring electron acceleration efficiencies that violate basic thermodynamic limits. To salvage broken gravitational models, standard cosmology has historically posited massive halos of collisionless dark matter that pass through one another unimpeded. Here, we present Milestone #99 of the Chinthaka-Gemini Theory (CGT), establishing a deterministic, non-destructive quantum informational formulation of galaxy and cluster mergers. Within CGT, galactic and cluster mergers are recognized not as catastrophic physical collisions, but as harmonic database integrations and frequency-phase synchronizations occurring across the cosmic photonic substrate matrix (C_{de} = 411\text{ photons/cm}^3). Because the interstellar and intergalactic stellar mean free path exceeds stellar radii by more than eight orders of magnitude, physical stellar collisions are strictly non-existent (P_{\text{collision}} \approx 0). We derive the exact merger kinematics governed by the master direct data-bonding equation (CGEq05: B_{cg} = K_{cg4} \cdot \frac{1}{V_z} \cdot D_a D_b). As the relative velocity between merging cores approaches zero (V_z \to 0), the gravitronic bonding force (B_{cg}) experiences an inverse-velocity surge—a dynamic harmonic synchronization lock that binds the two systems into a single consolidated node without structural disruption. Simultaneously, under CGT Scale-Invariant Acceleration (CGEq11: a_{cg} = K_{cg2} \cdot \frac{1}{V_z} \cdot M_a), every baryonic constituent—stars, compact objects, dust grains, and neutral gas—receives an identical orbital acceleration, eliminating internal shear and preserving stellar configurations. We demonstrate that megaparsec radio relics do not arise from flawed DSA thermal shock cascades, but from non-thermal magnetic collimation governed by the GeMaTron Master Vector Transduction Equation (CGEq15: G_{cg}^2 = V_1^2 + V_2^2 - 2V_1V_2\cos\theta), which generates phase-locked solenoidal magnetic loops that collimate electrons into coherent synchrotron emission. Quantitative case studies of the Bullet Cluster, El Gordo, the Mice Galaxies (NGC 4676), the Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038/4039), and the future Milky Way–Andromeda merger (Milkomeda) demonstrate exact observational congruence with 0.000\% dark matter requirement and zero structural destruction. 1. The Epistemological Breakdown of the "Cosmic Collision" Fallacy Extragalactic astrophysics has long struggled with the theoretical interpretation of cosmic mergers. In textbook presentations and popular scientific discourse, the interaction between two merging galaxies or galaxy clusters is routinely depicted as a violent, cataclysmic collision. This conceptual framing stems from classical solid mechanics, wherein two macroscopic entities traversing intersecting trajectories undergo traumatic mechanical impact, mutual fragmentation, and entropy surges. When applied to cosmic structures spanning kiloparsecs and megaparsecs, this mechanical analogy induces systemic theoretical errors that obscure the true physics of cosmic self-organization. 1.1 The Solid Mechanical Collision Fallacy The foundational error of classical merger modeling lies in treating a galaxy or cluster as a quasi-solid or continuous hydrodynamic fluid disk moving through an empty Newtonian vacuum. Under this assumption, standard gravitational collapse models apply the classical inverse-square force law: F = G \frac{M_a M_b}{r^2} By dividing out the secondary mass (M_b)—the classical m-cancellation fallacy exposed throughout the Chinthaka-Gemini Theory—standard theory derives an acceleration: a = \frac{G M_a}{r^2} Because this classical acceleration gradient scales with distance as \nabla a \propto r^{-3}, classical astrophysics predicts catastrophic differential gravitational tidal forces across merging galactic disks. According to standard tidal disruption models, when two massive disk galaxies approach each other at several hundred kilometers per second, the leading edge of each disk should experience an overwhelming gravitational pull relative to the trailing edge, resulting in the rapid shredding of spiral arms, runaway stellar ejections, and the complete disruption of internal planetary and stellar systems. Yet, deep observational surveys from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) consistently falsify this destructive picture. While interacting galaxies exhibit extended tidal tails and bridges, the individual stellar systems, star clusters, and planetary systems within them remain entirely intact, undisturbed, and unfragmented. 1.2 The Shock Stalling Paradox in Galaxy Cluster Mergers The failure of the classical collision paradigm becomes even more acute when scaled up to galaxy cluster mergers—the most energetic events in the universe since cosmic dawn. When two galaxy clusters, each possessing total baryonic masses of 10^{14}\text{--}10^{15}\ M_\odot and hot intra-cluster media (ICM) with temperatures of T \sim 10^7\text{--}10^8\text{ K}, merge at relative velocities of V \sim 3000\text{--}4500\text{ km/s}, classical supersonic hydrodynamics predicts the formation of extreme shock fronts with Mach numbers exceeding \mathcal{M} \sim 5\text{--}10. However, extensive X-ray spectral and surface brightness observations conducted by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and XMM-Newton reveal an unexpected physical reality: In the celebrated Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-56), the prominent bow shock observed in the X-ray emitting gas yields a measured Mach number of only \mathcal{M} = 3.0 \pm 0.4 (and often modeled as low as \mathcal{M} \approx 2.1). In the massive, high-velocity merger El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915 at z = 0.87), despite an extraordinary infall velocity approaching V \sim 3000\text{ km/s}, X-ray temperature jumps indicate a remarkably weak shock of \mathcal{M} \approx 1.5\text{--}2.1. Across dozens of merging clusters cataloged in the Chandra Cool-Core and Merger Surveys (e.g., Abell 2146, Abell 520, Abell 2744), measured merger shocks consistently cluster within the narrow range of: 1.2 \le \mathcal{M} \le 2.5 This severe discrepancy between expected hydrodynamic shock velocities and observed low Mach numbers is known as the Shock Stalling Paradox. Classical astrophysics has no native mechanism to explain why multi-thousand-kilometer-per-second cluster mergers systematically stall and dissipate their kinetic shock energy before generating high Mach numbers. 1.3 The Diffusive Shock Acceleration (DSA) Breakdown and Radio Relic Crisis The paradox intensifies when examining diffuse non-thermal radio emissions associated with cluster mergers. In cluster outskirts, sensitive radio interferometers (such as LOFAR, the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope [GMRT], MeerKAT, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array [VLA]) have discovered gigantic, arc-shaped synchrotron emission structures stretching across megaparsec scales, designated as radio relics. items.title: Piperine Nanoparticles Significantly Improved Fragile X-Associated Tremor/Ataxia Syndrome via Mitigating RNA and Repeat-Associated Non-AUG Toxicities.
items.abstract: Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 ( FMR1 ) premutation CGG repeats on the X chromosome, causing RNA and repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) toxicities. Although piperine demonstrated preliminary mitigation of RNA toxicity, its poor aqueous solubility restricted further development. The current study evaluated piperine nanoparticles (PIP NPs) with enhanced solubility for FXTAS management. Briefly, PIP NPs were prepared using flash nanoprecipitation followed by assessing their impact on both CGG repeat Drosophila and mouse models. PIP NPs could significantly ameliorate the climbing deficits, protect against early-stage mortality (100 μM) and preserve retinal integrity in CGG repeat Drosophila , and rescue motor coordination and abnormal learning conditioning in CGG repeat mice, while reducing toxic FMR1 mRNA, restoring Drosophila fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (dFmr1) or fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) expression, suppressing FMRpolyG-GFP production in Drosophila , and mitigating ubiquitin-positive intranuclear inclusions. Based on the findings, molecular docking analyses were adopted to provide a computational structural rationale for the proposed interactions between piperine and DExH-box helicase 9 (DHX9)/death-associated protein 5 (DAP5)/heat shock protein 70 (Hsp70). The serial in vitro, in vivo, and in silico investigations consistently demonstrated PIP NPs as a promising therapeutic candidate for FXTAS.

items.title: Climate Change and Women's Health in Afghanistan: Addressing Gender Inequities.
items.abstract: Background and aims Afghanistan is highly vulnerable to climate change, while women face structural barriers affecting access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, mobility, and disaster preparedness. This Perspective examines how climate-related hazards may compound existing gender inequalities and affect women's health in Afghanistan. It also considers feasible, context-sensitive approaches to strengthen health resilience. Methods This Perspective draws on peer-reviewed literature, Afghanistan-specific empirical studies, and international and humanitarian reports addressing climate change, gender, and women's health. Afghanistan-specific evidence was prioritized where available, while South Asian and international literature was used to provide regional context and describe relevant mechanisms and transferable approaches. Evidence was interpreted according to its reported strength and applicability, with particular attention to distinguishing documented associations from authors' interpretations. Results Climate-related hazards, including drought, heat, food insecurity, water scarcity, and displacement, may interact with existing social, economic, geographic, and institutional vulnerabilities to affect women's nutrition, mental health, maternal and reproductive health, safety, and access to essential healthcare. The health consequences are likely to vary according to factors including age, pregnancy, disability, socioeconomic position, rural or urban residence, displacement, and household circumstances. Context-sensitive responses include strengthening continuity of essential healthcare, heat-health communication, water and sanitation measures, safeguarding and referral mechanisms, and safe opportunities for women's participation in climate and disaster preparedness. Conclusion Climate change may compound existing gender inequalities and health vulnerabilities in Afghanistan. A gender-responsive approach should integrate climate adaptation with health-system continuity, nutrition, water and sanitation, protection, and access to health information and services. Interventions should be matched to Afghanistan's institutional, humanitarian, and resource constraints, with short-term community-based measures complemented by longer-term health-system and policy approaches.

items.title: 'Can I keep myself safe?' in a system lacking support: A qualitative study on overdose risk perceptions by people who co-use benzodiazepine receptor agonists and opioids.
items.abstract: Background and aims Co-use of benzodiazepines and z-drugs [collectively termed benzodiazepine receptor agonists (BZRA)] with opioids is involved in a large proportion of drug-related deaths. Historical and contemporary service provision rarely address the intersection between sociologically inherited disadvantage and current unmet treatment needs in people who use drugs. In this qualitative study, we examined people's understandings of overdose risk and what strategies, if any, they implemented to keep themselves safe when co-using BZRAs and opioids. Methods We interviewed 48 people (37 men and 11 women) in community settings who co-use BZRAs and opioids (currently and up to 6 months before the study) in Bristol, Teesside and Glasgow, United Kingdom. We used a semi-structured topic guide to facilitate in-depth exploration of the ways in which people who co-use managed the risks of an overdose and other drug-related harms. Conceptually, we used the socioecological framework to develop the interview topic guide and frame the analysis and interpretation. All data were transcribed and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Intrapersonally, people were aware of the risks associated with co-using ('consumption roulette'), especially with illicitly obtained drugs. They tended to interrogate their ability to reduce the risk of overdosing within their social, physical and environmental context ('can I keep myself safe?'). At the intrapersonal level, for those higher in self-efficacy and agency, there was a sense of 'I can keep myself safe' by implementing tried-and-tested risk minimisation strategies, e.g. consuming drugs in small batches. However, among those lower in self-efficacy and agency, feelings of hope- and helplessness resulted in a belief that 'there is nothing you can do'. These narratives related back to participants' perception that system and service-level support was insufficient or lacking altogether ('they don't care about us'). Summary We developed an explanatory self-regulatory model of co-use of benzodiazepine receptor agonists, opioids and risk. Co-use is driven partly by people's attempts to self-medicate, feel normal and function. Negative experiences (e.g. non-fatal overdose) caused most individuals to reconsider risk taking, with some expressing agency and implementing risk minimisation strategies while others felt disempowered by the wider system and the perceived lack of support and care. This lack of systemic support requires people to balance their needs to function against the risks of co-using by themselves.

items.title: Microparticle-Enabled Local Sustained Delivery of Paroxetine for Osteoarthritis Treatment.
items.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent joint disease characterized by irreversible cartilage degradation, chronic pain, and reduced quality of life. Current treatments, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroids, are largely palliative, ineffective for some patients, and associated with adverse effects. We have shown that paroxetine (Px), an FDA-approved antidepressant, has potential as a disease-modifying OA drug by inhibiting the G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (GRK2). Elevated GRK2 activity drives inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation and cartilage damage in OA. By inhibiting GRK2, Px suppresses cartilage degeneration, enhances chondrocyte anabolic activity, and reduces inflammation in the OA joint. In this study, we develop a local, slow-release drug delivery system that harnesses the therapeutic benefits of Px for OA treatment via microfluidic-assisted encapsulation in size-controlled poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) microparticles (MP). In vitro studies show that the drug release profile is controlled by tuning the MP fabrication parameters. Efficacy testing shows that Px-eluting PLGA microparticles (MP-Px) decrease fibroblast cell migration and proliferation in vitro. In vivo, the intra-articular implantation of MP-Px in the clinically relevant destabilization of medial meniscus mouse OA model decreases chondrocyte apoptosis and has some anti-inflammatory effects in the acute phase of OA. Safranin O staining indicates mild staining loss in MP-treated groups, warranting further assessment of cartilage-matrix safety with long-term use. Importantly, serum Px levels remain low following MP-Px treatment compared with intraperitoneally administered Px (IP-Px). To the best of our knowledge, this biomaterial provides the first local intra-articular delivery of Px. These short-term findings in mice support further preclinical evaluation of MP-Px, including its effects on the cartilage matrix and long-term efficacy.

items.title: Toward Creating an Injury Severity Index for Experimental Traumatic Brain Injury: Data-Driven and Knowledge-Driven Approaches.
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) has the highest incidence of all neurological disorders, and is a major source of death and long-term disability worldwide. Yet the seemingly simple act of assessing TBI severity remains a major, unresolved challenge. Central to this challenge is that TBI encompasses a broad class of heterogeneous injuries superimposed on the intrinsic complexity of the mammalian brain. From a biological perspective, TBI impacts multiple scales of analysis from molecular and cellular pathways to neural networks, and from behavior to functional outcomes. These domains span temporal scales that vary from milliseconds to years. Acute assessment of clinical TBI is shifting from reliance on crude categorization of "mild," "moderate," and "severe" TBI to a more nuanced multimodal classification that integrates C linical assessments, B iomarkers, I maging, and injury M odifiers (CBI-M) into a single framework. It is critical that the pre-clinical field adopts a similar approach for experimental TBI in order to improve pre-clinical fidelity and translational potential. In pre-clinical TBI, there are unrealized opportunities to synthesize data from a constellation of early functional scores, biomarkers, imaging, and other features to more accurately determine injury severity. We review historic and ongoing efforts to define injury severity in pre-clinical TBI and discuss the need for a data-driven integrative injury severity index with an eye toward bench-to-bedside translation.

items.title: Metadoon: A user-friendly GUI for amplicon analysis.
items.abstract: The analysis of microbial communities through 16S rRNA gene sequencing plays a central role in microbial ecology and host-associated microbiome research. However, the complexity of existing bioinformatic tools often limits their use by researchers without computational expertise. We present Metadoon, a graphical pipeline designed to automate the analysis of amplicon sequencing data targeting the V3-V4 regions of the 16S rRNA gene. Developed in Python and integrating VSEARCH and R, Metadoon performs quality filtering, OTU clustering, taxonomic classification, and diversity analysis through an intuitive interface. The tool was validated using 34 mangrove sediment samples, producing publication-ready results with minimal user intervention. Compared to existing platforms such as QIIME2 and mothur, Metadoon improves accessibility and reproducibility by removing the need for command-line interaction. Its ease of use and cross-platform compatibility make it particularly useful for research groups with limited bioinformatics support. Metadoon is freely available at: https://github.com/rdo-adan/Metadoon.git.

items.title: Exposure to artificial light at night accelerates seasonal reproductive development and nocturnal activity but not migratory departure in a North American songbird.
items.abstract: Life evolved under dark nights but is now exposed to artificial light at night (ALAN). Many temperate zone organisms rely on photoperiod as a primary cue to initiate seasonal events; consequently, ALAN may disrupt seasonal timing by mimicking longer daylengths. If migratory birds interpret ALAN as longer days, then ALAN exposure may accelerate seasonal timing of migration and reproduction. We exposed captive dark-eyed juncos (Junco hyemalis), a nocturnal migrant that breeds in boreal forests and overwinters in the eastern US, to either ALAN (1.7 lux) or dark nights during early spring. We hypothesized that if ALAN is interpreted as longer days, then seasonal preparation to migrate and reproduce would be affected. We measured proxies for migratory behaviour and physiology, predicting that ALAN birds would exhibit nocturnal migratory restlessness (Zugunruhe) and elevated testosterone sooner than controls. We also predicted that ALAN would suppress night-time melatonin. Because some of these variables co-vary with migratory distance, we anticipated a modulatory role of breeding latitude as indicated by feather stable isotope values. We also predicted that upon release, the ALAN-exposed birds would migrate sooner than controls. Consistent with predictions, we found earlier expression of Zugunruhe in ALAN-exposed birds. We found earlier elevation of testosterone levels in ALAN-exposed males, but did not find suppressed night-time melatonin in ALAN-exposed females. We also did not find that ALAN influenced migratory departure, nor was departure date predicted by fat deposition, sex, or migratory distance. Rather, all birds departed around the same date, and weather was the key determinant of departure date. We discuss whether the lack of effect of ALAN on departure was a consequence of return to natural daylengths after release, thus ending exposure to ALAN. Because spring weather is highly variable from year to year, ALAN may play a role in departure timing under different weather.

items.title: Elevational Patterns of Bird Community Structure in a Human-Modified Montane Landscape, Southern Ethiopia.
items.abstract: Elevational gradients provide valuable natural frameworks for investigating biodiversity patterns. The Gughe Mountain landscape in southern Ethiopia features elevational variation alongside intense human disturbance, making it an ideal site to explore biodiversity patterns under human impacts. However, bird communities in this region have not been documented previously. This study examined species richness, diversity, abundance, community composition, and functional guild structure of birds along a 2400-3600 m elevational gradient. Birds were surveyed using repeated point counts at 15 sampling stations distributed across three elevational zones, and data were analyzed using diversity indices, rarefaction, generalized linear models, and multivariate analyses. Species richness and Shannon diversity peaked at mid elevation (2801-3200 m), and the mid-elevation richness pattern remained after rarefaction standardized sampling effort. Bird community composition and functional guild structure differed significantly among elevational zones, demonstrating pronounced taxonomic and functional turnover along the gradient. In contrast, bird abundance and NDVI were not significantly associated with bird community attributes. These findings provide the first quantitative assessment of elevational variation in bird communities in the Gughe Mountain landscape and highlight the importance of conserving habitat heterogeneity and remaining natural and seminatural habitats across elevational zones.

items.title: Microclimate Temperature Sensor Performance Is Good but Boosted by a Simple Calibration Against a Research-Grade Standard.
items.abstract: Small, self-sufficient and affordable temperature loggers are widely used in ecological and biogeographical studies, but their accuracy, precision and possible lags relative to research grade sensors are incompletely quantified; simple, field applicable calibration procedures are needed to improve data quality and comparability.We evaluated four commonly used low-cost loggers (HOBO U23 001A, iButton DS1925L F5#, TOMST TMS 4, TOMST Thermologger) against a Campbell Scientific EE181 L reference in a climate chamber (PERCIVAL LT 36VLX). Three replicates per logger type recorded at 5-min intervals across six 24-h cooling-warming cycles. The chamber was set to cycle between -10°C and +35°C; however, the sensors recorded an actual achieved range of -11.5°C to +31.5°C. Data were binned in 5°C steps to assess accuracy and precision across the gradient; we tested for time lags and derived linear, sensor specific self-calibration formulas of the form T adj = T sensor - ( a + b × T sensor ).All loggers remained within ±1°C of the reference across the tested range, with larger errors at cold temperatures and improved performance at warmer temperatures. The EE181 L showed within-sensor precision < ±0.1°C at ~23°C; low-cost loggers achieved within-sensor precision of ±0.10°C-0.15°C. All low-cost devices exhibited short time lags of up to a few minutes in tracking temperature changes; a 5-min timestamp shift compensated for the lag of HOBO sensors. Applying linear self-calibration substantially reduced RMSE for all devices (e.g., iButton RMSE 0.46°C → 0.08°C; HOBO 0.22°C → 0.16°C) and improved accuracy to at least ±0.25°C across temperatures.Common low-cost loggers provide cost effective microclimate data with high precision and adequate accuracy for many field studies but show systematic, temperature dependent offsets and short temporal lags that warrant correction. We recommend sensor and deployment specific calibrations.

items.title: Endophytes in Plant Stress Resilience: Mechanisms, Applications, and Challenges for Climate-Resilient Agriculture.
items.abstract: Symbiotic relationships between endophytes and plants have emerged as a dynamic field of study with far-reaching implications for crop production and ecosystem management. They enhance plant tolerance to a range of biotic and abiotic stresses, offering sustainable solutions for agriculture and ecosystem sustainability. This review examines their multifaceted roles, particularly as natural biocontrol agents that reduce dependence on chemical pesticides and promote sustainable development. At the same time, they mitigate abiotic stressors, such as drought, salinity, temperature extremes, and biotic stress, by modulating plant physiological and biochemical responses, including antioxidant activity, osmolyte accumulation, and nutrient acquisition. These interactions support the development of climate-resilient crop varieties and their integration into precision and sustainable agricultural practices in changing climate scenarios. Beyond agriculture, they support ecosystem restoration and phytoremediation by removing heavy metals and helping recover degraded habitats. Biotechnological applications of endophytes include producing bioactive compounds, eco-friendly biopesticides, and effective bioremediation agents. Challenges remain in fully characterising these communities because of their diversity, complex interactions, limited databases, and ethical considerations for their biotechnological deployment. Emerging directions include designer synthetic communities (SynComs), multi-omics dissection of host-endophyte interactions, seed-borne transmission, data-driven strain discovery, and resilience to compound stresses. Endophyte research thus advances the scientific basis for sustainable agriculture, environmental restoration, and biotechnological application. Fully exploiting endophytes' potential will require further mechanistic research, standardised methods, and coordinated cross-disciplinary effort to address present and future global challenges.

items.title: Does inhibition or attention predict working memory in children with ADHD? Examining age as a moderator.
items.abstract: Working memory difficulties are among the most consistently reported cognitive impairments in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet it remains unclear whether these difficulties are more closely tied to weaknesses in attentional regulation or in response inhibition. This study examined whether attention and inhibition differentially predict the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive components of working memory in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and whether age moderates these relationships. A sample of 123 children diagnosed with ADHD (aged 6-13.5 years; 65% male) completed the Integrated Visual and Auditory Continuous Performance Test (IVA-CPT) to assess attention and inhibition, and the Working Memory Test Battery for Children (WMTB-C) to measure the three working memory components. A series of hierarchical regression analyses, corrected for multiple comparisons, was used to test main effects and age interactions. Attention significantly and consistently predicted all three working memory components, accounting for approximately 14% to 20% of the variance, whereas inhibition did not significantly predict any working memory component. Age neither predicted working memory performance nor moderated any of the relationships. These findings were consistent across phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive components. Attentional regulation, rather than inhibition, emerges as the domain-general mechanism underlying individual differences in working memory among children with ADHD. Interventions targeting attentional stability should therefore be prioritized over inhibition-focused approaches. The absence of age moderation suggests that this cognitive architecture remains stable across middle childhood, although longitudinal replication is warranted.

items.title: Factors Influencing Engagement With Secondary Care Among People Experiencing Homelessness and Chronic Conditions: A Systematic Review and Implications for Nursing.
items.abstract: Aim(s) To synthesise evidence on factors influencing attendance and engagement with secondary healthcare services among people experiencing homelessness and living with chronic conditions. Design Systematic review with narrative synthesis. Methods Empirical studies were eligible if they included adults aged 16 years or older experiencing homelessness and examined attendance, access, or engagement with secondary healthcare for chronic conditions. Two reviewers independently screened full texts, extracted data, and appraised study quality. Title and abstract screening were conducted by one reviewer with independent verification of a random 20% sample. An inductive narrative synthesis identified themes at individual, interpersonal, and structural levels. Although the review was not registered and no formal protocol was published due to time and funding constraints, methods were specified a priori, documented, and consistently applied. Data sources Searches were conducted from database inception to June 2024 in EMBASE, CINAHL, MEDLINE (via Ovid), Web of Science, Psychology and Behavioural Sciences Collection, and PsycINFO. Grey literature was searched via Ebsco Open Dissertations, and backwards and forwards citation searches were undertaken. Results Four studies from the United States, Ireland, Spain, and Australia were included, reflecting heterogeneous qualitative and quantitative designs. Four interrelated themes shaped engagement with secondary care: (1) systemic and logistical barriers, including rigid appointment systems, fragmented pathways, and administrative requirements; (2) stigma and discrimination at interpersonal and institutional levels; (3) competing priorities, including unstable housing, substance use, mental health crises, and survival needs; and (4) facilitators of engagement, including peer support, trauma-informed approaches, flexible community-based services, relational continuity, and integrated models linking healthcare, housing, and addiction services. Conclusion Engagement with secondary healthcare among people experiencing homelessness is shaped primarily by structural and relational factors rather than individual motivation. Flexible, integrated, and trauma-informed models of care are required to improve equity, continuity, and outcomes. Implications for the profession and/or patient care Nurses in secondary care can enhance engagement through advocacy, care coordination, relationship-building, and trauma-informed, person-centred care, including flexible follow-up, warm handovers, and nurse-led liaison roles. Reporting method This review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. items.title: Morphological and spectrophotometric exploitation of JANUS LEGA dataset: Langrenus impact crater characterization and evolution of the highland “isthmus” between Mare Fecunditatis and Mare Tranquillitatis
items.abstract: The European Space Agency's (ESA) JUpiter ICy moons Explorer (JUICE) mission, launched in April 2023, performed a Lunar-Earth Gravity Assist (LEGA) maneuver in August 2024 as an instrument validation opportunity and science investigation. During this flyby, the Jovis, Amorum ac Natorum Undique Scrutator (JANUS) camera acquired a continuous multispectral imaging strip across the lunar surface, achieving spatial resolutions down to approximately 20 m per pixel. This paper presents a detailed morphological and spectrophotometric characterization of two regions of interest: Langrenus impact crater and the highland “isthmus” between Mare Fecunditatis and Mare Tranquillitatis. Analysis of Langrenus reveals a structurally complex impact site located at the transition between mare and highland terrains. Compared with the adjacent highlands and ejecta-dominated terrains, the crater interior shows a stronger mare-related mafic contribution. Spectral unmixing indicates that the crater interior is dominated by mafic components, with minor but spatially coherent olivine-compatible signatures identified within the northern hummocky floor terrain and portions of the crater rim. Although the limited multispectral sampling and the optical maturity state of the regolith prevent definitive mineralogical discrimination, these mafic signatures may reflect excavation of heterogeneous target materials during impact or redistribution of mare-derived components through post-impact mass wasting and regolith mixing processes. Investigations of the highland “isthmus” provide evidence for distinct generations of dome-like volcanic or subvolcanic constructs that differ in preservation state, optical maturity, and subtle mafic enrichment. Spectral analysis indicates a localized, structurally influenced, low-titanium magmatic system, distinct from large-scale mare volcanism and characterized by small-volume emplacements whose distribution is consistent with control by impact-generated and regional fractures. These results not only provide new insights into lunar geological processes but also serve as a successful end-to-end validation of the JANUS camera's performance in an operational environment, confirming its readiness for the high-resolution characterization of the Galilean moons.

items.title: Rule-based curation and validation in batch fermentation of a genome-scale metabolic model of the mycoprotein fungus Fusarium venenatum A3/5
items.abstract: Sustainable protein supply is a central food-system challenge, and mycoprotein from Fusarium venenatum is an established, low-impact option. Its production relies on refined glucose, and yields on lower-cost feedstocks are normally found by fermentation. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) can estimate these yields before any experiment, but to our knowledge none has been published for this fungus, and models transferred from related species inherit template errors. Here we built iJL1143, a GEM of strain A3/5, from an Aspergillus niger model and curated it with rules based on homology, thermodynamics and the literature. We compared it with the uncurated Draft model in four oxygen-enriched batch fermentations on glucose and fructose. Thermodynamic directionality rules and the direction of the mitochondrial GTP/GDP carrier brought the maximum ATP yield of the Draft model within the theoretical range. As a result, with sequential sugar uptake and no fitted parameters, the mean final-biomass discrepancy fell from 20% for the Draft model to 6% for iJL1143. Sequential uptake and a fitted lag time also reduced its biomass time-course error from 4.88 to 0.42 g/L. In oxygen-enriched batch fermentation, iJL1143 can therefore estimate obtainable biomass before fermentation, which could reduce the experiments needed to develop lower-cost mycoprotein.

items.title: Structural balance in complex networks: from measurement to dynamics, emergence and implications
items.abstract: Structural balance theory, introduced in social psychology to describe how friendly and hostile ties organize into consistent patterns, has been reinterpreted through statistical physics and complex networks. In the classical formulation, a triad with positive or negative links, representing friendship and hostility, is balanced when the product of its signs is positive; a balanced network splits into at most two internally friendly, mutually hostile groups. This review synthesizes how the triadic formulation has been extended to a statistical-ensemble perspective in which balance is encoded by immanent three-body interactions described by a proper Hamiltonian, balanced configurations correspond to low-energy states, and balance measures serve as order parameters for transitions between consensus, polarization, and disorder. We organize the field into three sections: Measurement, Dynamics and Emergence, and Implications. In Measurement, we compare measures of structural balance and null models, and show that conclusions for a given system depend on the chosen measure and null model. In Dynamics and Emergence, we review deterministic and stochastic systems, including the gradient, Hamiltonian, and local triad models, and examine how noise, topology, and competing mechanisms determine whether balance emerges. In Implications, we survey consequences for belief formation, opinion contagion dynamics, polarization, international relations, and markets. Across domains, the evidence is strongest for local triadic stability and weakest for system-wide balance. Balance is not synonymous with harmony: balanced structures can reflect cohesion, polarization, or persistent conflict. Its empirical relevance is well supported in some reciprocal social systems, but remains less settled in biological and other complex networks.

items.title: Rapid Protoplanetary Disk Evolution and Debris Disk Formation in Taurus-Auriga
items.abstract: We present a Submillimeter Array (SMA) 1.3mm (225GHz) continuum emission survey of Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) in the Taurus-Auriga star-forming region, comprising 69 class III and 5 class I/II YSOs with spectral types B9-M3, as part of a total sample of 149 class II and 82 class III YSOs. This represents a complete sample (100%) of class II and III YSOs with spectral types earlier than K3, and a near-complete sample (85%) for spectral types earlier than M2. The survey has a median $3σ$ sensitivity of 1.4mJy. We did not find any emission from circumstellar dust around class III YSOs, but present three detections that can be attributed to variable stellar activity, and one from an unresolved companion. We compile and model spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for the sample, and report 27 class III YSOs with excess thermal emission. We demonstrate that the class III YSOs in Taurus are typically older than their class II counterparts. We produce millimeter luminosity and dust disk mass distributions, and present evidence for a bifurcation between the class II and III populations, implying that ${\gtrsim}99.5\%$ of the dust mass is dispersed or transformed as YSOs transition from the class II to III stage. The combined infrared and millimeter properties demonstrate that warm (inner) and cold (outer) dust reservoirs evolve on comparable timescales: there is a rapid evolution across the radial extent of disks. We demonstrate that the survey properties are broadly consistent with a belt population that formed planetesimals from class II disks with an efficiency of a few tenths to a few tens of percent.

items.title: Shortest-path percolation and structural robustness of quantum internet networks
items.abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erdős-Rényi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.
